Denoising diffusion and latent diffusion models for physics field simulations
abstract: Accurate prediction of physical fields is critical in various engineering applications, including thermal management in electronic systems, airfoil shape optimization in aerospace, and flow field control in hypersonic vehicles. This study employs the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) for predicting the temperature field caused by the thermal diffusion, and the flow fields spanning from incompressible to hypersonic regimes. A conditional DDPM framework is first validated with a steady-state thermal diffusion problem by predicting the temperature distribution around a plate with holes. Strong agreement with ground truth data is shown with an average error of approximately 0.013 for plates with a central circular hole. The model also delivers high accuracy in critical regions, such as near the inner circular or square holes. Its performance is further evaluated on incompressible flow around an airfoil and hypersonic flow over a compression ramp, confirming robust predictive capability across diverse flow conditions. Additionally, a latent-space implementation of DDPM is introduced, which employs an Autoencoder (AE) for dimensionality reduction and reconstruction of the physical data. The resulting Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) maintains reconstruction quality comparable to the standard DDPM while substantially reducing the computational cost of the diffusion training process. When applied to hypersonic flow over a compression ramp in the original parameter space, LDM predictions align well with ground truth, achieving a deviation of only 4.28% in separation length estimation. This work confirms the high predictive accuracy of the DDPM framework and highlights the efficiency gains from performing diffusion in a learned latent space. The findings establish an efficient framework for high fidelity generative modeling of complex thermal/flow fields.

abstract: • Aerodynamic performance is assessed along deformation paths, not endpoint geometries. • L/D increases monotonically along the deformation path toward the endpoint optimum. • A saturation region emerges beyond λ ≈ 0.8; incremental gains fall below 1%. • Morphing limit λ* ≈ 0.96 requires near-full deformation to recover 90% of L/D gain. • Endpoint optimality alone is insufficient to assess morphing suitability. Morphing-airfoil studies often assess aerodynamic optimality at isolated target geometries, implicitly assuming that optimized shapes remain continuously reachable from baseline airfoils. This practice can obscure the distinction between endpoint-optimal airfoils and configurations that remain aerodynamically suitable throughout the deformation process. The present work evaluates aerodynamic performance explicitly along continuous deformation from baseline airfoils to endpoint-optimal configurations. Multiple baselines, geometric parameterizations, deformation paths, local perturbations, and Reynolds numbers are considered to examine the robustness of the resulting aerodynamic behavior. Aerodynamic trends are first evaluated using XFOIL and subsequently examined using Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations. Deformation-based indicators are further introduced to provide a first-order engineering interpretation of the aerodynamic benefit achieved along the prescribed morphing path. Across all cases considered, aerodynamic efficiency increases during deformation, reaching up to 38% improvement at the endpoint-optimal configuration, approaches a saturation region beyond λ ≈ 0.8 where incremental gains fall below 1%, and degrades by approximately 7% under further deformation beyond the optimum. While these trends are consistent with classical lift–drag trade-offs, the results show that endpoint optimality alone does not ensure suitability as a morphing target. Aerodynamic behavior under continuous deformation, characterized by the normalized aerodynamic gain A(λ), the deformation metric D̄(λ), and the practical morphing limit λ*, should therefore be evaluated alongside endpoint optimality as an additional criterion when identifying viable morphing-airfoil configurations. Concretely, a candidate configuration should be accepted as a morphing target only if λ* falls within the achievable actuation range and A(λ) does not degrade significantly before that level is reached.

A design-oriented IBM–WMLES framework for rapid parametric mapping of turbine-cascade wake aerothermodynamics
abstract: A novel design-oriented computational framework based on wall-modeled large-eddy simulation (WMLES) coupled with a sharp-interface immersed boundary method (IBM) is proposed to enable rapid parametric mapping of unsteady aerothermal behavior in gas-turbine components. Rather than using scale-resolved simulations solely for detailed flow analysis, the present approach targets engineering outputs—compact, interpretable wake descriptors and surrogate response surfaces that can be queried within preliminary design and trade-study loops. The methodology is demonstrated on the LS89 transonic turbine cascade by varying two practically relevant drivers: inflow turbulence intensity and wall thermal condition. A GPU-optimized solver is used to generate a database of 64 WMLES cases at a per-case wall-clock turnaround that becomes compatible with systematic parametric campaigns—a regime previously accessible only to Reynolds-averaged-based workflows. The resulting scale-resolved fields are condensed into a hierarchy of spatial and temporal metrics representative of wake mean state and unsteady content, and these metrics are approximated through Chebyshev surrogate models defined over the parameter domain. The analysis indicates that wall thermal conditions predominantly control the mean thermodynamic wake state, whereas increasing inflow turbulence intensity redistributes unsteady pressure energy from high to intermediate Strouhal ranges and reduces spectral coherence. Overall, the proposed workflow provides a practical route from high-fidelity unsteady simulations to design-ready maps and response surfaces, bridging the gap between WMLES-level physics and parametric decision-making in gas-turbine design.

A design and PCA-based optimization framework for variable geometry turbine blade profiles
abstract: Variable geometry turbines (VGTs) are widely used in variable cycle engines to modulate core airflow. During mass flow regulation, the guide vane rotation induces pronounced changes in outlet flow angle and profile loading, which can degrade regulation accuracy and adaptability across multiple operating conditions. To address this challenge, this work developed an aerodynamic design optimization framework for VGT guide vane and rotor profiles. For guide vane profile design, a corrected deviation angle model was proposed and embedded in a workflow that couples parametric profile generation with an iterative calculation of the guide vane rotation angle. This enabled the guide vane to meet the prescribed outlet flow angle target at both the closed and open settings, and high-speed linear cascade experiments confirmed prediction-measurement agreement within 0.6°. For multi-condition aerodynamic performance improvement, a PCA (Principal Component Analysis) based optimization method was developed using Kriging surrogates and a multi-objective search, where design space was re-parameterized by principal component analysis to support surrogate retraining. Compared with opti-mization in the original design space, the proposed PCA-based strategy is robust and can achieve a comparable Pareto-front hypervolume using 46% fewer samples. The extracted principal components further enhance in-terpretability by revealing how key geometric variations affect profile loading and loss for both guide vane and rotor. Overall, this study offers a new perspective on multi-condition optimization of blade profiles and provides critical support for developing high-performance variable geometry turbines.

title: Integrated aerostructural design of composite aircraft using inertia relief and multi-objective optimization
abstract: Reducing structural weight and improving performance efficiency are main objectives in next-generation aircraft. Following that, this study has been conducted with the objective of designing a composite aircraft using novel integrated aerostructural design framework that combines inertia-relief-based load estimation, fully coupled static aeroelastic analysis, and surrogate-assisted multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MBO). This study has been conducted in three major steps: (1) inertia relief analysis for load factor estimation, (2) structural sizing of composite aircraft through a fully stressed design (FSD) approach, and (3) MBO incorporating composite materials; carbon fiber–reinforced polymers (CFRPs) and carbon fiber-reinforced thermoplastics (CFRTPs) combinations which offer substantial performance advantages. In this study, Boeing 737-class configuration is used as the reference model. In inertia relief analysis, aerodynamic loads from inviscid Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) were coupled with linear static structural analysis to evaluate load factors estimation which are subsequently incorporated into structural sizing through linear static structural analysis coupled with an iterative fully stressed design (FSD). Finally, MBO enabled aeroelastic consistency across generations, producing Pareto-optimal trade-offs between structural weight and aerodynamic drag. The optimized designs achieved a 20–25% reduction in structural weight while satisfying strength, stiffness, and stability requirements, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework for lightweight composite aircraft development.

title: Flow separation and control on a 35% thick wind turbine airfoil: experiments, simulations and data driven analysis
abstract: Modern wind turbine blades increasingly employ very thick airfoil profiles, particularly near the blade root, due to structural, manufacturing and transport constraints. These profiles are prone to flow separation, which leads to reduced performance and unstable aerodynamic loading. This type of flow is commonly controlled by passive Vortex Generators (VGs). The three-dimensional (3D) and unstable character of the flow, with or without VGs, makes it challenging to model physically or computationally and has not been sufficiently studied. This work highlights the intricacies of the 3D separated flow over very thick wind turbine airfoils and illustrates the need for rigorous analysis tailored to engineering applications. We investigate the flow over a 35% thick airfoil (DU00-W2-350), with and without flow separation control, using wind tunnel experiments, Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes simulations and data driven analysis methods. We analyse force symmetry and correlations, pressure distributions, and flow instability metrics, employing Hidden Markov Models to identify and quantify unstable flow regimes. The results demonstrate that the unstable and asymmetric loading on the airfoil is effectively suppressed by the presence of VGs on both sides of the airfoil. Numerical results show strong agreement with experimental data when full-span 3D CFD models are used, while lower-cost 3D-slice models are shown to accurately capture performance trends. The paper suggests that when airfoils experience 3D separation advanced metrics should be considered instead of the commonly used time averaged values. Further, it is shown that affordable, limited-width computational modelling is sufficient in terms of flow control efficiency prediction.

Nonlinear energy sink for passive mitigation of propeller whirl flutter
abstract: The electrification of aviation propulsion has resulted in new aircraft configurations that typically feature lightweight wings with high aspect ratios, along with multiple propellers distributed along the wingspan. Since the propellers are flexibly attached to the wing, an aeroelastic instability known as whirl flutter can occur. The rotating blades generate additional forces and moments, and due to gyroscopic effects, the propeller hub exhibits a whirling motion. Therefore, it is essential to explore various techniques to mitigate this aeroelastic instability. This paper examines the impact of a nonlinear energy sink (NES) on reducing the whirl flutter of a basic propeller-nacelle model. The proposed approach considers a propeller with pitch and yaw degrees of freedom, while modeling the dynamical contributions of the wing structure with equivalent nonlinear stiffness and viscous damping. The structural model of the propeller is coupled with a cubic nonlinear energy sink to passively mitigate oscillations. An initial characterization of the uncontrolled system is performed through frequency domain analysis, resulting in the creation of a velocity-damping-frequency diagram. The paper discusses a nonlinear adaptation of the propeller-nacelle model and conducts a bifurcation analysis using numerical continuation to characterize the dynamic behavior of the propeller-nacelle-NES system. The effects of attaching the NES are analyzed through bifurcation, parametric investigations, and energy transfer analysis of the device design parameters.

Kinetic mechanisms of single-pass ICRH and energy conversion in high-power magnetoplasma rocket: a hybrid PIC-MCC/FDFD study
abstract: The efficient coupling of ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) and magnetic nozzle acceleration is pivotal for high-power magnetoplasma propulsion, yet the kinetic mechanisms governing microsecond-scale energy surges remain poorly understood. This study investigates radio-frequency (RF) wave-particle interaction and energy conversion dynamics using a self-consistent kinetic model integrating a full-wave finite-difference frequency-domain solver with a hybrid Particle-in-Cell/Monte Carlo Collision (PIC-MCC) framework. Simulations in a realistic meter-scale magnetic topology (peak field: 2.8 T) reveal that the strong Doppler shift induces an upstream migration of the resonance layer, creating distinct non-Maxwellian suprathermal tails. Crucially, this work challenges the traditional collisionless assumption by demonstrating that collisional effects are essential for thrust generation. The integration of MCC reveals that pitch-angle scattering effectively breaks the adiabatic magnetic moment conservation constraint, facilitating rapid thermalization of perpendicular energy into directed axial energy. Consequently, the collision-inclusive model predicts a 36% increase in exit axial kinetic energy (0.1454 keV) and a theoretical specific impulse of 2696 s. Furthermore, extending the operational envelope reveals a critical power saturation mechanism. While absorbed power initially follows ideal I2 scaling, excessive RF current leads to severe finite Larmor radius (FLR) wall interception, degrading the system into a dominant ”wall heating” regime. This confirms that simply increasing input current is insufficient for scaling to megawatt levels. Instead, optimizing the magnetic field gradient and nozzle geometry to accommodate the expanding ion Larmor radius is the decisive path for maximizing thrust efficiency in future deep-space missions. Ultimately, this research confirms the pivotal role of collisional effects in breaking adiabatic constraints to enhance energy conversion. Moreover, by revealing the power saturation mechanisms governed by FLR effects, these insights provide essential kinetic criteria for optimizing magnetic topology and nozzle geometry, laying the groundwork for realizing megawatt-class propulsion in future deep-space missions.

title: Nonlinear dynamic analysis of a spline-connected shaft system under maneuvering flight

Time-dependent controllable set for contingency return trajectories under spatiotemporal constraints in CR3BP
abstract: In crewed lunar missions, when a failure or other emergency occurs, the spacecraft must accurately return to a designated landing site at a prescribed epoch or within a specified time window, thereby satisfying spatiotemporal constraints. To address the challenges of designing and analyzing contingency return trajectories under spatiotemporal constraints (CRTSC) and to determine their time-dependent controllable set (TDCS), this study establishes a systematic modeling and calculation framework. First, the definition and mathematical formulation of the controllable set are proposed and applied to CRTSC analysis under spatiotemporal constraints. Then, a re-entry pseudo-parameter method is developed to parameterize the CRTSC. Based on inverse integration in the circular restricted three-body problem (CR3BP), a differential correction technique is employed to refine the terminal state of the trajectory, forming a solution strategy for calculating the TDCS of CRTSC. Finally, extensive numerical simulations are conducted to investigate the topological characteristics of the TDCS and the influence of different constraint conditions on its parameter characteristics. The results indicate that, within the departure TDCS, the three-dimensional (3D) distribution of the perilune point and vacuum perigee longitude and latitude, together with the Jacobi integral, exhibits a tube-like structure. The findings provide a theoretical foundation for the design and analysis of contingency return trajectories in future crewed lunar missions.

title: Neural-network-based aerodynamic modeling and fixed-time neuro-adaptive control of a novel “diamond-wing” morphing aircraft
Experimental demonstration of a decentralized electromagnetic formation flying control using alternating magnetic field forces
abstract: Electromagnetic formation flying (EMFF) is challenging due to the complex coupling between the electromagnetic fields generated by each satellite in the formation. To address this challenge, this article uses alternating magnetic field forces (AMFF) to decouple the electromagnetic forces between each pair of satellites. The key idea of AMFF is that a pair of alternating (e.g., sinusoidal) magnetic moments results in a nonzero time-averaged interaction force if and only if those alternating magnetic moments have the same frequency. Hence, the approach in this article is to drive each satellite's electromagnetic actuation system with a sum of sinusoids, where each frequency is common to only a pair of satellites. Then, the amplitudes of each sinusoid are modulated (i.e., controlled) to achieve the desired forces between each pair of satellites. The main contribution of this article is an experimental demonstration of 3-satellite decentralized closed-loop EMFF using AMFF. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first demonstration of AMFF with at least 3 satellites in open or closed loop. This is noteworthy because the coupling challenges of EMFF are only present with more than 2 satellites, and thus, a formation of at least 3 is necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of AMFF. The experiments are conducted on a ground-based testbed consisting of 3 electromagnetically actuated satellites on linear air tracks. The closed-loop experiments demonstrate decentralized EMFF with AMFF where the maximum steady-state formation error is less than $\pm $0.01 m and the settling time is less than 30 s. These experiments validate the decoupling of intersatellite forces through frequency-multiplexed AMFF. The closed-loop experimental results are compared with the behavior of numerical simulations.

title: A review of trajectory planning for high speed vehicles: Current advancements and future prospects
Impact of wire mesh casing treatment on compressor rotating instability and stall patterns
abstract: Addressing the critical issues of rotating instability (RI) and stability degradation induced by large relative tip clearance in modern aero-engines, this paper presents an experimental investigation conducted on a low-speed axial compressor test rig. Utilizing circumferential dynamic pressure array measurements and modal decomposition techniques, the study systematically examines the impact of wire mesh casing treatment (WMCT) on the flow field characteristics and stall mechanisms under large clearance conditions. The results indicate that under the smooth wall (SW) baseline, the RI evolves from a discrete peak type to a broadband hump type disturbance as throttling proceeds, subsequently triggering a progressive stall. In contrast, the WMCT effectively suppresses the broadband unsteady disturbances in the near-stall region. This suppression enables the RI to maintain a distinct spike morphology up to the stability limit, eventually precipitating an abrupt spike-type stall. Flow field analysis further reveals that by inducing a secondary leakage vortex structure, the WMCT significantly attenuates the intensity of pressure fluctuations in the blade leading-edge region and inhibits their circumferential propagation capability. Consequently, effective control over the unsteady flow instability associated with large tip clearances is achieved.

Dimensional fidelity and hydraulic performance assessment of additively manufactured polymer pump components for rapid design validation
abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM) offers new opportunities for rapid prototyping of complex hydraulic components, enabling accelerated design iteration and experimental validation. However, the functional suitability of polymer AM technologies for hydraulic performance assessment remains insufficiently quantified, particularly for compact centrifugal pump components. This study presents a systematic experimental trade-off analysis of several polymer-based additive manufacturing technologies for the rapid prototyping of centrifugal pump impellers and volutes. The investigation combines dimensional metrology, geometric fidelity assessment, and hydraulic testing against a conventionally machined metallic reference. Multiple AM technologies and materials were evaluated with respect to surface quality, dimensional accuracy, and their impact on pump pressure rise, hydraulic efficiency, torque, and power consumption. The results show that AM components can reproduce the global hydraulic behaviour of the reference pump, preserving stable pressure flow characteristics and head capability. Polymer volutes introduce additional hydraulic losses leading to reduced efficiency, while polymer impellers maintain or increase pressure rise but require higher torque and power due to increased dissipation. Among the investigated technologies, PolyJet manufacturing using VeroUltra and Digital ABS materials provides the best compromise between dimensional fidelity, geometric reliability of critical features, and hydraulic performance. The findings demonstrate that carefully selected polymer additive manufacturing technologies can enable reliable rapid functional evaluation of centrifugal pump components for early-stage design validation, with predictable performance deviations primarily governed by surface-related hydraulic losses.

abstract: Unsteady shock–boundary-layer interaction on the lower surface of a transport-aircraft wing can be caused or amplified by ultrahigh-bypass-ratio underwing nacelle installation. This work analyzes the resulting buffet dynamics on the Airbus XRF1 configuration at a Mach number of 0.84, a Reynolds number of 3.3 × 10 6 , and − 4 ∘ angle of attack using scale-resolving delayed detached eddy simulations and unsteady pressure-sensitive paint measurements. Coherent structures are extracted employing a data-efficient multi-taper spectral POD. Dominant modes occur in the Strouhal number range St ∈ [0.1, 0.3]. Surface modes reveal wave-like shock motions that originate near the pylon–wing intersection and propagate inboard toward the fuselage. These shock oscillations are linked to unsteady flow separation downstream of the shock. Additional dominant modes show spanwise oscillations of the separated flow region and shock oscillations phase-linked to shear layer instabilities. The modal analysis of volume data reveals pressure waves connected to these modes traveling upstream above and below the wing.

Extended state observer enhanced constrained LPV-MPC for robust quadrotor trajectory tracking under wind disturbances
abstract: Robust trajectory tracking for quadrotors under wind disturbances requires control frameworks that explicitly handle constraints while mitigating disturbance. This study explores an important yet neglected design aspect in constrained robust control: the establishment of the minimum thrust constraint, U1, min. Utilizing a cascaded control architecture—combining outer-loopfeedback linearization with an inner-loop Linear Parameter-Varying Model Predictive Control(LPV-MPC) augmented by an Extended State Observer (ESO)—we evaluate the performance trade-off between a theoretical lower bound (derived from actuator limits) and a practical bound(necessary for hovering, U1, min). Simulation outcomes under wind gusts indicate that the theoretical limit enhances disturbance rejection by 12.4 percentage points relative to the practical limit, attaining a three-dimensional root-mean-square error (3D RMSE) of 0.286 m as opposed to 0.293 m. Both configurations satisfy actuator and safety constraints. This research raises U1, min, from a mere implementation aspect to a purposeful design consideration, offering practitioners a framework based on evidence to emphasize either disturbance rejection or natural hover stability.

title: Wall Inspector: Quadrotor control in wall-proximity through model compensation
abstract: The safe operation of quadrotors in near-wall urban or indoor environments (e.g., inspection and search-and-rescue missions) is challenged by unmodeled aerodynamic effects arising from wall-proximity. It generates complex vortices that induce destabilizing suction forces, potentially leading to hazardous vibrations or collisions. This paper presents a comprehensive solution featuring (1) a physics-based suction force model that explicitly characterizes the dependency on both rotor speed and wall distance, and (2) a suction-compensated model predictive control (SC-MPC) framework designed to ensure accurate and stable trajectory tracking during wall-proximity operations. The proposed SC-MPC framework incorporates an enhanced dynamics model that accounts for suction force effects, formulated as a factor graph optimization problem integrating system dynamics constraints, trajectory tracking objectives, control input smoothness requirements, and actuator physical limitations. The suction force model parameters are systematically identified through extensive experimental measurements across varying operational conditions. Experimental validation demonstrates SC-MPC's superior performance, achieving 2.1 cm root mean squared error (RMSE) in X-axis and 2.0 cm RMSE in Y-axis position control - representing 74% and 79% improvements over cascaded proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, and 60% and 53% improvements over standard MPC respectively. The corresponding mean absolute error (MAE) metrics (1.2 cm X-axis, 1.4 cm Y-axis) similarly outperform both baselines. The evaluation platform employs a ducted quadrotor design that provides collision protection while maintaining aerodynamic efficiency. To facilitate reproducibility and community adoption, we have open-sourced our complete implementation, available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SC-MPC-6A61.

Integrated multi-technique experimental setup for wind tunnel investigation of side jet interaction with crossflow
abstract: This paper presents the design, implementation, and preliminary validation of a novel integrated experimental setup for high-fidelity investigation of side jet interaction with subsonic, transonic, and supersonic crossflow in the VTI T-38 blowdown wind tunnel. The setup enables, for the first time on a sting-mounted slender missile model, simultaneous acquisition of global aerodynamic forces and moments, detailed surface pressure distributions in the jet interaction region, and schlieren flow visualization, while supplying high-pressure air to interchangeable Mach 1 and Mach 4 nozzles.A custom five-component flow-through internal strain-gage balance was developed to route the high-pressure jet supply without compromising force measurement accuracy. Thirty-four static pressure taps around the nozzle are linked to a compact on-board pressure scanner, complemented by the wind tunnel parallel-beam schlieren system.Preliminary tests on the baseline model configuration without side jet provided essential reference aerodynamic data, including base-pressure-corrected axial force, Mach-dependent center-of-pressure migration, and characterization of transient starting and stopping loads. Static calibration of the jet supply system quantified pressure losses, thrust characteristics, and nozzle operating regimes.By overcoming longstanding limitations in combining accurate global force measurements with high-pressure secondary flow on sting-mounted models, the setup delivers consistent, high-density multi-faceted datasets in a single test run. These data are expected to significantly improve quantitative evaluation of reaction control jet efficacy, enhance understanding of jet-crossflow interaction mechanisms, and support reliable validation of CFD codes for next-generation agile missiles and spacecraft across diverse flight conditions.

Calibration method of spacecraft–inertial sensor center-of-mass offset for the Taiji gravitational wave detection mission under science mode
abstract: Accurately calibrating the center-of-mass (CoM) offset between the spacecraft (SC) and the inertial sensor test mass (TM) is crucial for space-based gravitational-wave (GW) antennas, such as LISA and Taiji. Current calibration methods require additional spacecraft maneuvers that disrupt science data continuity and inter-satellite links, compromising the coherence of gravitational wave signals. Here, we present a maneuver-free calibration scheme that directly estimates the CoM offset vector using only standard science-mode measurements from inertial sensors, interferometers, and differential wavefront sensors. By embedding the CoM offset induced coupling acceleration as an extended state in a model-based adaptive Kalman filter, we achieve estimation accuracy of 0.01-1.5 mm across all axes with a maximum error below 1%. This approach enables continuous, high-precision calibration during nominal observation runs, ensuring continuous and coherent gravitational wave data collection while maintaining the required precision, and also facilitating advanced DFACS functions such as performance evaluations and fault diagnosis. For LISA-like missions, where data continuity is paramount for detecting faint gravitational wave signals, this method will enhance scientific output and reliability.

title: Neural-network-based event-driven robust control for distributed formation of multiple quadrotors
abstract: The actual work investigates the distributed and finite-time formation control of a multi-agent system (MAS) composed of vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) vehicles subjected to unknown and time-varying disturbances. The attitude of each VTOL is initially stabilized through the design of a robust control strategy. Then, in order to achieve consensus-based formation and trajectory-tracking for the MAS with reduced burden communication, an event-triggered non-singular fast terminal sliding-mode control (NFTSMC) strategy is synthesized. Additionally, a radial basis function neural-network (RBFNN) capable of estimating external disturbances is designed for robustness enhancement purposes. The closed-loop system stability is proved by employing the Lyapunov theory, and the minimal inter-event execution is verified to be lower-bounded, excluding the Zeno behavior. Numerical and experimental results validating the effectiveness of the proposed control scheme are presented considering a fleet of aerial robots.

title: Deep-learning of satellite aerodynamics in very low Earth orbit with partial-physics pretraining

Feasibility and trade-offs in the design of an airship for Martian exploration
abstract: The rapid growth of the field of airship technology over the last few years for Earth missions, in turns enabled by the development of electric motors employed in a distributed fashion as a means for both propulsion and control, is fueling the investigation of the adaptability of this type of flying platform for several tasks. Through the energy harvesting capability achieved with solar cells, the already inherently superior endurance of airships could be extended in principle to the order of months, thus producing a highly-effective platform especially for high-altitude, low-payload monitoring tasks. The spill-over of these analyses to other planetary scenarios featuring a significant atmospheric layer is straightforward - in principle. Several shortcomings affecting the design of airships on Earth have to be analyzed as well in the generally more requiring non-terrestrial environments, coping with additional specific scenario constraints. This research, grounded on a consolidated methodology previously introduced and employed for the sizing of diverse airships for Earth missions, discusses such additional constraints and the features of an airship design procedure needed to cope with them. Furthermore, a specifically emended design methodology is employed to analyze in a parameterized fashion the effect on the airship sizing of some key technology and mission design assumptions, yielding an assessment of the feasibility and critical points. This research is aimed to answering three pivotal questions about the operational feasibility of an airship for Martian exploration. Firstly, to what extent can established sizing frameworks for terrestrial high altitude airships be adapted to the Martian environment. Secondly, what are the primary technological constraints that dictate the overall feasibility of the concept. Finally, whether a solar-powered design optimized for a specific mission, in favorable yet realistic conditions, be achievable. When placed in the context of the available literature concerning Martian airships, this work provides a clear insight on the global feasibility of such a mission, highlighting the technological bottlenecks possibly preventing the practical realization of an LTA concept for Martian exploration.

Origin and control of pseudo-rotating spiral jets
abstract: Active flow control (AFC) methods for jet-type flows have been extensively explored since the 1970s. Spectacular examples demonstrating the AFC power and the beauty of fluid mechanics include bifurcating and blooming jets. Recent advances in machine learning-based optimization have enabled efficient exploration of high-dimensional AFC, revealing control solutions beyond human intuition. The present paper focuses on one such discovery: the pseudo-rotating spiral jet. This phenomenon manifests as separate branches disconnected from the main jet stream, formed by vortical structures aligned along curved paths rotating around the initial jet axis. Applying the large eddy simulation (LES) method and a high-order numerical code, we investigate the origin of these jet-type patterns and formulate new rules for their control, showing that spiral jets belong to a family of multi-armed jets observable only at specific control settings. Furthermore, we demonstrate how human perception of three-dimensional imagery depends on the observable domain and vortex lifetime. We show that the rotation of spiral arms - despite having a well-defined frequency - is an illusion arising from the tendency to connect neighboring moving objects into continuous patterns. In contrast to the chaotic behavior of small-scale turbulence, we found that the large-scale flow motion induced by AFC, operating in a deterministic manner, is fully predictable. Through theoretical derivation and analysis of 3D LES results, we develop a remarkably simple yet precise kinematic model that captures the formation and motion of the vortical paths. This model replicates the outcomes of complex flow simulations, reproduces the apparent jet shape, and facilitates the identification of the actual pattern. The analysis of time-averaged data shows that, for a specified set of control parameters, the jets exhibit an unprecedented tendency to increase the entrainment rate (up to 9 times that of the classical jet), accompanied by a simultaneous 5-fold rise in turbulent kinetic energy, resulting in intensified mixing. Analysis of a passive scalar field reveals a substantially more uniform distribution, with up to a sevenfold improvement over the classical jet at five nozzle diameters, and nearly perfect mixing achieved at ten diameters. These findings open new perspectives for both academic researchers and industrial engineers, particularly in combustion science, cooling systems, and jet propulsion, where control of the mixing process is a critical factor for flame stabilization, heat exchange, and noise mitigation.

Multidisciplinary design optimization of distributed electric propulsion aircraft with trim and flying qualities constraints using surrogate models
abstract: Hybrid-electric regional aircraft characterized by distributed electric propulsion offer promising benefits but introduce strong couplings problems between aerodynamics, structures, propulsion, and power systems, requiring a multidisciplinary design and optimization (MDO) approach to capture relevant trade-offs. This work presents an extended MDO framework applied to the Clean Aviation HERA configuration, developed within a collaboration between Politecnico di Milano and Airbus Defence and Space. The framework enhances traditional aero-structural optimization considering the use of the aerodynamic solver DUST, based on Vortex Particle Method (VPM) and by explicitly incorporating stability, control, and automatic trim requirements as design constraints. To limit the computational cost of aerodynamic simulations, surrogate models based on supervised machine learning regression and design of experiments (DOE) are employed within a multi-fidelity strategy. Results show consistent performance improvements in trimmed flight conditions, with successful enforcement of stability and flying qualities constraints. Furthermore, comparison between surrogate-based and high-fidelity optimizations highlights both the accuracy of the reduced-order models and their effectiveness in lowering computational costs.

Fusing CFD and measurement data using transfer learning
abstract: Aerodynamic analysis during aircraft design usually involves methods of varying accuracy and spatial resolution, which all have their advantages and disadvantages. It is therefore desirable to create data-driven models which effectively combine these advantages. Such data fusion methods for distributed quantities mainly rely on proper orthogonal decomposition as of now, which is a linear method. In this paper, we introduce a non-linear method based on neural networks combining simulation and measurement data via transfer learning. The network training accounts for the heterogeneity of the data, as simulation data usually features a high spatial resolution, while measurement data is sparse but more accurate. In a first step, the neural network is trained on simulation data to learn spatial features of the distributed quantities. The second step involves transfer learning on the measurement data to correct for systematic errors between simulation and measurement by re-training a subset of the entire neural network model. This approach is applied to a multilayer perceptron architecture and shows significant improvements over the established method based on proper orthogonal decomposition by producing more physical solutions near nonlinearities. In addition, the neural network provides solutions at arbitrary flow conditions, thus making the model useful for flight mechanical design, structural sizing, and certification. As the proposed training strategy is very general, it can also be applied to more complex neural network architectures in the future.

Study on ignition and combustion enhancement characteristics of gliding arc plasma in confined spaces
abstract: To meet the high-reliability ignition requirements of rocket engines, based on the combustion chamber of a rocket engine, ignition and combustion experiments of a gliding arc plasma were conducted in a confined space. The results indicate that, in the confined space, successful ignition mainly occurs under fuel-lean conditions. The boundary constraints cause the combustion reaction to concentrate toward the central region, with heat release concentrated in the core combustion zone, which is significantly different from the combustion heat release characteristics observed in an open environment. Therefore, targeted investigation of ignition characteristics in confined spaces is necessary. The gliding arc plasma igniter can achieve reliable ignition in the confined space of a rocket engine, with an optimal ignition equivalence ratio range of 0.57~0.68. The active species generated by the plasma exert a combustion enhancement effect during the ignition process. Methane flow rate plays a key role in determining the ignition equivalence ratio range. When the oxidizer flow rate is fixed, a higher methane flow rate results in a narrower ignition range, indicating that this ignition method is more suitable for low-flow-rate, low-thrust rocket engines. For high-flow-rate engines, optimization of the equivalence ratio and an increase in igniter power are required. Appropriately extending the combustor length can significantly improve ignition performance.

Role of thermal radiation in HTP-based small-scale hybrid rocket engines
abstract: Thermal radiation is acknowledged as a contributing mechanism in hybrid rocket engines, yet its quantitative impact across different operating regimes, particularly at small geometric scales, has not been systematically assessed. In this work, the role of radiative heat transfer in a 10 N-class hybrid rocket engine is investigated through a coupled Computational Fluid Dynamics and Gas-Surface Interaction framework, including a participating-medium radiation model that accounts for gas-phase radiation from CO 2 and H 2 O. Numerical simulations are validated against experimental firing tests and used to examine how chamber pressure, propellant combination, and engine size influence the wall heat balance and fuel regression behavior. For hydrogen-peroxide-based configurations operating in the 10 N thrust class, radiation provides a limited contribution to wall heating, remaining below 5% of the total wall heat flux under practical operating conditions. Increasing chamber pressure enhances the radiative heat flux but does not substantially alter its relative weight within the accessible operating envelope. When the same configuration is operated with gaseous oxygen, the radiative fraction increases from 4.5% to 17.5%, reflecting the strong influence of combustion temperature on radiative heat transfer even at small scale. A comparison with a dynamically comparable 1 kN-class firing condition further indicates that larger characteristic dimensions are associated with a rise of the radiative contribution up to 28.1%, consistently with the increased optical thickness of the configuration. Overall, the study establishes a consistent framework to identify when radiative heat transfer can be neglected in small-scale hybrid rocket engines and when it must be explicitly accounted for in this propulsion class. The results contribute to addressing the limited characterization of radiative effects in small-scale hybrid propulsion systems and provide a validated reference for the design and modeling of CubeSat-class hybrid rocket engines.

The kenemostat: Structural feasibility of a vacuum-buoyant geodesic vehicle including global buckling
abstract: A kenemostat — from the Greek kenon (void), anemos (wind), and statos (standing) — is a lighter-than-air vehicle that achieves buoyancy by enclosing a total vacuum and navigates by riding wind fields at selectable altitude. The primary structure is a geodesic polyhedral frame with I-beam edges in compression and a sealing skin. Two structural variants are analyzed: (A) a stiffened shell with the skin bonded to the frame, and (B) a detached membrane with the skin in pure biaxial tension against the frame edges. Both member (Euler) buckling and global (shell) buckling are treated. The equivalent continuum shell stiffness of the geodesic lattice is derived, yielding global buckling pressures of approximately 3 atm (Variant A) and 2 atm (Variant B) at frequency f = 3 for edges sized by member buckling alone. A beam-element FEA of the 92-vertex, 270-edge geodesic icosahedron validates the load model. Frame mass scales as R^3/sqrt(f); a compressive stress check bounds viable frequency to f = 2-4 for CFRP. With CFRP-class materials the critical circumradius is 12-20 m; CNT composites reduce it to approximately 7 m. A self-equalizing pulley cable provides internal bracing at negligible mass. Beyond break-even, payload grows cubically: approximately 4 tonnes at R = 20 m, 60 tonnes at R = 40 m.

Dual-biomimetic conceptual design of a Blended Wing Body Unmanned Aerial Vehicle inspired by eagle and manta ray
abstract: Blended-wing-body (BWB) unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are attractive for regional logistics because of their high aerodynamic efficiency and internal volume, yet practical concepts are often limited by coupled low-speed stall/trim constraints and weak directional stability in tailless layouts. This work proposes a mission-driven dual-biomimetic conceptual design framework for a 200-kg-class BWB cargo UAV inspired by manta rays (planform shaping, smooth lifting-body blending and large leading-edge radius morphology) and eagles (spanwise scaling, wingtip, and tail). The biomimetic translation is cast into transferable non-dimensional geometry descriptors, including planform/segmentation ratios, sweep/twist, leading-edge-radius ratio, winglet height ratio, and V-tail volume coefficients. A controlled comparative matrix is evaluated using steady RANS CFD (Spalart–Allmaras) to isolate the incremental effects of wing–body planform shaping, leading-edge-radius strategy, winglets, V-tail integration, and surface smoothing, followed by a twin-engine installation assessment accounting for nacelle external drag. Relative to a conventional-geometry control, the biomimetic planform reduces C_(D,c) by ~11% and increases 〖(C_L/C_D)〗_c by ~13%. Enforcing r_LE/c≥2% increases C_(L,max) by ~7.8% and delays stall by ~1°. Winglets slightly improve induced-drag efficiency but yield negligible net 〖(C_L/C_D)〗_c gain. A compact V-tail reverses adverse directional stability to favorable behavior and reduces cruise trim offset mainly through interference-driven wing–body pressure redistribution. Surface smoothing provides the largest cruise benefit (≈13% lower C_(D,c)), dominated by reduced pressure drag. The resulting configuration satisfies the prescribed mission constraints and yields reusable, non-dimensional design guidelines for BWB UAV conceptual design.

title: Fully-featured digital twins of in-service high-pressure turbine blades for high-fidelity CFD analyses
abstract: The high-pressure turbine blades of modern jet engines are inevitably subject to deformation and deterioration during their service life due to the extreme conditions under which they operate. Their hollow design with multiple internal cavities allows for effective internal and external cooling strategies, helping the component to withstand the increasingly high temperatures produced by modern combustors. Knowledge of the geometric variations experienced by these blades during service is crucial for designers to estimate the residual service life and aerothermal performance of the component. This important task has recently been achieved by running numerical flow simulations on the scanned, digitalized versions of the geometries. For cost effectiveness, time savings, and practical reasons, the scanned geometries do not capture the complex internal channels of the component. This part of the geometry is vital to perform higher-fidelity assessments, such as conjugate heat transfer simulations, which model both internal and external flows. This study proposes the first automatic methodology for reconstructing the internal geometry of a turbine blade scan by linking it to the external deformation field, paving the way for systematic generation of fully-featured digital twins of scanned in-service blade geometries. The internal deformation and reconstruction methodology is first presented in detail, then validated on a simplified test-case, and finally applied to a real high-pressure turbine blade scan from a modern jet engine. The resulting reconstructed geometry is used to assess the residual aerothermal performance of the scanned blade.

Numerical and experimental comparative analysis of synthetic jet-based wingtip vortex control
abstract: This study presents a combined numerical–experimental investigation of synthetic jet-based active control of wingtip vortices, with the aim of assessing the predictive capability of an unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes framework against Stereoscopic Particle Image Velocimetry measurements. The performed analyses consider both baseline (jet-off) and controlled (jet-on) configurations at a fixed momentum coefficient Cµ = 0.2% and two di-mensionless frequencies, f + = 0.071 and f + = 0.55. Regarding the baseline case, the simulations accurately reproduce the overall vortex roll-up and cap- ture the vortex trajectory well in the near field, while increasing discrepancies arise downstream due to enhanced numerical diffusion and the intrinsic limitations of eddy-viscosity turbulence models. Under actuation conditions, the time-averaged results indicate a weakening and diffusion of the primary vortex. Both forcing frequencies promote the formation of a co-rotating jet-induced vortex, with the higher frequency yielding a more distributed attenuation. A quantitative comparison of the geometrical characteristics of the vortex core, based on an elliptical Gaussian fitting model, shows that numerical simulations capture the main trends in vortex growth and vorticity peak reduction, although vortex circulation and core diffusion are generally overestimated. Phase-locked analyses further demonstrate that the numerical model reproduces the main periodic modulation of the vortex strength induced by the synthetic jet, particularly during the blowing phase. Overall, the results of the study confirm that present numerical simulations provide a reliable first-order tool for assessing synthetic-jet control of wingtip vortices, while highlighting the need for improved wake resolution and higher-fidelity approaches to achieve fully quantitative agreement.

abstract: This paper presents a constraint-aware control framework for underactuated aerial manipulators, enabling accurate end-effector trajectory tracking while explicitly accounting for safety and feasibility constraints. The control problem is formulated as a quadratic program that computes dynamically consistent generalized accelerations subject to underactuation, actuator bounds, and system constraints. To enhance robustness against disturbances, modeling uncertainties, and steady-state errors, a passivity-based integral action is incorporated at the torque level without compromising feasibility. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through high-fidelity physics-based simulations, which include parameter perturbations, viscous joint friction, and realistic sensing and state-estimation effects. This demonstrates accurate tracking, smooth control inputs, and reliable constraint satisfaction under realistic operating conditions.

Hammershock analysis of S-shaped air intake at subsonic mach number
abstract: This study investigated hammershock events in the RAE M2129 S-shaped intake at a subsonic freestream Mach number. Numerical simulations were performed with ANSYS Fluent and OpenFOAM employing hybrid RANS–LES turbulence modelling. Two surge signatures, with identical peak overpressure ratios, but different rise and recession times, were analysed. A characteristic-based, partially non-reflecting, outlet treatment was adopted to minimise spurious acoustic reflections. The results indicated that the rise time governed the intensity and propagation speed of the primary compression wave, whereas the recession time controlled post-ejection flow recovery and separation persistence. Both solvers reproduced the main physical features of the transient event, although quantitative differences were observed in pressure peak values and shock front advancement.

The concept and feasibility study of multimode acceleration coaxial (MAC) thruster
abstract: A multimode propulsion concept, termed the Multimode Acceleration Coaxial (MAC) thruster, is proposed for in-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing (ISAM) missions. These missions require three key capabilities: high impulsive thrust for proximity operations, high specific impulse for orbit maneuvers, and electrostatic discharge (ESD) mitigation for safe docking. The MAC thruster adopts a coaxial architecture consisting of a “nozzled” hollow cathode, an annular discharge channel, and magnetic circuits. The key novelty lies in the integration of Hall, CC discharge, and gas-jet modes within a single device, enabled by the dual use of the hollow cathode as both a neutralizer and a high-flow-rate propellant injector. A breadboard model (BBM), developed based on the ν800 JAXA 1 kW-class Hall thruster technology, was experimentally investigated, achieving a specific impulse of up to 1620 s and a thrust exceeding 0.5 N. The results demonstrate that each operating mode exhibits distinct performance characteristics tailored to corresponding ISAM mission requirements, highlighting the capability of a single thruster to operate across a wide operational envelope. It is thus demonstrated that the MAC thruster provides an integrated propulsion solution with shared propellant, enabling enhanced mission flexibility while reducing spacecraft system complexity in future ISAM applications.

Large Eddy simulation and data-driven surrogate modeling of high-pressure cryogenic oxygen jets in crossflow
abstract: In this work, the mixing characteristics of a transcritical liquid oxygen jet injected into a vitiated crossflow are investigated at an operating pressure of 100 bar. A comprehensive parametric analysis is performed using Large Eddy Simulations (LES) coupled with tabulated chemistry to decouple the effects of the momentum flux ratio (J) and the jet Reynolds number (Rej). Results indicate that while J primarily governs global jet penetration, Rej significantly affects the near-field topology. At low Reynolds numbers, thermal expansion effects dominate over inertia, leading to a pronounced radial spreading of the dense core, whereas higher Reynolds numbers extend the liquid-like core length. To enable rapid design space exploration, the high-fidelity database is leveraged to train a resolution-invariant surrogate model based on Fourier Neural Operators (FNO). The proposed model accurately infers the time-averaged scalar field and jet trajectory for unseen operating conditions, capturing the non-linearities more effectively than classical empirical correlations. The surrogate demonstrates a speed-up of several orders of magnitude compared to the CFD solver, proving to be a robust tool for the preliminary design of high-pressure propulsion systems.

title: A zonal hybrid parameterization framework for high-fidelity geometric reconstruction and aerodynamic consistency of turbine blade profiles
abstract: Existing turbine blade parameterization methods are often hard to preserve aerodynamic consistency while achieving high-fidelity geometric reconstruction, particularly in geometrically sensitive regions. To address this limitation, a zonal hybrid parameterization framework is proposed for the aerodynamically consistent and high-fidelity reconstruction of turbine blade profiles. Based on the distinct geometric characteristics and aerodynamic sensitivities of the leading-edge, mid-chord loading, and trailing-edge regions, the blade profile is described using a zonal formulation, in which these three regions are represented by a local analytical ellipse, cubic-spline baselines superposed with localized perturbation functions, and a rho-conic analytical curve, respectively. The resulting framework defines a low-dimensional design space with 17 explicit design variables. The inverse reconstruction problem is then cast as a bounded black-box optimization problem and solved using an increasing-population covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy initialized by Latin hypercube sampling. Results for the GE-E3, T106C, and VKI-LS89 profiles demonstrate that the proposed framework more faithfully preserves key aerodynamic features, including leading-edge acceleration, separation-sensitive surface-flow characteristics, transonic shock structures, and wake-loss distributions, while also delivering higher geometric reconstruction accuracy than two widely used parameterization methods. Overall, the proposed framework provides a unified and practical basis for aerodynamically consistent profile reconstruction and parameterization analysis, with potential for future optimization-oriented applications.

Assessment of easily accessible and proprietary models of departure aircraft performance using open flight tracking data and a mixed analysis-synthesis approach
abstract: Predicting the environmental impact of civil air traffic around airports requires reliable modelling of aircraft operations, especially for departures due to their high engine thrust near the ground. Assessing currently available aircraft performance models is difficult without proprietary FDR (flight data recorder) information, but the recent availability of open flight tracking data has prompted formulation of a reliable modelling tool for flight operation reconstruction using a mixed analysis-synthesis approach (MASA) previously developed by the authors. The MASA tailors prescribed ANP (aircraft noise and performance) procedures to actual flight operations, and allows assessing different performance models without using FDR data. In this work, an upgraded MASA is used to compare the departure performance predictions of BADA4, a restricted-access proprietary model, with those based for thrust on ANP, more easily accessible, and for fuel burn on the open-data ICAO Doc 9889 method. The thrust estimation is conducted using either the ANP or BADA4 sub-model, with a hybrid sub-model also tested, while extension to fuel burn is performed including Doc 9889 and BADA4 methods. After processing over 11,000 flight-tracked departures, the resulting trajectory errors and modelled thrust outputs show good reliability of ANP especially near the take-off, while BADA4 appears more accurate in higher-altitude climb phases. For fuel burn, the open-data method yields values nearly 40% below BADA4, but the underestimation is halved when compared to literature FDR data. These results demonstrate that easily accessible thrust and fuel flow models paired with flight tracking data can provide satisfactory predictions of departure aircraft performance.

title: Continuous parameterisation of wing movable layout for optimisation
abstract: This paper presents a novel methodology for continuous parameterisation of movables, which takes advantage of the ability of the doublet lattice method to describe aerodynamic forces using downwash. The movables are described in the continuous space using a downwash distribution generated using a B-spline surface. The parameterisation allows for any number of control surfaces to be positioned along the trailing edge of the wing. A high aspect ratio strut-braced wing aircraft model has been used to determine the handling qualities and manoeuvre load alleviation performance at different flight conditions, demonstrating and assessing the methodology for modelling movables distributions. The results in the paper demonstrated a successful application of a novel continuous movable parameterisation methodology, which can be applied to an aircraft for which only the planform and initial structural parameters are known. Furthermore, the results obtained with the continuous parameterisation advocate for the use of movables which can change their shape in the spanwise direction.

The influence mechanism of inlet operating conditions and load distribution on the scaling effect of subsonic compressor cascades
abstract: At present, the F or G-class gas turbines have been applied at the industrial power plant, and J-class heavy-duty gas turbines are being researched. The design mass flow rate of the J-class heavy-duty gas turbine is approximately 1000 kg/s. During the verification stage of compressor components, engineers have to face a great challenge in conducting full-scale geometric experimental studies. Therefore, scale-down testing based on aerodynamic similarity offers an economical and practical alternative. Specifically, the V103 compressor cascade is selected as the research object, this paper uses the RANS (Reynolds Averaged Navier–Stokes) numerical method to investigate the influence mechanisms of the inlet incidence angle, inlet Mach number (flow compressibility), and the different load distributions on the scaling effect of the compressor cascades. The results show that for the large incidence angle at off-design operating conditions, the scaling effect results in a 26.25% difference in the relative total pressure loss; and a 4.5% difference in the static pressure ratio. The scaling effect causes significant differences in the suction peak pressure at the leading edge of the cascade. The scaled-up model will increase the leading edge aerodynamic load, and the reason is attributed to the increased boundary layer edge curvature on the suction surface. For incompressible flow conditions, the influence of the scaling effect on the suction peak pressure is not significant. The compressible flow theoretical analytical solution indicates that for compressible flow, when the inlet flow Mach number approaches sonic conditions, the influence of the scaling effect on the suction peak pressure becomes more significant. For cascades with different geometric load distributions, the influence of the scaling effect on suction peak pressure is related to the position of the maximum load. As the maximum load of the cascade shifts backward, the suction peak pressure difference caused by scaling effects also shifts toward the mid or rear part of the profile. The scaling effect has a more significant influence on the profile loss and incidence range of the aft load cascade. This work provides a useful highlight for the preliminary design of industrial heavy-duty gas turbine compressors.

Deep neural network surrogates for next-generation twin-engine STOL airlifter design
abstract: The operational demands of Agile Combat Employment and fleet recapitalization are driving interest in next-generation tactical transports. While twin-engine solutions promise reduced operational and maintenance costs compared to four-engine baselines, they present significant design challenges for achieving robust Short Take-Off and Landing ( stol ) performance from austere, semi-prepared runways. This work addresses the inherent antagonism between maximizing payload and minimizing critical field length through a certification-constrained multi-objective optimization framework. A high-fidelity dataset of approximately 16,500 converged designs was generated using the Pacelab APD & SysArc conceptual design suite to train a Deep Neural Network surrogate model with high validation fidelity against physics-based predictions. The surrogate was integrated with an NSGA-II genetic algorithm to efficiently map the multi-objective Pareto front, bounded by key constraints including One Engine Inoperative climb gradient, minimum control speed margin, static stability margin, and maximum takeoff weight. The resulting Pareto front reveals direct trade-offs between runway performance and payload capacity for twin-engine, T-tail C-130J-class configurations. This optimization workflow, combining certification constraints with surrogate modeling, accelerates conceptual design of stol transports, reduces early design risks, and extends to adjacent mission profiles and design space explorations.

title: Investigation of creep life optimization of a high-pressure turbine rotor blade with ribbed internal cooling channels
Aerothermal squealer tip optimization via direct manipulation of free form deformation method
Ultra-high-bypass-ratio fan flutter prediction using non-linear fluid–structure interaction model
abstract: Next-generation turbofan engine designs have shifted toward higher bypass ratios and lower fan pressure ratios to improve specific fuel consumption. This trend results in larger fan diameters, thinner blades, and the extensive use of composite materials, thereby making aeroelastic instabilities induced by fluid–structure interaction more pronounced. Although the traditional energy method is widely adopted, it lacks the capability to capture complex blade motions and entails prohibitive computational cost. To address these limitations, this study develops a high-efficiency nonlinear fluid–structure interaction (FSI) framework based on a standing-wave-to-traveling-wave transformation. By tracking modal displacements using standing-wave mode shapes, the proposed approach enables the simultaneous extraction of aerodynamic damping for multiple nodal diameters within a single computation. The method is validated on an ultra-high-bypass-ratio (UHBR) fan (ECL5, designed by Ecole Centrale de Lyon, where comprehensive experimental measurements were also carried out) using a Unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (URANS) solver coupled with an implicit Newmark-β structural integration scheme. Compared with the conventional energy method, the proposed framework achieves a computational cost reduction of more than 90% while maintaining nearly identical damping predictions for the least stable modes. Flutter analysis performed along the high-loaded working line from 80% to 104% design speed indicates that ND1 is the least stable nodal diameter, but positive aerodynamic damping is maintained throughout. The results further reveal that fluctuations in aeroelastic stability are closely associated with acoustic resonance transitions (cut-on/cut-off) within the fan duct. In particular, for ND2 and ND3, a rapid decrease in aerodynamic damping is observed once their characteristic frequencies exceed the upstream cut-on frequency. Overall, the proposed efficient FSI framework provides a reliable and practical tool for rapid aeroelastic stability assessment of advanced fan stages.

title: Path-following guidance for unmanned aerial vehicle with bounded lateral acceleration
abstract: This paper addresses the three-dimensional path-following guidance problem for unmanned aerial vehicles under explicit actuator constraints. Unlike conventional approaches that assume unbounded control inputs or handle saturation heuristically, the proposed method incorporates bounded lateral acceleration directly into the guidance design. A nonlinear guidance framework is developed employing a nested saturation-based control technique. The proposed guidance strategy guarantees bounded control inputs while ensuring exponential convergence of cross-track errors to zero. The formulation is applicable to general smooth paths and is systematically extended from planar to three-dimensional scenarios using a path-tangent coordinate framework. Rigorous stability analysis based on Lyapunov theory establishes convergence and feasibility properties of the closed-loop system. Numerical simulations on representative paths, including straight-line, circular, and sinusoidal paths, demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior tracking performance, reduced control effort, and robustness against disturbances compared to existing guidance laws. The simplicity of the design and its compatibility with practical actuator limits make it suitable for real-world UAV applications.

title: Deep reinforcement learning empowers autonomous decision-making in intelligent air combat: challenges, breakthroughs, and prospects
Reduced-order modal analysis of circumferential flame propagation during ignition in a toroidal vortex combustor
Bridging the domain gap in spacecraft pose estimation: A novel image generative model
Efficient and sustainable surface modification of TC17 dual-phase titanium alloy via dual-frequency ultrasonic cavitation for green aerospace propulsion
Aerodynamics and stability of tailless UCAV in ground effects
abstract: Tailless UCAVs are stealth, high subsonic configurations used for deep penetration in the contested airspaces. These configurations have wing with moderate leading edge sweep angle with no definite fuselage and lack both horizontal tail vertical tail which makes the aerodynamics of these configurations very unique. The increase in autonomous UAVs in recent times have led to renewed interest in this class of configurations. The understanding of the behavior of the UCAVs near the ground have a profound impact on the development robust control schemes for the take-off and landing which are very critical mission segments for the UCAVs. The current literature on the ground effects focusses mainly on conventional configuration or high swept delta wings. The absence of distinct horizontal or vertical tail makes these configurations marginally stable in both the longitudinal and the lateral-directional plane. These attributes of the tailless UCAV make the aerodynamics and stability to be highly coupled in nature. This work focusses on understanding the aerodynamic behavior of a typical tailless UCAV near the ground and its influence on the stability characteristics. RANS CFD analysis is carried out at different ground heights, angle of attack side slip angle. Studies are also carried to understand the effect of roll orientation effect on the ground effects. The lift coefficient was observed to decrease near the ground at lower angle of attack and increase at high angle of attack. The region between the ground and aircraft acts like a venturi at low angle of attack. At high angle of attack, ramming effect is observed increasing the pressure on the bottom surface. The drag coefficient does not change at lower angle of attack and significant reduction is observed at higher angle of attack due to the reduction in the induced drag. The directional stability of this configuration is almost close to neutral stability due to absence of vertical tail and the UCAV shows a reduction in directional stability near the ground. The rolling moment due to side slip angle shows a stable behavior near the ground. The roll orientation of the UCAVs impacts the rolling moment behavior near the ground providing increased rolling moment (roll stiffness) near the ground which has a tendency to counter the direction of the roll. The dynamics of the tailless UCAV near the ground has interesting behavior near the ground. The short period mode has stabilizing behavior near the ground whereas the Dutch roll tends to be slightly unstable near the ground. The roll orientation of the UCAV seems to impact the Dutch roll mode changing from slightly unstable to a slightly stable behavior. The aerodynamics and stability aspects are highly coupled for tailless UCAV. The understanding of tailless UCAV near the ground will be key for development of control schemes for robust take-off and landing of these Configurations.

title: A geometric approximation-based airfoil data augmentation for airfoil classification
abstract: This paper proposes a Geometric Approximation-based Airfoil Data Augmentation method and applies it to the classification of transonic airfoils. The method comprises two stages: geometric approximation and sample screening. Specifically, the geometric approximation stage employs an optimization-based strategy to generate a large set of candidate samples, while the sample screening stage filters for feasible intermediate airfoils based on geometric tolerance to maintain sample validity. Samples augmented via this approach preserve critical geometric features of the target airfoils while expanding dataset diversity, consequently improving the classification performance for transonic airfoils. Experimental validations on the UIUC dataset quantify the accuracy improvements achieved by the proposed method; furthermore, the method exhibits favorable generalization capabilities and enables reliable labeling of unlabeled data.

title: Effect of a bluff body shape on a recirculation zone topology and mixing characteristics
abstract: The objective of this study is to determine how the cross-sectional shape of a bluff body controls the topology of the downstream recirculation zone and the associated mixing characteristics in turbulent non-reacting flow. Four bluff bodies with identical cross-sectional area are examined: circular (Crc-BB), square (Sqr-BB), triangular (Tri-BB), and hexagram-type star (Str-BB) geometries. A combined experimental and numerical approach is employed, with particle image velocimetry (PIV) used for velocity field measurements and high-order large-eddy simulation (LES) for detailed flow analysis. The numerical results show good agreement with the experimental data, both in terms of the mean velocity and fluctuation profiles. We demonstrate that the BB shape has a strong impact on the downstream recirculation zone in different aspects. Non-circular geometries, particularly Tri-BB and Str-BB, imprint their cross-sectional shape onto the flow, with effects persisting over several equivalent BB diameters. These shapes disrupt the formation of the Kelvin–Helmholtz vortex ring observed in Crc-BB and instead promote streamwise-aligned vortices that originate at sharp corners. This leads to significant modifications in flow statistics, including reduced velocity fluctuations along the axis, enhanced inward radial motion, and increased entrainment. All non-circular BBs improve entrainment rate compared to the circular case, with Str-BB yielding the highest increase of more than 7%. Such an increase would be highly significant in reactive configurations, potentially corresponding to a comparable rise in oxidizer transport toward the reaction zone. Additionally, Tri-BB and Str-BB promote more uniform turbulence levels within the recirculation zone, which may help prevent localized hot spots and support stable combustion.

title: Robust optimal formation control for fixed-wing UAVs with external disturbances via reinforcement learning: Theory and experiment
Autonomous multi-site sampling on asteroids via landmark rehearsal-aware hopping trajectory planning
Impact of data dimensionality reduction on vibration-based structural health monitoring for flexible satellites
abstract: Sensing approaches based on compressed data have been studied and applied in Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) for data acquisition and analysis. However, their use in the space domain remains relatively unexplored. This study investigates the Symbolic Aggregate approXimation (SAX) technique as a data compression method in structural damage identification for space systems. The SAX-based approach transforms raw time series data into symbolic representations, significantly reducing data dimensionality. This compression is adopted to retain critical information in vibration signals while shortening the input sequence length. Applied to a spacecraft scenario featuring large solar panels monitored by distributed accelerometers, the method demonstrates enhanced classification performance compared to a prior benchmark in a more challenging multi-class damage identification problem. The data reduction is evaluated in combination with bi-LSTM, GRU and TCN network architectures to assess the robustness of the SHM approach across different models, highlighting the dual benefits of improving damage identification accuracy and computational efficiency during training.

An analysis of engine nacelle compartment leak and explosion hazards for a hydrogen-fuelled aircraft
abstract: The introduction of hydrogen as a fuel source in aircraft poses significant design and safety challenges, particularly regarding the consequences of hydrogen leaks in confined engine nacelle compartments. This study presents a detailed CFD-based analysis of hydrogen leak dispersion and explosion hazards in a simplified annular nacelle geometry, addressing a critical gap in aviation safety knowledge. STAR-CCM+ was used to simulate hydrogen dispersion, examining the influence of leak location, orientation, mass flow rate, and ventilation rate on the formation of flammable gas regions. FLACS-CFD was employed to predict explosion overpressures resulting from ignition of stoichiometric hydrogen-air mixtures. The work provides original contributions to hydrogen safety in aviation by quantifying tolerable leak limits and ventilation requirements, demonstrating that air-based ventilation alone may be insufficient for managing larger leaks. The results show that even small hydrogen leaks (> 0.1 g/s) can form flammable clouds capable of producing hazardous overpressures, especially under turbulent or congested conditions. Explosion simulations revealed that a 1 g stoichiometric (29.5% v/v) hydrogen-air cloud (occupying ∼1% of the 3.8 m 3 compartment volume) can exceed tolerable overpressure thresholds (> 0.1 barg) unless large pressure relief vents are used. The potential impact of the findings is to offer guidance for the safety design, certification, and regulatory development of future hydrogen-fuelled aircraft engine powerplants.

title: Safe path planning for fixed‑wing UAVs in dynamic urban wind fields
Element-level finite-element-informed machine-learning surrogates for failure-index prediction in a composite wing box with intralaminar damage
abstract: This study develops and numerically assesses finite-element-informed machine-learning surrogates for predicting five classical failure indices in a composite wing-box substructure containing prescribed intralaminar stiffness degradation. A damage-oriented database is generated by varying damage position, extent, and intensity over rib, skin, and spar regions of an equivalent-orthotropic finite-element model. Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and a multilayer perceptron are trained and evaluated using a common data-partitioning and cross-validation framework, with separate attention to the upper end of the failure-index range. The tree-based ensembles consistently outperform the neural-network benchmark; the Max Stress index is the most accurately reproduced, whereas the Christensen index and spar-dominated cases remain more difficult, particularly for failure-index values above 0.7. The results establish the feasibility of rapid numerical screening within the adopted model assumptions.
