Numerical study of particle-gas choked flow in dense-phase powder conveying
abstract: Maintaining dense-phase gas–solid choked flow at the outlet of a powder delivery system is crucial for the efficient and stable operation of powder-fed engines. In this study, a coupled computational fluid dynamics–discrete element method (CFD–DEM) approach is employed to simulate the two-phase flow in the choked nozzle outlet region, aiming to elucidate the underlying transport mechanisms. The results reveal the existence of a maximum particle mass flow rate in the two-phase choked transport regime, which corresponds to an accumulation-controlled regime that is independent of the incoming flow conditions and enables more efficient and stable delivery. Significant inter‐phase and intra‐phase non‐uniformities are observed in both velocity and particle distribution. Notably, these non‐uniformities emerge before the nozzle throat, contradicting the homogeneous flow assumption commonly used in flow rate predictions. Compared to a straight pipe of equivalent diameter, an appropriately designed downstream expansion angle enhances the maximum mass flow rate by increasing the particle velocity near the throat, while also improving the solid‐to‐gas mass flow ratio and flow stability. The effect of increasing upstream gas pressure on the mass flow rate is similar across different expansion angles; however, a straight pipe configuration amplifies flow instability under high‐pressure conditions. By elucidating these governing mechanisms, this study advances the fundamental understanding of dense-phase choked flow and provides engineering‐oriented insights for the optimization of powder delivery systems.

Assessment of blade tip timing data from three novel bladed disk simulators based on a finite element modal model
abstract: The emergence of blade tip timing (BTT) data simulators, providing timing samples from their known blade tip vibration output, has been primarily driven by the necessity of developing and evaluating BTT signal processing algorithms, avoiding costly experimental set-ups. Apart from the realism required of its mathematical model, the simulator is required to produce data from all blades, and various configurations of probes, in feasible time frames, including the effect of axial deformation on the timing data. It should also have the capability to produce data with errors comparable to speed-dependent noise in real data. The novel contribution of this paper is the presentation of three novel bladed-disk simulators that address these requirements, and their validation in a novel type of study that considers all blades of an aero-engine compressor, and which uses a commercial BTT software package to process the data and identify an excited blade mode-family member. Simulated data with speed-dependent errors amounting to 10% noise-to-signal ratio are successfully processed, resulting in mean errors of 2.4%, 0.15% in resonant amplitude and frequency across the blades. The simulated BTT data are shown to correctly distinguish between two excited mode-pair members differing by just 1% in natural frequency. Correlation with experimental BTT data is also presented.

Aerodynamic interference in multi-propeller-wing configurations: A UVLM-based decoupling analysis of time-averaged and unsteady loads
abstract: This paper presents a unified aerodynamic interference framework based on the Unsteady Vortex Lattice Method (UVLM) to quantify the complex coupling effects in multi-propeller-wing configurations of distributed propulsion systems. By incorporating numerical interference switches, the framework systematically isolates the contributions of propeller slipstream, wing-induced upwash, and inter-propeller interactions. The method's accuracy is validated against wind tunnel data and high-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). Application to a multi-propeller-wing array demonstrates that a counter-rotating configuration yields superior aerodynamic performance compared to a co-rotating setup, driven by more favorable slipstream interactions. Furthermore, a mechanism decoupling analysis identifies the distinct physical origins of unsteady loads, isolating the primary aerodynamic drivers responsible for wing lift variations and propeller phase synchronization. Ultimately, this framework provides a physics-based, modular tool for the aerodynamic design and optimization of Distributed Electric Propulsion (DEP) systems.

title: Fast prediction of film cooling effectiveness on turbine blades under radiation effects based on regional distribution characteristics
Performance and flow power analysis of ejector-augmented ducted fans
High-fidelity prediction of turbine blade surface temperature fields under sparse measurements using an ensemble gradient-aware attention U-net
abstract: As a key component of aero-engines, turbine blades operate in high-temperature environments for long periods, and their temperature distribution directly affects engine performance and safety. However, in practical engineering, sensor deployment is limited, resulting in sparse collected data. Additionally, in high-gradient regions, the insufficient effective information severely impacts the accuracy and reliability of traditional reconstruction methods. To address the above issues, this paper proposes an end-to-end method for reconstructing the surface temperature field of turbine blades under sparse measurement conditions. This method constructs a unified reconstruction framework consisting of "sparse data input—gradient-aware residual and attention fusion network—gradient-constrained hybrid loss—Bootstrap data augmentation—global temperature field output". By introducing the physical prior of temperature gradients, it synergistically enhances the feature learning of high-gradient regions at both the network structure and loss function levels, while maintaining the smoothness and physical consistency of the global temperature field. The results show that the proposed method can achieve high-fidelity reconstruction of the blade surface temperature field under sparse measurement conditions. The prediction results are highly consistent with high-precision numerical simulations, with the maximum absolute error not exceeding 15 K, and the prediction errors of most measuring points controlled within ±0.2%. Although the maximum absolute error does not exceed 15K, this error value is controlled within the sensitivity threshold that affects the lifetime of engine. Therefore, this predictive model can be reliably used to define the safe operating boundary of the engine, providing a high confidence decision-making basis for the key trade-off between performance optimization and life management, and avoiding performance losses caused by overly conservative design. Compared with traditional reconstruction methods, the maximum prediction error is reduced by approximately 75%. Further ablation analysis verifies that gradient-aware modeling, attention mechanism, and Bootstrap augmentation strategy all play key roles in improving reconstruction accuracy and stability.

title: Validation of icing solution predicted by FENSAP ICE on hexahedral meshes undergoing morphing
abstract: This article summarizes work done in terms of validation of recent capabilities of a commercial-of-the-shelf numerical tool, dedicated for icing simulations, namely, Ansys FENSAP-ICE 2024R1. The basis for validation is the experimental data from icing wind tunnel shared by AIAA as part of the Second Ice Prediction Workshop (IPW-2). This research is focused in particular on multi-shot ice accretion simulation to reproduce 29 minutes of swept wing exposure to icing conditions. Significant effort was put on the fine mesh generation process aiming for topology producing high quality hex elements aligned orthogonally with expected flow paths. Our study consists of two multi-shot analyses to compare an effect of finer time-step duration applied in the sequence, to capture finer development of ice roughness and smaller ice features on clean surface of the skin. In general, predicted ice shapes match, in an average sense – to 3D scans of ice, provided within IPW-2. The ice mass is overestimated by 10% to 25% between shots compared to experimental data. Also, 3D features like ice scallops are not clearly captured with given surface mesh size. Some fine differences exist between sequences using finer and coarser shot time durations applied.

Investigation on reactive jet and ignition performance of a compact pre-combustion igniter
abstract: To provide ground-based fundamental data supporting reliable reignition under extreme high-altitude conditions, this study presents the design and experimental investigation of a compact pre-combustion igniter. A ground-based experimental platform was established to systematically study the spectral characteristics, jet dynamics, and ignition performance of the igniter. Optical emission spectroscopy revealed the generation of abundant active species, including the N₂ second positive band and NO-γ band. The vibrational temperature initially increased, then decreased, and finally stabilized with increasing gas flow rate, reaching a maximum of 12853 K. Jet visualization experiments showed that both jet flame length and stiffness increased notably with gas flow rate, with a maximum increase in jet stiffness of 169%, indicating effective resistance to crossflow interference. Comparative ignition tests showed that at combustor airflow rates of 250 m³/h and 300 m³/h, the pre-combustion igniter reduced ignition delay time by 37.5% and 28.3%, respectively, compared to a conventional spark igniter. Furthermore, the lean ignition limit was extended by an average of 25.97%, with a maximum improvement of 57.06%. The pre-combustion igniter enhances ignition reliability and adaptability through sustained jet flame, injection of active species, and turbulence intensification, demonstrating performance advantages under ground conditions that are qualitatively indicative of its potential for high-altitude applications

Multi-impact lifecycle assessment of innovative powertrain architectures for urban air mobility
abstract: Urban Air Mobility (UAM) emerges as a viable solution for future mobility needs, interesting for highly crowded and congested cities. However, to align with European Union sustainability goals, it is fundamental to investigate and identify the most suitable architecture solutions for this new sector. This study conducts a multi-impact lifecycle assessment of different sustainable architectures. Several drone solutions are sized and evaluated across key environmental categories, considering both current and foreseen scenarios. The work analyses hybrid-electric, full-electric, and hydrogen-based configurations by examining resource utilization, manufacturing, energy/fuel cycles and utilization stages, even fueled with synthetic fuels. Results highlight that e-fuels might decarbonize the sector (achieving reductions of 60–80% relative to electric and green hydrogen fuel cell solutions) but behave worst in other categories, while overall, green hydrogen fuel cell and renewable electricity are the best ones in four out of the five considered categories. These findings sustain the informed design of low-impact UAM solutions aligned with European Union’s sustainability goals.

title: Combining bionic blade design with fluidic oscillators for separation and loss suppression in high-lift low-pressure turbines
Characteristic scale identification of recirculation zone and outlet distribution regulation for a novel triple-swirler combustor
abstract: To bridge the gap in quantifying the relationship between combustor recirculation zone characteristic scales and outlet temperature fields, this study proposes a three-dimensional identification method based on ellipsoid equivalence. By quantitatively extracting characteristic length, width, and height via cross-section analysis, a correlation between the recirculation zone vortex core scale and temperature uniformity is established. Investigations on a novel triple-swirler combustor demonstrate that a radial angle of γ=60° maximizes the characteristic height, significantly enhancing radial mixing and heat diffusion. This configuration optimizes uniformity, reducing the OTDF and RTDF to 0.20 and 0.09, respectively. It is revealed that the characteristic length controls the high-temperature zone's axial position, the height regulates the radial temperature gradient, and the width dictates circumferential uniformity. Optimal exit temperature distribution therefore requires coordinated control of the three-dimensional recirculation-zone scales, maintaining a compact axial structure while appropriately expanding the radial and circumferential scales. This study provides a quantitative theoretical framework and an engineering-oriented solution for precise control of combustor exit temperature distributions.

title: Context-aware Koopman stochastic MPC for spacecraft attitude control with time-varying inertia
abstract: When a servicing spacecraft captures a non-cooperative target, the combined spacecraft undergoes abrupt inertia changes that are poorly known a priori.Such uncertainty complicates enforcing attitude keep-out zone (KOZ) constraints, which protect sensitive sensors from bright celestial objects.Probabilistic constraint enforcement can reduce the conservatism of worst-case guarantees while maintaining a prescribed safety level; however, evaluating chance constraints through nonlinear dynamics in real time remains computationally demanding.This paper introduces a context-aware Koopman stochastic model predictive control (CAK-SMPC) approach. A Mamba-based context encoder continuously encodes recent state–input history into a context vector, enabling rapid adaptation to time-varying inertia without explicit system identification or online retraining. Conditioned on this representation, a Koopman variational autoencoder lifts the nonlinear dynamics into a latent space that evolves linearly within each control horizon. The resulting linearity enables closed-form Gaussian covariance propagation, reducing KOZ chance-constraint tightening to a convex quadratic program solvable in real time.In 500 Monte Carlo trials under both fixed and time-varying inertia, CAK-SMPC achieves near-zero KOZ violation rates with worst-case computation times well within the control period, whereas four baseline methods incur substantial violations under model mismatch.

title: Accuracy assessment of noise prediction of propellers via numerical simulation, analytical methods, and experimental campaigns
abstract: This work focuses on the assessment of the accuracy of numerical predictions and experimental campaigns on providing aerodynamic characteristics and acoustic emissions of an isolated benchmark propeller. An experimental campaign is carried out with a benchmark model low-Reynolds propeller (89,000 tip Reynolds number) of 0.3 m diameter operating at high RPM, equivalent of a tip-Mach number ($M_t$) of 0.37 and an advance ratio ($J$) of 0.4. Measurements are conducted in the anechoic A-Tunnel, an open test-section wind tunnel, confined by an anechoic chamber. Simulations are carried out with the commercial software PowerFLOW and aimed at reproducing the propeller geometry and conditions. BEMT-based noise estimations are also carried out and used as reference results for the discussion. The study focuses on the assessment of uncertainties of the experimental campaign, and the current accuracy of numerical and analytical predictions, creating a complete picture of the discrepancies expected in similar setups when predicting and experimenting with propeller noise along with the potential sources of errors. Results point to the accuracy of the three methodologies in assessing the overall noise emissions. This follows the precise description of the integral aerodynamic loads on the propeller and the dominant first tonal components of the noise signature. Similarly, the velocity field obtained from the methodologies compares well. Nevertheless, precise descriptions and measurements of the higher harmonics of the tonal emissions and of the broadband noise levels are still lacking and demonstrate the need for improved experimental and numerical methodologies to allow accurate cross-validation between the methodologies.

Enabling large-scale Newton–Krylov turbomachinery aerodynamic analysis through subspace recycling
Coupled heat transfer with pyrolysis and flow matching of ammonia/kerosene in double-layer regenerative cooling channels
Robust prediction of aircraft aerodynamic loads with quantified uncertainty
abstract: Accurate prediction of external aircraft loads before and during flight testing is critical to ensure safety and reduce the need for costly test repetitions. Advances in sensor technologies allow for real-time collection of structural health data from numerous points on the aircraft. The load data are autocorrelated and include structural noise due to aircraft vibrations, especially during high-speed high-angle-of-attack maneuvers, aspects that are often dismissed in the literature. Prior studies on aircraft load prediction mainly remove noise from flight data to improve model accuracy. To address these shortcomings, we model both the denoised load signal and structural noise to capture the full range of load envelopes during test flights. To this end, first load signals are denoised and the performance of time agnostic machine learning models (Elastic Net and Random Forest) and a time-aware deep learning model (Gated Recurrent Unit with Multilayer Perceptron (GRU-MLP)) are compared. Next, the boundaries of structured noise components and transient spikes are modeled using quantile regression. This two-prong approach provides both point estimates and uncertainty-aware load envelopes that bound the full range of possible load behaviors. The results show that the best model in capturing load is GRU-MLP, capturing approximately 95% and 90% of two load components predicted: bending moment and torsion. Additionally, the nominal 80% predicted noise boundaries empirically cover 85% of the actual data with a tight interval width of 1 z-score unit. Modeling the load and noise separately and simultaneously provides greater transparency on average and transitional loads in test flights, where both the nominal behavior and variability are essential.

Quantum annealing–based black-box optimization for aerodynamic shape design
abstract: This study proposes a topology optimization framework for aerodynamic shape design based on FMQA (factorization machine with quantum annealing). To address the limited capability of existing topology optimization in exploring global optima, this study aims to enhance global search performance by incorporating quantum annealing. In FMQA, machine learning is used to construct a combinatorial optimization model that is solved by quantum annealing. The proposed method is applied to the optimization of a single-element airfoil, and both QUBO (quadratic unconstrained binary optimization) and Ising formulations are investigated. The results show that the Ising model outperforms the QUBO model due to its higher learnability in machine learning. The effect of regularization is also examined, demonstrating that it suppresses overfitting and leads to smoother, physically meaningful geometries. The optimal geometry includes a Gurney flap-like structure at the trailing edge, which significantly improves aerodynamic performance. The results highlight the potential of the proposed FMQA-based topology optimization framework for discovering high-performance and non-intuitive aerodynamic designs.

title: Modeling of three-dimensional probabilistic sand rebound in aero-engine sand protection systems
Numerical investigation on fuel jet mixing control and ignition in supersonic cavity combustor based on plasma energy deposition
abstract: Under supersonic conditions, the short residence time poses challenges, such as inadequate fuel mixing, ignition difficulty and poor flame stability, in the scramjet engine. This puts forward new demands for flow control technologies. The mixing control and ignition process of a rear-wall ethylene jet in supersonic cavity combustor are numerically investigated based on two types of plasma actuators, namely direct current discharge (DCD) actuator and laser energy deposition (ED) actuator. Results indicate that DCD actuator placed on the lower wall facilitates the fuel transport toward the cavity front wall and prolongs the residence time, whereas it exhibits opposing effects when placed on the upper wall. ED actuator located within the cavity enhances fuel transport to the front wall and extends the residence time, demonstrating greater flexibility in flow control. A single-pulse laser energy deposition located inside the cavity successfully ignites the ethylene-air mixture, which undergoes sequential processes of flame kernel propagation and quenching, reignition, and stable non-premixed shear-layer combustion.

title: Asymmetric nozzle guide vane pair design for high-pressure turbine aerothermal performance
abstract: To reduce the aerothermal penalties caused by lean-burn combustor exit distortions, this study proposes an asymmetric nozzle guide vane (NGV) pair design where adjacent vanes are independently shaped. For a practical 1:2 combustor-to-NGV ratio, this method allows for localized control of inlet hot streaks and residual swirl, which directly affects convective heat transfer and aerodynamic losses. Unsteady CFD simulations of the NGV–rotor coupling using the HYDRA solver show that tangential lean asymmetry shifts the exit pressure and temperature fields, helping to prevent the radial migration of hot fluid towards the casing. As a result, thermal loading in the casing region and heat flux at the rotor tip leading-edge are reduced, despite a slight increase in heat transfer through the NGV passage. At the stage level, this redistribution results in an improvement of around 0.5 % in non-adiabatic efficiency under positive swirl conditions, increasing to nearly 1.8 % when the swirl orientation is reversed. These findings confirm that asymmetric vane pairing is an effective passive method for managing heat-transfer redistribution and enhancing aerothermal performance under realistic combustor inflow conditions, thereby broadening the design options for next-generation high-pressure turbine optimization.

title: High-precision three-dimensional full-scale deployable testing methodology for thrust pointing assembly mechanism

Geometry-aware, CAD-free, and differentiable closed-form surrogates for lifting surface mass estimation via symbolic regression with autonomous similarity scaling
abstract: Accurate structural mass estimation of lifting surfaces is required throughout aircraft design, yet existing methods cannot simultaneously provide closed-form geometric descriptors, physically consistent similarity scaling, and exact differentiability without repeated three-dimensional geometry instantiation. This work presents a symbolic-regression (SR) framework for segment-level mass estimation of solid, skin-laminated, shell, and wing-box lifting surfaces, using external surface area and enclosed volume as governing mass descriptors and quasi-analytical rib and spar volume expressions for internal contributions. A parameterized wing-segment dataset was generated in OpenVSP over the 2–25 kg MTOW range, consistent with harmonized UAV regulatory frameworks, using planform variables and Class–Shape Transformation airfoil coefficients to cover the admissible geometric envelope. From this database, closed-form SR models and a Bayesian-optimized deep neural network (DNN) benchmark were trained on identical data partitions, with compact reduced models subsequently derived via partial-elasticity analysis. The SR models provide CAD-free, closed-form, and exactly differentiable surrogate equations, with dimensional-homogeneity filtering on the Pareto front enforcing physically consistent similarity scaling, recovering dimensional laws autonomously—without repeated geometry instantiation. Full SR surrogates achieved R 2 ≥ 0.9997, while elasticity-guided reduced models preserved R 2 ≥ 0.9994. In external validation over CAD-reconstructed aircraft spanning 1.9–3, 629 kg, SR yielded mean segment-level errors of 1.80 % for surface area and 0.96 % for enclosed volume, outperforming the DNN (1.84 % and 1.61 %) while reducing evaluation time by up to 63 × . Reduced models achieved mean errors below 1.40 %, and quasi-analytical internal estimates remained below 3.64 %. Experimental validation on the fabricated Fénix UAV wing confirmed a total mass error of 2.74 %, with component-level errors below 3.80 %.

title: Development of state-space propeller aeromechanical models for substructuring and control
abstract: This paper presents an efficient formulation for developing propeller aeromechanical models in state-space form, enabling their integration into dynamic substructuring frameworks and facilitating control system design. Propellers are modeled with rigid blades under axial-symmetric flow conditions, accounting for both inertial and unsteady aerodynamic forces. The latter are computed in the frequency domain using a vortex particle method and subsequently recast in the time domain via Rogers’ rational function approximation, yielding a compact set of aerodynamic lag states. The resulting framework supports rapid aeroelastic analyses of eVTOL configurations with multiple propulsors, while also allowing integration of control inputs such as collective pitch and rotational speed. The methodology is validated through the whirl flutter analysis of a propeller–pylon system and the stability assessment of a wing with distributed electric propulsion. Results show excellent agreement with reference solutions, with discrepancies below 3% in the whirl flutter stability maps and below 2% in the predicted flutter speed and frequency of the wing configuration. Finally, as a proof-of-concept demonstrating compatibility with aeroservoelastic analysis, an active flutter-suppression system based on thrust modulation of multiple propellers is developed, effectively stabilizing the system at critical flutter conditions and restoring the nominal trim state.

Closed-form unsteady thin-airfoil theory for high-amplitude problems
abstract: A closed-form formulation for unsteady forces on airfoils experiencing massive flow separation is highly sought after due to its relevance in various engineering applications. This study presents an explicit unsteady thin-airfoil theory for massively separated flows. The proposed formulation incorporates a critical leading-edge suction parameter (LESP) directly into the explicit Theodorsen/Wagner vortex-sheet framework, thereby extending closed-form unsteady thin-airfoil theory to massively separated flows while retaining its analytical nature. Once the critical LESP is reached, the LESP is assumed to remain constant until flow reattachment. We validate the theory against experimentally measured unsteady forces reported in the literature for four kinematic families undergoing large-amplitude motions with massive flow separation. The inclusion of the critical LESP substantially improves the prediction accuracy compared with the conventional formulation, particularly in separated-flow conditions. The theoretical predictions are analyzed in the context of measured forces and flow visualizations to interpret the underlying physical mechanisms governing unsteady force generation.

A locally validated surrogate-assisted design strategy for a hypersonic waverider under coupled aerodynamic and aerothermal constraints
abstract: Hypersonic waverider design requires aerodynamic efficiency and aerothermal feasibility tobe resolved within a coupled and physically interpretable framework. This study presents abounded local design investigation for a hypersonic waverider at Mach 10, 30 km altitude,and 𝛼 = 4◦, using a physics-based evaluation chain, local design-space refinement, target specificsurrogate modeling, and post-optimization full-physics reevaluation. The local problem is defined by four geometric variables: shock angle 𝛽, width-to-length ratio 𝑊∕𝐿, leading edgeradius 𝑟𝑙𝑒, and shaping exponent 𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟. The results show that 𝛽 and 𝑊∕𝐿 act primarily as aerodynamic performance drivers, whereas 𝑟𝑙𝑒 acts mainly as a thermal-feasibility variable with only weak influence on 𝐿∕𝐷 over the examined local range. The best feasible solution is boundary-controlled rather than interior, occurring near the upper bounds of 𝛽, 𝑊∕𝐿, and 𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟 , and near the smallest thermally admissible value of 𝑟𝑙𝑒. Two final reference designs are retained: a peak feasible point and a recommended nominal point. The nominal design preserves nearly the same aerodynamic efficiency as the peak feasible design while increasing the thermal margin from 0.19 to 4.04 W/cm2. A local surrogate framework trained only within the trusted four-dimensional design box reproduces the optimizer-relevant structure of the problem under random hold-out, blocked hold-out, and post-opt reevaluation. Both retained reference points are also shown to remain within the admissible hypersonic flight corridor. These results establish a physically interpretable and locally validated surrogate-assisted design strategy for hypersonic waverider development under coupled aerodynamic and aerothermal constraints.

title: Saturation-predictable prescribed performance hierarchical control for fly-around formation via secure distributed and edge-based event-triggered mechanisms
abstract: In light of the critical role of multi-spacecraft fly-around formations for observing non-cooperative targets, ensuring robust control under input saturation, communication delays, and false data injection (FDI) attacks remains a pivotal challenge. To address these issues, this paper develops a saturation-predictable prescribed performance hierarchical control scheme via secure distributed and edge-based event-triggered mechanisms. The main advantages of the proposed framework include a proactive performance boundary expansion mechanism driven by a dynamic multi-reservoir echo state network (DMESN), which inherently prevents singularity risks caused by abrupt actuator saturation. Furthermore, a hierarchical anti-disturbance strategy, incorporating confidence factors and predictive delay compensation, successfully isolates FDI attacks and curbs disturbance propagation. Finally, an edge-based self-triggered protocol ensures geometric rigidity while significantly alleviating communication burdens without requiring continuous state monitoring. Both numerical simulations and semi-physical air-bearing robot (ABR) experiments are performed for effectiveness verification.

Reliable buckling load prediction for Ariane 6 test article: Experimental validation of the vibration correlation technique
abstract: The recent progress of the vibration correlation technique (VCT) has consolidated its viability as a non-destructive experimental procedure for determining the in situ buckling load of unstiffened and skin-dominated stiffened downscaled cylindrical shells. Building on this foundation, the present paper aims to further validate the technique for full-scale, qualification-relevant applications, assessing its robustness in the context of design-proof testing of launcher structures. The specimen investigated is a full-scale launcher tank barrel, representative of the lower section of the hydrogen tank of Ariane 6’s first stage. The barrel, composed of four aluminum panels welded together, was tested for buckling at IMA Dresden under the coordination of MT Aerospace AG (MTA) as part of Ariane 6 structural qualification campaign. The experimental campaign involved the first application of the VCT to full-scale buckling tests with combined axial–bending loads, carried out in two configurations: (1) using three out of four actuators evenly spaced around the circumference, and (2) using two actuators from the same setup. For each configuration, non-contact vibration measurements were taken at various load levels. These measured natural frequency variations, along with linear buckling loads obtained from finite element (FE) models, were used to evaluate the robustness and practical applicability of the VCT. The experimental results confirm VCT as a reliable non-destructive technique for estimating the buckling load of imperfection-sensitive, full-scale cylindrical shells. To complement the experimental investigations, a numerical framework is proposed, employing high-fidelity FE models with stochastic, Fourier-based imperfections and realistic loading via a UAMP subroutine in Abaqus, enabling reliable buckling predictions even in the absence of measured imperfection data.

Reinforcement learning-based multi-objective control of aerospace electro-hydrostatic actuators
abstract: Due to the inherent trade-off among high-accuracy tracking, fast dynamic response, and high efficiency, improving the overall control performance of variable pump displacement and variable motor speed (VPVM) driven electro-hydrostatic actuator (EHA) systems remains challenging. This paper proposes a reinforcement learning (RL) based data-driven control strategy for VPVM systems to achieve an adaptive balance among these conflicting objectives without relying on a fully identified high-fidelity system model. A conventional proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controller is adopted as a baseline safety controller to ensure feasible and robust operation. Building on this baseline, an actor–critic RL framework based on value-iteration Q-learning is introduced to learn an online flow-allocation strategy. The learned policy autonomously coordinates motor speed and pump displacement, enabling a favorable compromise between high-precision trajectory tracking, fast dynamic response, and reduced motor thermal load. System-level properties of the proposed controller are analyzed, establishing Bellman suboptimality and convergence of the approximate value function. Extensive experiments conducted on a VPVM test bench under steady-state, dynamic, and load-spectrum operating conditions validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that, compared with conventional control strategies, the proposed approach significantly reduces motor current and heat generation while maintaining high control accuracy and favorable dynamic response, thereby improving overall system efficiency.

title: Deformation reconstruction and optimal strain sensor placement for mesh antennas using RBF interpolation and QR decomposition dimensionality reduction
Learning aerodynamic optimization of three-dimensional high-lift configurations based on reinforcement learning in two-dimensional flow field environment
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated significant potential for learning and leveraging experience in aerodynamic design optimization. Through extensive agent-environment interactions, generalizable optimization policies can be acquired. However, applying RL to three-dimensional (3D) aerodynamic optimization remains challenging due to the high computational cost of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) during training. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel RL-based 2D-to-3D framework that trains an optimization policy in a low-cost 2D CFD environment and directly deploys it to 3D high-lift configurations. The policy is trained using the Double Deep Q-Network algorithm, requiring only 483 samples of 2D aerodynamic data. Velocity field features are extracted through Two-Directional Two-Dimensional Principal Component Analysis to provide physical information for the agent’s decision-making. This physics-informed policy learning strategy underlies the generalizability of the learned policy across various flow conditions and its direct application to 3D configurations without further learning. While the optimal design parameters can differ substantially between 2D and 3D configurations, the velocity field features linked to aerodynamic performance, which have been learned by the agent in 2D environment, show remarkable similarity when both configurations attain their optimal states. Results show that the proposed framework efficiently trains an optimization policy applicable to various 3D high-lift configurations at minimal computational cost. The policy exhibits high efficiency and strong generalizability in optimizing both 2D and 3D high-lift configurations under varying flow conditions, flap deflections, and wing planforms.

title: Aeroacoustic analysis of tip-joined blade propeller
abstract: This study presents an experimental aeroacoustic investigation of a tip-joined blade (TJB) propeller, compared with 2- and 4-bladed configurations under identical operating conditions and matched thrust. The influence of blade azimuthal angles (30 ∘ , 60 ∘ , and 90 ∘ ) was also analyzed to precisely quantify the acoustic benefits of the TJB propeller. Experiments were conducted in an anechoic wind tunnel to quantify and separate tonal and broadband contributions in the acoustic spectra at various radiation angles. At 4,000 rpm and an advance ratio of J = 0.4 , the TJB produced equivalent thrust to the baseline 2-bladed propeller, with only a 2.8% difference. Under these conditions, it exhibited the strongest first tonal peak at 133 Hz, 2 dB higher than the baseline propeller, while broadband noise above 9 kHz was the lowest among all configurations. The TJB, with slightly reduced propulsive efficiency (56.7% for the 4-bladed 90 ∘ to 54.5% for the TJB), showed the highest tonal overall sound pressure levels (OASPL) across all directivity angles. This behavior is attributed to aerodynamic interactions between the forward and rearward blade segments, similar to the scissor 4-bladed 30 ∘ configuration, which also displayed elevated tonal levels. However, the broadband levels of the TJB remained lower than those of the 4-bladed configurations and comparable to the 2-bladed propeller. These trends are associated with reduced trailing-edge noise resulting from the sweeping of the blade elements necessary to form the joined-blade structure. Overall, the results indicate that the TJB propeller provides broadband noise reduction benefits, despite no observed advantage in tonal noise.

title: Experimental and numerical investigation of the benefits of serrated trailing edges on an axial compressor
Aeroelastic analysis of propeller blades near stall
abstract: Modern electric vertical take off and landing aircraft concepts are pushing propellers into operating regimes that have high disk-loading and at the same time they are required to be more efficient and quieter, in order to operate in large numbers and in densely populated areas. A solution to do this is to make the blade sections thinner. However, these thinner blades are likely more susceptible to stall flutter. Previous work by Higgins, has shown that more propeller research is needed in an experimental and simulation capacity. Many of the known studies were conducted pre-war and the results are not relevant to modern propeller designs. This research considers a composite modern set of propeller designs and examines the stall flutter behaviour that takes place. In this work 3D finite element models are used to represent the blade structure and a modal approach is adapted for coupled fluid structure interactions. The scale adaptive simulation turbulence model is employed to provide a better representation of the stalled flow behaviour, which is typically lacking in lesser fidelity studies. This work is in agreement with experimental studies and suggests that the stalled flow forces the blade to oscillate about its modal frequencies. To the best of our knowledge, such simulations have not yet been reported in open literature.

Orbital-structural coupling effects in tethered space systems using unified elastic dynamic modeling
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of accurately predicting the strongly coupled orbital and structural dynamics of tethered space systems, such as momentum exchange tethers and tethered spacecraft formation flying. Conventional modeling approaches typically rely on artificial rigid-flexible partitioning between spacecraft and tethers, complex interface constraints, and non-physical coordinate transformations, which hinder their ability to simultaneously capture elastic tether deformation, spacecraft structural dynamics, orbital motion, and environmental disturbances within a unified framework. To overcome these limitations, a high-fidelity unified elastic dynamic modeling approach based on the Nodal Position Finite Element Method (NPFEM) is proposed. By expressing all kinetic and potential (gravitational and elastic) energies exclusively in terms of finite element nodal positions, the proposed framework preserves elasticity in both the spacecraft and tether while eliminating explicit separation of rigid-body variables and complex interface constraints. Orbital disturbance effects are directly and consistently incorporated at the element level with nodal position information, allowing the governing equations to be assembled directly from individual contributions. Rigid-body motion and elastic deformation of spacecraft and tethers are subsequently reconstructed algorithmically from the nodal state for physical interpretation. The proposed modeling framework is validated through three representative tether mission scenarios, including a tether system in its local vertical, a momentum exchange tether and a hub-spoke tether formation. The results demonstrate robust capability in capturing strongly coupled orbital–structural interactions and critical transient responses in large-scale tethered systems, thereby enabling higher-fidelity analysis and supporting design automation for applications such as momentum exchange, formation flying, and space debris removal.

Artificial neural network fine-tuning to increase accuracy of low-thrust space trajectory cost approximators
abstract: The use of artificial neural networks (ANNs) to approximate the cost (propellant mass or time of flight) of low-thrust trajectories has become increasingly prevalent in recent years, outperforming other methods such as analytical approximations or shape-based approaches both in CPU time and accuracy. An ANN requires a set of data on which it is to be trained—in the case of low-thrust trajectory approximators this is produced by pre-optimising a large number of trajectories between randomly generated orbits. Whilst this number is substantially smaller than the total number of trajectories that the ANN will approximate in its usage period, the computational cost associated with generating this training database is still significant (typically many days). This paper proposes that instead of generating a large dataset of optimal trajectories as in a conventional method, the ANN can first be pretrained on a large dataset of sub-optimal trajectories (‘low-resolution’ model) that can be produced very quickly. Once pretrained on this sup-optimal database, a small number of optimal trajectories (the ‘high-resolution’ model that ultimately needs to be approximated) can be generated and the pretrained ANN is fine-tuned on this small dataset. It is shown that such an approach enables reaching a high accuracy of fit to the high-accuracy trajectories in a significantly shorter time than if the ANN were trained directly on them with no pretraining.

A hybrid AI framework for hypersonic flow physics: Bridging experiments and numerical simulations
abstract: The characterization of hypersonic flow physics in high-enthalpy regimes is one of the crucial challenges in fluid dynamics, where strong thermochemical non-equilibrium effects, steep gradients, and extreme flow conditions significantly limit both experimental and numerical approaches. Experimental campaigns in facilities such as SPES (Small Planetary Entry Simulator) provide valuable insights into these complex physical phenomena, but are inherently limited by sparse spatial resolution and measurement noise. On the other hand, high-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations can resolve detailed flow physics, yet their high computational cost severely restricts their use across wide parametric spaces. To address these limitations, this work introduces a hybrid Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework based on Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) for reconstructing key hypersonic flow field quantities from limited and heterogeneous datasets. The approach combines high-fidelity CFD data with experimental measurements obtained at the SPES facility of the University of Naples Federico II, enabling a physically consistent integration between numerical and experimental representations of the flow. Validation on unseen cases demonstrates that the proposed model accurately predicts the main thermochemical quantities, achieving errors within a ± 10% range. These results highlight the potential of physics-driven, data-integrated AI models as efficient tools for analyzing complex hypersonic flow physics, as well as for supporting the design and optimization of future experimental campaigns.

Improved stability-based transition transport model for airships incorporating wall heating effects
abstract: Laminar drag reduction is a critical technology for enhancing the endurance and station-keeping capabilities of airship platforms. However, existing transport-based transition models fail to account for the premature transition induced by wall heating, a limitation that significantly hinders the robust engineering application of laminar-flow technology in realistic thermal environments.To address this deficiency, this study first develops stability-based correction for transition modeling that explicitly incorporates wall-to-freestream temperature ratios. Leveraging the Falkner--Skan--Cooke (FSC) equations and linear stability theory (LST) with the $e^N$ method, we derive physics-based correlations for the transition criteria as functions of the temperature ratio, pressure gradient, and turbulence intensity. These corrections are integrated into a simplified stability-based transition transport model proposed by \citet{franccois2023simplified} and validated against the classic Schubauer and Klebanoff flat-plate experiments, demonstrating accurate prediction of transition locations under adiabatic, heated, and cooled conditions. Crucially, wind-tunnel experiments on a heated airship model show that wall-heating sensitivity is strongly influenced by local pressure-gradient variations, which is due to Reynolds-number-driven transition-location shifts. The proposed model successfully reproduces the experimentally observed transition advancement caused by wall heating. This framework, covering both heating and cooling regimes, provides a capability to support future laminar-flow control technologies based on wall-temperature modulation.

Surrogate-based constrained optimization of camber-morphing airfoils: Onset location as a design variable and quantification of adaptive versus robust morphing strategies
abstract: Camber morphing offers a continuous and seamless alternative to hinged control surfaces for improving airfoil aerodynamic efficiency across varying flight conditions. Despite extensive study of morphing amplitude as an optimization variable, the chordwise onset location, the point along the chord at which camber deformation begins, is almost universally treated as a fixed structural parameter rather than a co-optimized design variable. Furthermore, the pitching-moment change induced by morphing, which directly constrains longitudinal trim authority, is rarely enforced as an explicit inequality constraint during optimization. To the best of the authors' knowledge, no prior study has simultaneously treated chordwise onset location and morphing amplitude as co-optimized variables under a hard stability constraint while quantifying the aerodynamic trade-off between adaptive and robust morphing strategies. This work addresses that gap through a surrogate-based constrained optimization framework in which both morphing amplitude and chordwise onset location are continuous design variables subject to |ΔCm| ≤ 0.04. In the most favorable case, adaptive morphing increases the NACA 2412 lift-to-drag ratio from 40.6 to 101.5 (ΔL/D = 60.9, +150%) relative to the unmorphed baseline, while all reported percentage gains are accompanied by their corresponding absolute L/D values. Transition SST CFD validation at Re = 10⁶ confirms the selected optima to within 6.0%, and four additional Re = 10⁵ adaptive-optimum simulations agree with the XFOIL/RBF reference within 2.8–5.8%. Averaged over the four Re = 10⁶ conditions at CFD fidelity, the mean per-condition L/D gain of the adaptive strategy over the fixed robust configuration, defined here as the adaptability value, reaches 18.3%, with a maximum of 38.1% at α = 2° Critically, the robust configuration degrades L/D by 20.7% below the unmorphed baseline at α = 6°, demonstrating that a fixed morphing preset can actively harm high-incidence performance. These findings establish chordwise onset location as a consequential aerodynamic design variable and provide a physically grounded basis for evaluating when adaptive morphing is justified under stability constraints.

title: CASPEX: An end-to-end causal–physics explainable framework for trustworthy spacecraft health monitoring
abstract: Future spacecraft increasingly depend on onboard autonomy to ensure reliable operation under limited communication, complex subsystem interactions, and strict computational constraints. Effective health management must therefore provide not only early anomaly detection but also physically consistent root-cause diagnosis at the subsystem level. However, existing approaches either lack fault propagation awareness or produce diagnostic outputs that are not consistent with spacecraft dynamics. This paper presents CASPEX, a real-time causal–physics framework for autonomous spacecraft health monitoring. The proposed architecture integrates anomaly detection, dynamic causal graph learning, and physics-consistent attribution within a unified onboard pipeline to identify fault origin, propagation pathways, and subsystem-level impacts. A dual-module design supports low-latency intervention-aware diagnosis for isolated faults and detailed causal–physics analysis for complex multi-fault conditions. The framework is validated using high-fidelity multivariate telemetry generated in the Basilisk simulation environment, covering reaction wheel, power, and attitude control subsystems across single- and multi-satellite scenarios. Results show reliable identification of upstream fault sources, a 38–52% reduction in non-physical diagnostic attributions, and improved consistency with system behaviour. The operational module executes within 47–69 ms and the detailed analysis within 150–210 ms on a Cortex-A72 processor, demonstrating real-time onboard feasibility. The proposed approach provides physically grounded, interpretable, and computationally efficient fault diagnosis, supporting trustworthy autonomous operation for next-generation spacecraft and distributed satellite systems.

abstract: Significant research has addressed solar-sail transfers in heliocentric settings, whereas planet-centered transfers have received comparatively little attention. However, most solar-sail missions flown to date have operated in Earth-centered orbits and are likely to continue to do so, highlighting the importance of planet-centered sailing in the future of this new and promising technology. This work fully characterizes the co-planar multi-revolution circular-to-circular (MC2C) transfers, which enable motion between co-planar circular orbits and are therefore regarded as one of the “simplest” possible planet-centered solar-sail transfers. Using an indirect optimization approach, the performance of the MC2C transfers (i.e., achieved radius change in a fixed transfer time) is computed for various initial sun-orbit geometries. As a result, the best and worst transfer geometries (which depend on the illumination conditions of the orbital plane) are identified, enabling the construction of the performance envelopes that relate radius change to transfer time. These envelopes provide a simple graphical tool to obtain such metrics without having to optimize a single trajectory, greatly enhancing the workflow during early mission design. Through dimensional analysis, the envelopes are generalized to any sail design and any planet in the solar system, greatly broadening their applicability. Finally, the explanation of the physical mechanisms behind the best and worst geometries is provided through new concepts that are unique to solar sailing, like the “growth vector”. This explanation lies the foundation for the study of future, more complex planet-centered solar-sail transfers.

abstract: Based on the research background of high-performance distributed electric propulsion (DEP) fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), a data-driven aerodynamic modeling method is developed to address the design challenges of propulsion/aerodynamic coupling in the distributed propulsion wing (DPW) configuration which fully integrates the distributed propulsors and wing surfaces. To overcome the issues of limited data and insufficient understanding of physical mechanisms in practical engineering, physical prior knowledge is introduced, and a physics-informed grey-box aerodynamic model, named Focus-VI, is established based on extremely tiny datasets utilizing variational inference and attention mechanisms. Compared with the fully black-box multi-layer perceptron (MLP), Focus-VI demonstrates advantages in higher accuracy, stronger generalization ability, and certain interpretability, and can be effectively applied to the modeling, analysis, and optimization design of DPW.

Dynamic transport of charged lunar dust under lander plume impingement
abstract: Plume-induced dust transport is a major hazard during lunar landing, but the charging history of lofted grains is often simplified as a plasma-equilibrium problem. This assumption overlooks the rapid triboelectric charging produced by plume-driven dust collisions and its possible persistence after engine shutdown. This study develops a coupled multiphysics model for charged lunar dust transport under plume impingement during lunar landing. The model integrates plume-induced gas–solid interaction, triboelectric charging from dust collisions, shifted orbital-motion-limited plasma charging, and electrostatic dust transport. Verification against nozzle-exit measurements and published plume solutions confirms that the framework captures the main plume aerodynamics and provides a reliable basis for predicting dust motion. The results show that pre-shutdown dust ejection is mainly governed by aerodynamic forcing, whereas post-shutdown transport of fine grains is strongly affected by inherited triboelectric charge before the grains relax toward the plasma-controlled equilibrium state. This effect is highly size selective: it amplifies transport deviations mainly in the fine-grain regime rather than uniformly affecting all particles. Neglecting inherited triboelectric charge can lead to large prediction errors for submicrometer grains, with the divergence index reaching 144.6% for 0.1 μm particles. Under stronger electric fields, the sensitive range further extends toward 1 μm grains, whereas 100 μm grains remain nearly unaffected. Under the representative lunar plasma condition, the inherited triboelectric charge and plasma-equilibrium charge reach comparable magnitudes at a grain radius of approximately 2.27 μm, marking a charge-scale crossover rather than a transport threshold.

abstract: Deterministic CFD predictions for hypersonic cone-flare configurations ex-hibit large variation and uncertainties, even for canonical benchmark cases.This work quantifies how aleatory variability in freestream conditions, walltemperature, transport parameters, and nose bluntness propagates to design-relevant quantities of interest. Variation in these inputs is modeled usingprescribed probability distributions. A non-intrusive uncertainty propaga-tion framework couples the SU2 solver, using steady compressible RANSwith the SST turbulence model, to DAKOTA. Latin Hypercube Samplinggenerates 238 realizations of the seven-dimensional input space. These areaugmented through Bayesian adaptive sampling to a total of 269 simula-tions. From each simulation, six quantities of interest are extracted and usedto train a surrogate Kriging model. After model validation, 75,000 MonteCarlo evaluations of the surrogate enable efficient estimation of probabilitydistributions and Sobol global sensitivity indices of the quantities of interest.The results highlight the dominant effects of boundary-layer thermodynam-ics on thermal loads and separation behavior. This study demonstrates areproducible surrogate-based UQ workflow for hypersonic cone-flare RANSsimulations and motivates future extension to epistemic model-form and nu-merical uncertainty.

Design and analysis of a constraint driven distributed attitude observer for a three-vehicle constrained formation
abstract: This paper derives and analyzes a constraint driven distributed attitude observer, with direction constraints on the unit vector space, for a three-vehicle formation with unknown attitude dynamics. Each vehicle in the formation can measure its own angular velocity, one known inertial direction, such as a known magnetic field, and the relative directions to other vehicles in the formation. The relative direction measurements between two of the vehicles in the formation are not available. The observer design is based on the Lagrange-d’Alembert principle of variational mechanics, which is applied to a virtual system whose energy correlates to the attitude estimation errors. The energy-like term of this observer is driven to zero by introducing a dissipation term, thereby driving the estimation errors to zero. The observer improves on a prior “local” attitude observer by directly using the sensor measurements of all vehicles, rather than requiring the computation of a deterministic attitude solution. In addition, the observer is shown to be more robust in cases where the prior design estimate would diverge, and this is verified numerically. The local exponential stability is assured for almost all configurations, excluding only a zero measure subset, provided that the configuration rate of change is bounded. Finally, the convergence, the filtering ability, and the comparison with the prior “local” observer are evaluated by employing extensive Monte Carlo numerical simulations. The numerical results verify the theoretical stability conclusions. Significant improvements with respect to previous results are observed in a subset of degenerate and ambiguous configurations.

Influence of shock control bump geometry in impinging shock wave boundary layer interactions
abstract: The effect of shock control bumps (SCB) on oblique shock wave/turbulent boundary layer interaction is investigated in this experimental study. The primary goal of the study is to characterize how the oblique SWBLI flow structure changes with bump forebody geometry, and assess the resulting control effectiveness through its impact on the extent of flow separation. To study the effect, five bump geometries were designed with different values of the ramp angle, while the maximum crest height and afterbody shape are kept constant. The experiments were conducted under fully developed turbulent boundary layer conditions with R e θ = 21.8 × 10 3 and freestream Mach number of 2.0 for the interaction with 12 ∘ wedge angle and 41.5 ∘ incident shock angle. The control effectiveness is assessed from the size of the separated flow region, as well as the downstream boundary layer velocity profile development. For this, PIV is employed as the main diagnostic method to characterize the flow field. In addition, high-speed schlieren and oil-flow visualization measurements were performed to assess the effect of the SCB on the overall interaction structure. A significant reduction in the occurrence of reversed flow is observed when the bump is employed as a control device. Control effectiveness, assessed primarily through the integrated separated area A sep derived from the separation probability distribution, shows non-monotonic dependence on ramp geometry. This behavior is attributed to a trade-off between the pre-compression strength introduced by the bump leading edge and the increasing proximity of the leading edge shock to the main interaction region as the ramp angle steepens.

Reduced-order prediction of multi-jet flow control effects on vortex breakdown over delta wings from single-jet training
abstract: Vortex breakdown over delta wings strongly influences aerodynamic performance at moderate to high angles of attack. When active jet control is introduced, the flow response becomes highly sensitive to jet placement, making systematic exploration of multi-jet configurations computationally expensive. This study develops a reduced-order CFD-machine-learning framework to estimate multi-jet vortex behaviour using training data obtained solely from steady single-jet simulations. Analysis of the single-jet database shows that jets placed near the mid-span and close to the leading edge promote upstream migration of the breakdown, whereas jets positioned closer to the wing apex delay vortex breakdown. A reduced-dimensional representation of the flow is constructed to capture the dominant vortex structures, and the baseline CFD predictions are assessed against Particle Image Velocimetry measurements. Jet parameters are then mapped to this modal space to enable rapid reconstruction of planar velocity fields. Without retraining on combined-actuation cases, the single-jet-trained model is used to generate rapid superposition-based estimates for selected two-, three-, and four-jet configurations. The reconstructed fields preserve the main vortex topology, with error increasing gradually but remaining bounded as jet count increases. Full multi-jet CFD simulations are then used to verify the selected configurations and show that the physical response is cumulative but not strictly additive, exhibiting saturation and partial cancellation depending on the actuator arrangement. The proposed framework reduces the computational cost of steady RANS-based screening from 20–83 core-hours to approximately one minute on a single CPU core, enabling rapid screening of complex multi-jet flow-control strategies.

title: Short-term perturbed evolution of debris cloud in Eulerian-Lagrangian perspectives
Multi-fidelity load reconstruction in drone composite wings using in-service strain measurements
abstract: Accurate reconstruction of aerodynamic loads from sparse strain measurements is a longstanding challenge in structural health monitoring (SHM), particularly for lightweight composite wings in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) where space and weight constraints limit instrumentation. This work presents a data-efficient pipeline for UAV wing load reconstruction under sparse sensing, explicitly designed to operate with limited experimental data. The proposed framework uses a two-stage approach consisting of multi-objective optimization for sensor placement and a hybrid load reconstruction strategy that combines physics-based (low fidelity) with data-driven (high-fidelity) observations. In the first stage, the optimal strain gauge locations are identified numerically through a Pareto-based optimization that balances the number of sensors against reconstruction accuracy. Then, in the second stage, a multi-fidelity approach is developed for the reconstruction of the aerodynamic loads where a calibration matrix (CM), derived from finite element simulations, is combined with an artificial neural network (ANN) trained on limited experimental data to account for modelling discrepancies and improve prediction fidelity. The framework is validated both numerically and experimentally, using wind tunnel experiments on a composite UAV wing. The results show that the multi-fidelity framework improves load reconstruction relative to the CM-only baseline and is particularly effective when experimental data are limited. With only three wind-tunnel runs used for training, the multi-fidelity model reduced the mean MAE from 8.72 to 4.58 for lift and from 8.94 to 4.08 for drag. For lift, the corresponding mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) decreased from 49.23% to 18.44%. When ten training runs were used, the mean MAE was further reduced from 8.73 to 3.85 for lift and from 8.44 to 3.91 for drag, while the lift MAPE decreased from 47.51% to 12.92%. The proposed framework is also compared against a fully data-driven ANN trained on the same experimental datasets. Across the full data-availability study, the multi-fidelity approach reached accurate and stable predictions with fewer training runs than the ANN, which exhibited higher variability under data-scarce conditions. These results highlight the potential of the proposed framework as a promising basis for SHM and digital twin (DT) applications in aerospace structures.

An improved time-marching throughflow method for transonic flow analysis in highly loaded axial compressors
abstract: While computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-based two-dimensional (2D) throughflow methods are essential for the preliminary design of axial compressors, their application to highly loaded transonic regimes is frequently hindered by numerical instabilities and accuracy degradation. To overcome these issues, this study presents a time-marching throughflow method governed by the circumferentially averaged Euler equations. The innovativeness of this work lies primarily in two aspects. First, to improve the computational robustness, an adaptive time-dependent inviscid blade body force model is proposed, which dynamically couples with the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) stability condition, local flow parameters, and grid geometries. Second, the physical motivation for the use of the normal blockage factor to enhance the prediction accuracy is elucidated. This physically grounded correction effectively compensates for the excessive aerodynamic blockage introduced by the captured normal shock waves. The method is systematically validated against two benchmark transonic cases (NASA Rotor 37 and Stage 35) and further demonstrated on a 1.5-stage compressor with a high loading coefficient of 0.5. Results indicate that enhanced computational convergence is achieved when compared with the original inviscid blade body force model. The relative errors in predicting the choking mass flow rate are within 0.5% for the NASA cases and 1.7% for the 1.5-stage compressor, proving this method to be a highly capable and robust tool for modern transonic compressor design.

title: Cooperative integrated guidance and control for multiple hypersonic flight vehicles with prescribed time and performance
abstract: Recently, integrated guidance and control (IGC) has been widely employed to tackle cooperative guidance problems for multiple missiles. Nevertheless, achieving prescribed-time convergence within such a framework for multiple hypersonic flight vehicles remains a challenging and underexplored area. To address this issue, this paper systematically proposes a cooperative IGC scheme ensuring prescribed time and performance, while simultaneously accounting for composite disturbances (including unmodeled dynamics and external disturbances) and multiple practical constraints (such as field-of-view constraint and input saturation). Specifically, an IGC model is developed incorporating both actuator dynamics and input saturation, and a prescribed-time prescribed performance function, independent of initial conditions, is designed to constrain coordination and tracking errors. Based on the leader-follower architecture, the prescribed-time prescribed performance distributed cooperative guidance laws are proposed. This approach ensures coordination of both impact time and flight position, eliminating the reliance of traditional methods on precise time-to-go estimation, while simultaneously accounting for the field-of-view constraint and terminal guidance switching. Subsequently, based on the backstepping control, the prescribed-time prescribed performance robust tracking control laws are designed to ensure rapid tracking in each control loop. This design integrates an extended state observer with prescribed-time convergence to estimate and compensate for composite disturbances, alongside a high-order auxiliary system to handle input saturation. Furthermore, the stability of the closed-loop system with prescribed-time convergence and prescribed performance is rigorously proved using Lyapunov theory, and guidelines for controller parameter selection are provided. Extensive simulations validate the effectiveness and generality of the proposed method in cooperative strike missions against ground targets, demonstrating its capability to achieve high impact accuracy and coordination effectiveness while guaranteeing rapid convergence and low steady-state errors.

title: An Encke-inspired SGP4-based hybrid correction scheme for Galileo-type orbit prediction
abstract: A hybrid correction scheme that integrates SGP4 with the reference-orbit-and-deviation philosophy of Encke’s method is introduced for Galileo-type orbit prediction. In this framework, SGP4 produces the reference trajectory, while a neural network model forecasts the dominant residual component relative to this trajectory. Unlike the classical Encke method, the deviation equations are neither derived nor numerically integrated; instead, deviation propagation is replaced by a data-driven predictive model initialized with the first two revolutions of the residual series. Analysis of the GSAT0204 Galileo-type dataset identifies the argument of latitude as the dominant explanatory variable for SGP4 distance errors. This result is physically consistent, as the argument of latitude determines the satellite’s position along its orbital path, and TLE/SGP4 propagation errors are frequently dominated by the along-track component. Numerical experiments on 313 TLEs of GSAT0204 demonstrate that, within the examined Galileo-type orbital region, the proposed correction scheme reduces SGP4 distance errors in most cases. With periodic rectification, the effective prediction horizon extends from a few days to several weeks and, in many cases, beyond one month, with errors approaching those of an optimal correction benchmark. These results highlight the potential of integrating classical orbit-propagation techniques with machine learning to enhance prediction accuracy while preserving computational efficiency in space surveillance and tracking applications. Comprehensive validation across additional Galileo satellites and broader orbital regimes remains a subject for future research.

Trade-offs between plume collimation and axial thrust in a cusped field thruster with modified exit magnetic topology
abstract: This study examines how modifications to the exit magnetic topology influence the discharge behavior, plume structure, and thrust characteristics of a cusped field thruster (CFT). A conventional three-layer magnetic configuration and a modified four-layer design were experimentally compared. The three-layer configuration provides effective electron confinement but forms an inclined exit separatrix, producing a characteristic double-peak plume with relatively large divergence. In the four-layer configuration strengthens the cusped magnetic field near the outlet, reshaping the separatrix into a more vertically oriented cusp and modifying downstream electron accessibility. Magnetic-field simulations performed using a three-dimensional COMSOL model show good agreement with magnetic-probe measurements, validating the numerical design. Plume characteristics were measured using a Faraday probe mounted on a computer-controlled rotary stage over an input power range of 160–220 W. Results indicate that the three-layer configuration consistently produces a wide double-peak plume with a pronounced centerline ion-current deficit, whereas the four-layer configuration yields improved central plume filling and inward-shifted peak angles. At the same time, the four-layer configuration exhibits enhanced ion flux at large plume angles, indicating a redistribution of ion momentum rather than a uniform reduction in plume divergence. Performance measurements show that the four-layer configuration generates a higher total ion beam current, increasing from 0.742 to 0.945 A as power rises from 160 to 220 W, which leads to a higher ideal thrust potential. However, when plume angular distribution is considered, the measured axial thrust of the four-layer configuration remains lower than that of the three-layer design within the tested power range owing to redistribution of ion momentum into non-axial directions. Scaling analysis further indicates that the axial thrust of the four-layer configuration exhibits a steeper growth trend with input power, suggesting the possibility for improved axial-thrust performance at higher operating power beyond the present experimental range. The results demonstrate that exit magnetic-topology modification provides an effective means of tailoring plume structure and ion-acceleration behavior in CFTs, while highlighting the trade-offs among ion production, plume collimation, and axial momentum conversion. These findings underscore the importance of magnetic-field geometry in CFT optimization and provide an experimental basis for future magnetic-topology engineering aimed at improving axial thrust efficiency and scalability.

title: Geometrically nonlinear model of cable net and mesh for the manufacturing of large deployable mesh reflectors
abstract: The design and manufacturing of Large Deployable Mesh Reflectors (LDRs) require accurate prediction of the deployed configuration of cable-mesh assemblies and a reliable determination of their corresponding zero-stress geometry, which is essential for the fabrication of cutting patterns, cable rest lengths, and assembly tolerances. Most form-finding and unstressing techniques, traditionally developed for civil infrastructures, are hardly applicable to spaceborne reflectors, characterized by a complex assembly of cable nets, reflective meshes and ring trusses. This work presents an integrated two-stage methodology specifically tailored to LDRs. In the first stage, a form-finding strategy is developed resorting to an extended Force Density Method (FDM) capable of simultaneously accounting for front and rear cable nets, the reflective mesh, and the flexibility of the deployable ring truss. The final shape is optimized through a multi-objective gradient-based procedure enforcing both nodal adherence to the ideal parabolic contouring cylinder and homogenization of reaction forces at the supports, ensuring improved electromagnetic and structural performance. In the second stage, a geometrically nonlinear incremental-iterative procedure is introduced to recover the unstressed configurations of the front net, rear net, and mesh. Cable slackening, reactivation, and geometrically nonlinear effects are consistently handled. The proposed framework provides a unified and scalable computational tool for the accurate modeling, optimization, and manufacturing of large deployable mesh reflectors.
