Numerical investigation and wind tunnel test of a novel yaw actuator for flying wing aircraft
abstract: For balancing directional control and stealth of high-stealth flying wing aircraft, a novel yaw actuator based on dual synthetic jets is proposed. Reverse dual synthetic jet actuators (RDSJAs), installed at the middle of the wing, can replace mechanical control surfaces to achieve yaw control while maintaining favorable stealth characteristics. High-accuracy numerical investigations and wind tunnel tests are conducted to illustrate the flow control mechanism and acquire aerodynamic control characteristics. Reverse dual synthetic jets interact with the coming flow, improves the adverse pressure gradient over the upper surface, and then weakens the flow velocity especially near the leading edge and behind RDSJAs, and induces a lot of period alternate separated bubbles, which gradually expand, merge, and break down during the downstream evolution process. The injection of high-energy reverse jets obviously promotes the momentum exchange and energy dissipation near RDSJAs, and hence triggers the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, inducing the large-area separated domain behind RDSJAs. The decline of leading-edge suction and the improvement of low pressure behind RDSJAs make Cd and Cn increase, achieving yaw control without the movement of mechanical control surfaces. RDSJAs are suitable for yaw control at low to moderate angles of attacks (AOAs). At a trim AOA of 2°, RDSJAs can increase Cd by 55.7% and Cn by 134.4%. The optimal yaw control performance is achieved under high-frequency actuation with F⁺ = 7.2. Proportional control of aerodynamic loads can be realized by varying Cμ, and the fine tuning of aerodynamic loads can be achieved by adjusting the actuation frequency, actuation location, and modulation waveform.

title: Study on the coupling effect of typical geometric parameters on cooling effectiveness and thermal stress characteristics of double-wall cooling blades
Experimental study on nitrogen-fed 10 cm ECR gridded ion source for ABEP
abstract: Very low Earth orbit missions are limited by the aerodynamic drag of the rarefied atmosphere. Air-breathing electric propulsion (ABEP) can generate thrust by ionizing the orbital atmosphere to overcome this limitation, while also reducing the need for propellant reserves. This study experimentally evaluates a nitrogen-fed 10 cm electron cyclotron resonance (ECR) gridded ion source to investigate its application feasibility for ABEP through beam extraction experiments and Langmuir probe diagnostics. Within the stable operating envelope, the extracted beam current increases with input microwave power and nitrogen flow rate. The discharge characteristics are similar to the typical noble gas operation. However, a beam current drop appears at high nitrogen flow rate and is accompanied by an abrupt rise of the accelerator grid ion impingement current. The beam current drop is primarily attributed to the space charge limit rather than discharge extinction. Increasing the screen grid voltage shifts the onset of the beam current drop to higher nitrogen flow rate and expands the stable operating envelope. The grid holder length influences power coupling and beam extraction by changing the volume and shape of the plasma production region. Under the conditions that the nitrogen flow rate is 10 sccm and the input microwave power is 55 W, the ion source extracts a beam current of 258 mA, corresponding to a thrust of 8.8 mN and a specific impulse of 4311 s, which shows its potential in ABEP-based drag compensation applications.

title: Streamlined BCC lattice-core regenerative cooling channel with segmented airfoil-shaped strut cross‑section: Parametric design and thermohydraulic performance
Online decision switching for anti-UAV tracking based on reinforcement learning
Full aerodynamic model-based real-time 3D wind vector estimation without flow angle sensors for small UAVs
abstract: Autonomous energy-efficient flight for small unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) fundamentally relies on accurate real-time wind vector estimation. However, existing onboard methods are highly sensitive to low-cost sensor noise. Moreover, the error propagation mechanisms of simplified aerodynamic models remain unclear. To address these constraints, a real-time 3D wind estimation framework integrating a full aerodynamic model is proposed. Crucially, this framework relies exclusively on standard onboard sensors, completely eliminating the dependency on vulnerable flow angle sensors. As an auxiliary post-processing step, a lightweight Adaptive Moving Average Estimation module is introduced to balance noise suppression and dynamic wind tracking. Furthermore, the propagation mechanisms of aerodynamic model errors on estimation precision are systematically quantified for the first time. Multi-scenario simulations validate the high precision and robustness of the proposed method. Subsequent flight tests demonstrate its sim-to-real transferability, onboard real-time capability, and engineering feasibility, while explicitly clarifying practical error sources. This study provides a reliable autonomous wind perception solution, directly supporting energy-efficient flight and trajectory planning.

title: Design of a bio-inspired morphing airfoil mechanism using inverse kinematics and multi-objective aerodynamic shape optimization
Hydrogen-induced changes in flame topology, coherent structures, and instability development in a premixed swirl-stabilized combustor
abstract: Hydrogen is increasingly being used in the aerospace sector as a clean energy source. The premixed combustion of hydrogen–air mixtures in porous media has received considerable attention, with the aim of enhancing hydrogen energy conversion efficiency and mitigating environmental impacts. This work experimentally investigates the influence of hydrogen enrichment on the morphology, spectral response, and temporal coherence of premixed methane–hydrogen combustion flames in a swirl-stabilized combustor at atmospheric pressure. Three fuel compositions (0%, 30%, and 40% H₂ by volume) were tested at constant thermal power (4.6 kW) and equivalence ratio (ϕ = 0.8). Hydrogen addition produced more compact, intense, and symmetric CH* and OH* chemiluminescence fields, indicating increased reactivity and stronger localization of the reaction zone. However, this morphological compactness was accompanied by a marked increase in dynamic instability. The main acoustic peaks rose from about 225 and 195 Pa at 240 and 300 Hz in the methane flame to 526 and 496 Pa at 30% H₂, while at 40% H₂ the dominant peak shifted to 310 Hz and reached 581 Pa, together with a broader spectral distribution. SPOD revealed a progressive shift from low-frequency coherent structures to fragmented higher-frequency modes, with CH* and OH* dominant frequencies extending up to 207.5 Hz at 40% H₂. Temporal autocorrelation further showed a transition from stable periodic behavior at 0% H₂ to strong mid-frequency coherence at 30% H₂ and rapid decorrelation at 40% H₂. The results demonstrate that hydrogen enrichment simultaneously enhances flame compactness and amplifies unsteady flame–acoustic interactions, defining a clear trade-off between combustion reactivity and dynamic stability.

Design and optimization of a fuselage-integrated diverterless supersonic intake for ramjet vehicles

Parameter identification and uncertainty quantification for supersonic turbulence modeling via a multi-level optimization strategy in scramjets
A blade loading-driven multi-task optimization approach for a family of centrifugal compressors
abstract: In the design refinement process of a centrifugal compressor family, three-dimensional optimization is vital to maximize the compressor performance. Most studies tend to optimize each master stage sequentially, which consumes substantial time and computational cost, also prolonging the design process. To address this issue, this study introduces the concept of multi-task optimization to the design of a compressor family by using the Multi-Factorial Evolutionary Algorithm (MFEA) method to achieve concurrent three-dimensional optimization of compressors. This algorithm enabled parallel optimization by exploiting the underlying similarities inherent in the preliminary designs, and sharing implicit search directions across the compressor family during the optimization process. To further accelerate the convergence of the optimization, the linearized domain adaption (LDA) method was proposed to explicitly guide the search directions through analysis of blade loading distribution. Through optimizing four base stages, it was found that, compared to the conventional single-task optimization approach, MFEA accelerated the optimization convergence by 56.1%, while the LDA-guided MFEA method accelerated the convergence by 67.9%. On average, the design-point efficiencies of the four stages were enhanced by 1.7% through optimization. This confirmed that the multi-task optimization strategy can significantly improve the aerodynamic optimization process of families of centrifugal compressors, thereby saving significant computational time and cost.

title: Adaptive drag reduction using GA-based intelligent flexible flaps on Ahmed body under crosswind conditions
Assessment of hydrogen and kerosene combustion performance and emissions in an aircraft engine at different altitudes based on real engine data
abstract: The shift towards sustainable aviation fuels has heightened interest in alternative propulsion technologies. Hydrogen, being a carbon-free fuel, offers a promising avenue for reducing aviation emissions; however, its combustion properties differ markedly from traditional kerosene-based fuels. This study employs computational fluid dynamics to numerically examine the combustion performance and emissions of a commercial aircraft engine operating with kerosene and hydrogen across six flight levels (FL300-FL390). Key parameters analyzed include temperature distribution, species concentrations, turbulence kinetic energy, and pollutant emissions. Findings reveal that hydrogen combustion achieves higher peak temperatures and broader high-temperature regions than kerosene across the investigated cruise conditions. These combustor-level results indicate stronger local heat release and oxidation intensity under the simulated cases, but they are not interpreted here as direct evidence of superior whole-engine thermal efficiency. Hydrogen also produces a clearer thermal-NOx penalty at the lower flight levels, while eliminating carbon-containing exhaust species from the combustor products.

Generative augmentation of imbalanced flight records for flight diversion prediction: A multi-objective optimisation framework
abstract: Flight diversions are rare but high-impact events in aviation, making their reliable prediction vital for both safety and operational efficiency. However, their scarcity in historical records impedes the training of machine learning models used to predict them. This study addresses this challenge by proposing a generative augmentation framework for imbalanced aviation tabular records. The principal contribution lies in the design of a composite optimisation objective specifically tailored to flight data, which integrates four complementary quality dimensions into a single score used to guide automated hyperparameter search via the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) algorithm: realism, statistical similarity, fidelity, and predictive utility. These dimensions were selected and defined to reflect the operational and statistical requirements specific to aviation records, and were complemented by two descriptive evaluation dimensions, diversity and operational validity, forming a six-stage assessment framework. The composite objective was then used to tune three deep generative models, namely Tabular Variational Autoencoder (TVAE), Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN), and CopulaGAN, with Gaussian Copula (GC) serving as a statistical baseline. Results show that optimised models substantially outperform their default counterparts across all six assessment dimensions, and that augmentation with the resulting synthetic data improves diversion prediction compared to training on real data alone. These findings demonstrate that domain-adapted multi-objective optimisation is an effective strategy for generative augmentation of rare events in aviation, with applicability to other imbalanced tabular prediction tasks.

abstract: This paper proposes a deployable hierarchical control architecture for mission-level energy management in a series hybrid-electric distributed propulsion (DEP) aircraft, explicitly balancing safety and long-horizon optimality. The architecture integrates model predictive control (MPC) with a reinforcement learning-based Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) agent in a phase-adaptive hierarchical structure. MPC ensures conservative, constraint-aware authority during safety-critical phases (takeoff and climb), while the SAC agent provides fuel- and energy-optimal power allocation in less constrained regimes, particularly cruise. Outputs are continuously blended using flight-phase-dependent weights rather than hard switching, with automatic fallback to MPC-only operation upon SAC degradation. The SAC policy, trained off-policy over full missions, generalizes across conditions while strictly enforcing battery state-of-charge and thermal constraints. The energy management is decoupled from trajectory regulation, avoiding online constrained or optimal inner-loop propulsion or speed control. Aircraft velocity evolves naturally from thrust–drag dynamics, guided by a simple fixed-structure feedback controller enforcing predefined phase-dependent speed targets, preserving physical consistency without online constrained optimization. Results demonstrate that the hierarchical MPC-guided SAC framework achieves superior performance across stability, tracking, and efficiency, yielding an overall score of 0.88. By maintaining small SAC corrections between 0.3 and 0.4 in magnitude, the system ensures robust transitions between control authorities. For a 0.38-hour reference mission, the controller leverages low-demand phases for in-flight battery recharging, delivering 9.79 kWh at a peak power of 103 kW to maximize SOC recovery. Compared to MPC-only benchmarks, the strategy achieves a 5.75% reduction in fuel consumption and a 5.7% decrease in C O 2 emissions for both Jet-A and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). These findings establish that the integrated framework provides a robust, real-time solution for reducing emissions and extending battery longevity without compromising flight performance.

Effects of distributed propulsion on commuter aircraft longitudinal static stability and control
abstract: This paper presents wind-tunnel results quantifying the impact of a leading-edge distributed high-lift propeller system on the longitudinal stability and control characteristics of a generic 19-seat commuter aircraft model. The experimental campaign extends previous power-off tests on the same configuration to powered conditions, measuring lift, drag, and pitching-moment coefficients versus angle of attack and thrust coefficient at take-off flap setting. Results show that distributed propulsion affects longitudinal stability and control depending on thrust level and tail configuration---conventional aft-tail or T-tail---highlighting effects that are overlooked in literature. Static margin can be reduced by 8% or increased up to 6%, whereas the elevator control power can be doubled. Implications for tail sizing, pitch trim, and take-off performance are discussed.

abstract: Highly efficient thermal management systems are key to future environmentally-friendly turbofan engines. Using the bypass duct annulus surfaces for heat exchange promises an effective heat transfer and usage. Consequently, the heat transferring area is limited which calls for heat transfer enhancing surface structures. They are, however, inevitably exposed to airborne particulates which are ingested into the engine. Deposition of such particulates potentially degrades the heat transfer. We present an energy-based particle-wall interaction model including aerodynamic and liquid bridge forces. It not only allows for predicting the in-service performance degradation but also forms an important basis for the development of deposition-tolerant structured surfaces. The model is implanted in OpenFOAM. We demonstrate the model by predicting the deposition of Arizona Road Dust on a flat plate residing in a confined chamber featuring flow conditions and a particle-size distribution typical for a bypass duct of a turbofan engine. Good qualitative agreement was achieved between the numerically-predicted and experimentally-measured impact and deposition patterns when the action of fluid shear was properly estimated. Numerical predictions assuming rebound or all-escape conditions at the test chamber wall exhibited differences in particle impact and deposition distributions over the flat plate surface. As a consequence, the derivation of correlations from results obtained in a confined space requires a suitable correction of the effects induced by the test bed. The inclusion of capillary forces generated considerably-increased deposition in terms of both local levels and overall coverage ranges. This makes humidity an important parameter which characterizes the severity of engine operation.

Swirl-jet coupled flow and heat transfer in aircraft nacelle anti-icing D-duct
abstract: Anti-icing performance of the nacelle is critical to ensure the operational safety of aero-engines under atmospheric icing conditions. To overcome the issues of non-uniform heat transfer and localized hot spots inherent in conventional piccolo tube hot-air anti-icing systems, the swirl anti-icing system has attracted increasing attention as an efficient and lightweight alternative. This study systematically investigates the complex mechanisms of swirling flow and impinging jet heat transfer in an anti-icing D-duct. A coupled numerical model integrating internal-external flow fields and solid skin heat conduction is developed and validated. The flow structure in the D-duct cavity is analyzed in detail, and the flow characteristics of high-speed jets over complex curved surfaces are characterized. The swirling flow exhibits circumferential similarity and radial differences. After colliding with the wall, the jet forms local strong heat transfer and decays exponentially along the flow path and thus leads to the formation of hot spots. Based on parametric modeling and theoretical analysis, local convective heat transfer correlations tailored to the swirling flow region and jet impingement region are established respectively. The heat transfer correlations describing the circumferential and radial distribution characteristics of internal wall heat transfer in D-duct provide theoretical basis and engineering calculation methods for the optimal design of swirl anti-icing systems.

title: A phase-based framework for surge-wave classification in an axial compressor
Influence of shock wave configuration on near-wall flow in an aerospike nozzle
abstract: Aerospike nozzles represent a promising alternative for future propulsion systems, particularly in light of recent advances in additive manufacturing. The flow over the spike is primarily governed by a Prandtl–Meyer expansion, while the interaction between shock waves and spike geometry significantly influences the near-wall flow behavior. Due to the lack of a comprehensive methodology to analyze the influence of shock waves in aerospike nozzle flows, a model is developed to predict the origin and inclination of the oblique shock wave generated at the nozzle fillet. The model assumes that the incident shock wave is reflected at the spike surface, producing two distinct pressure peaks along the wall. In addition, an auxiliary model is proposed to account for deviations from the planar shape of the incident shock wave in the vicinity of the spike surface, enabling improved estimation of its effects on the flow field. Shock polar diagrams are employed to identify the most appropriate flow configurations near the reflection point, based on the von Neumann two- and three-shock theory. The results show good agreement with reference data in terms of the pressure distribution along the spike surface, demonstrating the capability of the proposed approach to capture the flow features under varying ambient pressure conditions.

abstract: Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is the most promising technical pathway to achieve the "Fly Net Zero" 2050 target. SAF can be permitted to use in civil aviation only if its impacts on engine operability, particularly lean blowout (LBO), are fully understood. In this paper, effects of fuels, including traditional aviation fuel RP-3 and two SAFs (named SAF-ZH and SAF-JH), on LBO limit are studied by measurement and theoretical analysis. Three types of combustor dome, i.e., dual-axial, dual-radial, axial-radial swirl cups are used. Significant physicochemical property differences exist among these three fuels. RP-3 exhibits the lowest LBO limit, whereas SAF-ZH shows the highest LBO limit, with SAF-JH showing the intermediate level. Fuel and configuration sensitivity analyses indicate that LBO behavior using SAF-ZH is predominantly fuel-controlled, while SAF-JH exhibits joint fuel-configuration dependence. The droplet concentrations at the flame root are approximate under the operating conditions near LBO for both dual-axial and dual-radial swirl cups to ensure the minimum fuel consumption to maintain combustion. The dual-radial swirl cup achieves larger SMD reduction due to the more entrained small droplets by stronger recirculation and further achieve higher evaporation and lower LBO limit. Both SAFs may demonstrate better compatibility with dual-radial and axial-radial configurations. Superior flow stability can partially offset LBO deterioration caused by less favorable chemical factors. In terms of upstream propagation of the flame cluster, the flame using RP-3 exhibits the lowest average propagation speed, and the use of dual-radial swirl configuration can lead to the highest propagation speed among the investigated combustors.

Phase-parameterised gaussian process for predicting UAV aerodynamic loads in operational turbine wakes
abstract: ABSTRACT Operational inspection of wind turbines using uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) is an attractive method for reducing offshore operation and maintenance costs, but robust flight in the turbine near-wake remains challenging due to the presence of strong unsteady disturbances that can degrade stability and quality of the inspection. This paper presents a control-oriented modelling framework for predicting UAV aerodynamic loads in operational turbine wakes with faster-than-real-time capability. A free-vortex-wake representation is used to capture the dominant near-wake physics, and a phase-parameterised Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) surrogate model is employed in a wake-aligned coordinate system to exploit the periodic structure of the induced velocity field. The surrogate model is coupled to a nonlinear, physics-informed rotorcraft flight dynamics model to predict wake-induced force perturbations on a quadrotor UAV. The approach is validated against data obtained from an experimental campaign with a scaled three-bladed turbine and a 250 mm-class quadrotor mounted on a load cell. The relevant data and experimental settings are reported as a reference for future research. Across lateral and vertical traverses in the near wake, the predicted streamwise and vertical force components agree with measurements in both magnitude and trend. A frequency-domain error attribution analysis shows the turbine–UAV interaction component, and the results indicate the measured spectral peaks at the turbine rotational and blade-passing harmonics are consistent with the simulations. The present formulation is primarily intended for wake conditions with coherent low-order periodic content, and its prediction fidelity may degrade under strongly turbulent or weakly phase-coherent inflow. Within this scope, the results demonstrate that phase-parameterised GPR surrogates can provide accurate, data-efficient, uncertainty-aware wake disturbance predictions suitable for real-time simulation platforms supporting UAV autonomy and control development for operational turbine inspection.

A conjugate heat transfer solver using tabulated chemistry for radiative cooling supersonic nozzles
abstract: A computational program for analyzing compressible reactive flow with conjugate heat transfer (CHT) was developed using the tabulated chemistry method. The developed program was applied to solve a supersonic nozzle problem incorporating radiative cooling. The time-saving benefits of the tabulated chemistry method were maximized in this compressible reactive flow with conjugate heat transfer problem. The temperature of the R-42 engine nozzle wall cooled by blackbody radiation was 648 K lower at the combustion chamber and 1645 K lower at the exit compared to the adiabatic wall–shifting equilibrium conditions. As the wall temperature decreased sharply due to radiative cooling, the density of the flow near the wall increased. Furthermore, the thickness of the velocity boundary layer and the thermal boundary layer decreased, resulting in higher flow velocities. Meanwhile, as the cooling caused changes in the density and internal energy ranges, the scale of the solution had to be expanded. The developed framework provides an efficient and physically consistent approach for analyzing thermal–fluid interactions in compressible reacting flows with heat loss. It also establishes a thermodynamic tabulation framework for future non-adiabatic compressible flamelet modeling.

Design space exploration of hybrid electric propulsion architectures on regional turboprop aircraft
abstract: Electrified Aircraft Propulsion (EAP) holds significant potential to reduce fuel consumption, emissions, and operating costs. With expanded design freedom and uncertainty in technological advancement, it is essential to systematically investigate EAP design to quantify the influence of powertrain electrification, identify promising candidates, and understand key design trade-offs. This paper presents a system-level design space exploration of two parallel hybrid architectures integrated into two regional turboprop aircraft models based on the ATR 42 and the DHC-7. The conventional aircraft models are first resized with advanced non-EAP technologies to establish a consistent reference. Parametric parallel hybrid electric propulsion architectures with two- and four-propulsor configurations are developed and characterized using high-level sizing and operational design variables. Constrained optimizations are performed at projected 2030, 2040, and 2050 electric technology levels, followed by a sensitivity study. Results suggest drastically different hybridization strategies and significant trade-off between the goals of minimizing fuel burn and minimizing total energy consumption, especially at lower technology levels. The different propulsive efficiencies resulting from different propulsor sizing strategies lead to lower optimal cruise hybridization for the four-propulsor configuration and impose a stricter lower bound on the motor size for the electric taxi. The electric technology variables are found to primarily affect weights, fuel burn, and energy consumption, but not point performance metrics. The results provide a quantitative assessment of the potential benefits and limiting factors of proposed EAP architectures across multiple technology horizons, offering design guidelines and insight into how advancing electric technologies shape future aircraft design.

Subsystem-level aerodynamic optimization with max-Q-based system integration and flight testing of an experimental sounding rocket
abstract: The current paper presents a max-Q anchored subsystem level aerodynamic optimization of the experimental sounding rocket Vayuvega, thrustMIT’s supersonic experimental sounding rocket developed for the International Rocketry Engineering Competition 2025 for the 30,000 ft Commercial Off The Shelf (COTS) category. Unlike conventional top-down rocket design approaches, which begin with vehicle-level requirements and progressively refine subsystems, the present study adopts a bottom-up subsystem-level optimization strategy in which key aerodynamic components are individually optimized prior to full vehicle integration and flight testing. Using a myriad of low and mid-fidelity tools, three central components governing the rocket’s aerodynamics, the nosecone, boattail, and fins, were optimized with target parameters like drag reduction, increased stability margin, and high factors of safety for flutter conditions. Results indicated that the component-wise optimization and complete integration is a viable and cost-effective approach. Flight testing showed that the rocket achieved an apogee of 29432 ft, and had a deviation of 2.55% from the predicted trajectory and achieving the highest apogee in the 30k COTS category, thus demonstrating a robust methodology for the aerodynamic optimization in future experimental sounding rockets and provide a reliable and efficient apporach for resource-constraint teams involved in experimental rocketry as compared to top-down approaches which are generally resource-heavy and computationally expensive.

Influence of endwall clearance on the aerodynamic performance of a spherical-endwall variable-geometry turbine
abstract: Variable-geometry turbines achieve flow matching over a wide operating range by adjusting the guide-vane stagger angle. However, the endwall clearance and pivot-shaft structure introduced by vane rotation can significantly affect aerodynamic performance. In this study, a two-stage variable-geometry turbine with spherical endwalls is investigated using steady numerical simulations based on ANSYS CFX and the SST turbulence model. The effects of guide-vane rotation angle, endwall clearance height, and pivot-shaft location on the flow characteristics and aerodynamic performance are systematically analyzed. The results show that endwall clearance height and guide-vane rotation angle are the dominant factors affecting aerodynamic performance. As the clearance height and vane closing angle increase, both the total pressure recovery coefficient of the adjustable guide vane and the total-to-total efficiency of the two-stage turbine decrease. The outlet mass flow rate is mainly controlled by the guide-vane rotation angle. The pivot-shaft location also modulates the loss characteristics, especially under large closing-angle and clearance conditions, where the trailing-edge pivot configuration produces the most severe loss. Flow-field analysis indicates that low total-pressure recovery and high entropy increase are mainly observed near the hub and tip endwall regions and in the downstream wake region. A response surface model further reveals the nonlinear coupling effects among clearance height, rotation angle, and pivot-shaft location. These findings provide guidance for endwall optimization and multi-parameter matching design of spherical-endwall variable-geometry turbines.

DIFNet: Decentralized information filtering fusion neural network with unknown correlation in sensor measurement noises
abstract: In recent years, decentralized sensor networks have garnered significant attention in the field of state estimation owing to enhanced robustness, scalability, and fault tolerance. Optimal fusion performance can be achieved under fully connected communication and known noise correlation structures. To mitigate communication overhead, the global state estimation problem is decomposed into local subproblems through structured observation model. This ensures that even when the communication network is not fully connected, each sensor can achieve locally optimal estimates of its observable state components. To address the degradation of fusion accuracy induced by unknown correlations in measurement noise, this paper proposes a data-driven method, termed Decentralized Information Filter Neural Network (DIFNet), to learn unknown noise correlations in data for discrete-time nonlinear state space models with cross-correlated measurement noises. Numerical simulations demonstrate that DIFNet achieves superior fusion performance compared to conventional filtering methods and exhibits robust characteristics in more complex scenarios, such as the presence of time-varying noise. The source code used in our numerical experiment can be found online at https://wisdom-estimation.github.io/DIFNet_Demonstrate/.

Airship dynamics in a tethered docking maneuver
abstract: In the context of the currently growing interest of industry and research towards the field of controlled airships, in particular in association to unmanned flight, the availability of methods and tools for the analysis of specific maneuvers faced by airships over their typical mission profile constitutes a relevant asset. The inherent dynamics of this class of flying vehicle, dominated by buoyancy and the aerodynamics of their envelope, produces a peculiar response especially in terminal maneuvers and in the docking phase. The latter is often carried out with the help of tethering cables, which further influence the dynamic behavior of the airship, in a way depending on the number and physical characteristics of the cables, the tethering points on board, the rewind velocity, etc. For a better understanding of the airship response in this type of maneuver, mid-fidelity dynamic models of both the airship and tethering cables are employed in this research. They are applied in a first stage to understand the effect of tethering cables on the dynamics of the airship, through a detailed linear analysis. The latter is performed in a parameterized fashion, studying the effect of different parameters on dynamic stability. Then the analysis of the outcome of fully non-linear simulations of an airship anchored to the ground via a rewinding tethering cable is proposed, showing the effect of different simple control logics on the behavior of the airship during an idealized docking manevuer. The proposed modeling and analysis methods allow to efficiently study the behavior of steerable lighter-than-air vehicles in terminal maneuvers, with a detail sufficient for airship design and characterization phases, also making for an interesting asset in the compliance-checking phase with respect to regulatory requirements.

Failure mechanisms and dimensionless protection criteria for recovery platforms under heavy rocket plume impingement
abstract: This study investigates the complex flow evolution and thermal load distribution induced by multi-nozzle gas jet impingement on platforms during heavy-lift launch vehicle recovery. A high-fidelity numerical model is developed based on the three-dimensional compressible Navier–Stokes equations and the realizable k-ε turbulence model. A structured hexahedral grid is used to discretize the computational domain, and the numerical method is validated against Planar Laser-Induced Fluorescence (PLIF) experimental data for under-expanded impinging jets. The effects of descent altitude, horizontal drift distance, and protective wall height on flow characteristics and thermal environment are systematically examined. The descent process can be divided into three stages: high-altitude free expansion, transitional impingement, and near-ground wall-bounded flow. As the altitude decreases, the flow structure evolves from regular Mach disks to fragmented shock waves and large-area wall-attached jets, accompanied by a significant expansion of the high-temperature region on the platform surface. Horizontal drift leads to two distinct physical mechanisms that undermine the protective effect of the wall. Under moderate relative drift, this mechanism manifests as a vortex-overtopping mode, in which the shear layer at the wall top destabilizes and forms a cascade of vortices. This establishes a steady cross-wall energy transport pathway, substantially increasing the peak heat flux in the equipment zone. Under large relative drift, a shear-dispersion mode occurs, reducing the peak heat flux by over 80% and shifting the threat from concentrated transport to dispersed dissipation. These two mechanisms can be unified by the drift ratio (H is the landing altitude and S is the horizontal drift distance). For a wall height of 1 m, the critical value is . When is below this value, the wall effectively blocks the high-temperature gas; when exceeds this value, the protective function is compromised. The parameter is defined as the critical dimensionless protective wall height. In the present configuration, , which corresponds to a physical height of 3.5 m. At this critical state, the peak heat flux for the vortex-overtopping mode is reduced by 99.1% compared with the failure condition. Consequently, the cross-wall energy transport pathway is severed, and the protection mechanism shifts fundamentally from magnitude suppression to mechanism elimination. Overall, this study reveals the physical mechanisms of protection failure under horizontal drift, establishes a dimensionless failure criterion based on the relative drift ratio, and proposes a universal dimensionless critical wall height, offering engineering guidance for the design of thermal protection systems for reusable launch vehicle recovery platforms.

abstract: This study presents the design and preliminary verification of a wireless power transmission (WPT) system based on high-power laser emission from lunar orbit. The system comprises a constellation of satellites in quasi-frozen lunar orbits, equipped with high-efficiency fiber lasers that convert solar energy into optical power. This energy is beamed to the Moon’s surface, where it is received and converted into electricity by photonic power converters (PPCs) located near strategic infrastructure zones. The paper focuses on key subsystems relevant to satellite design and testing, including laser payload integration, beam collimation optics, thermal management, and pointing accuracy control using Fine Steering Mirrors. A full satellite model is dimensioned, and its inertia matrix is derived to support attitude control design under realistic external disturbances such as solar radiation pressure and the lunar gravity gradient. Experimental validation of PPC performance under different laser power densities is conducted to assess efficiency and thermal behavior. Results confirm the feasibility of laser WPT for lunar environments and provide critical input for subsystem qualification and mission planning. The study advances the design and subsystem-level testing of satellite-based laser WPT architectures for lunar power stations, with a focus on orbital dynamics, laser integration, thermal management, beam steering, and power conversion.

Process parameter matching design of aero-engine high-speed radial oil-collecting rings based on stacking model
abstract: Ensuring the reliability of main-shaft bearings operating under high DN values is crucial for modern aero-engines. However, in the high-speed rotating environment of aero-engines, complex multi-parameter interactions limit the improvement of oil collection efficiency for radial oil-collecting rings. This study proposes a radial oil ring process parameter matching design framework based on stacked ensemble learning technology. The stacking model integrates Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) and CatBoost as base learners and employs Random Forest (RF) as the meta-learner, effectively capturing the nonlinear relationships among five process parameters. Interpretability analysis based on the RF-Stacking model indicates that nozzle angle and velocity ratio play dominant roles in oil collection efficiency, jointly determining geometric overlap and effective interception rate. Interaction effects further reveal highly efficient coupling regions among parameters. Additionally, supplementary experiments validate the model’s accuracy. Finally, by replacing the Random Forest meta-learner with a Ridge Regression model and combining it with the Sparrow Search Algorithm (SSA) for extrapolative optimization, an unprecedented highest oil collection efficiency was achieved in parameter design (predicted value of 79.57%, actual value of 78.50%). Compared to the pre-optimization state, oil collection efficiency was significantly improved, setting a new known record. This study provides a new paradigm for efficient parameter matching design of radial oil collection rings.

Optimal trajectory planning for flexible truss assembly based on nonlinear model predictive control
abstract: With the continuous advancement of space technology, on-orbit assembly of truss structures using robotic manipulators is expected to become an important development trend. Unlike rigid payloads, large-scale lightweight trusses exhibit significant elastic vibrations during assembly, which can compromise end-effector accuracy and pose risks of structural fatigue if not effectively suppressed. This paper proposes vibration-suppression optimal trajectory planning for robotic manipulators during the assembly of flexible truss structures. First, a coupled rigid-flexible dynamic model of the robot-truss system is established, and the interaction mechanism between the manipulator end-effector motion and truss vibration is derived in task space. On this basis, a nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) frameworkis proposed to optimize the assembly trajectory under multiple constraints, including vibration suppression, actuator physical limits, and obstacle avoidance. By simultaneously evaluating the tracking errors and structural modal energy, the method achieves active vibration suppression during the planning stage. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively suppresses multi-modal vibrations, ensures smooth and safe end-effector motion, and outperforms trajectory planningmethods without optimization.

title: CFD identification of acceleration-dependent aerodynamic derivatives and equivalent added-mass effects in hybrid buoyant–lifting vehicles
abstract: This work presents a computational-fluid-dynamics-based methodology for identifying acceleration-dependent aerodynamic derivatives and equivalent added-mass effects in hybrid buoyant--lifting vehicles for high-altitude pseudo-satellite (HAPS) applications. The approach combines unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes simulations of prescribed harmonic rigid-body motions with Fourier-based system identification to extract both velocity- and acceleration-dependent aerodynamic coefficients.The methodology is first validated on a prolate spheroid, for which analytical potential-flow solutions are available. The CFD-identified acceleration derivatives show very good agreement with theoretical predictions, supporting the accuracy of the proposed approach.The method is then applied to a hybrid closed-wing HAPS configuration to obtain a complete six-degree-of-freedom set of aerodynamic derivatives and equivalent added-mass coefficients. Owing to the lifting nature of the configuration, the acceleration-dependent terms cannot be interpreted as purely inertial contributions, but rather as equivalent terms including both fluid-inertial and unsteady aerodynamic effects.The results reveal significant translational and rotational contributions, together with non-negligible coupling terms arising from the interaction between buoyant volume and lifting surfaces. Comparison with potential-flow estimates confirms the overall structure of the equivalent inertial couplings, while highlighting deviations associated with the lifting character of the configuration.A simplified longitudinal flight-dynamics analysis shows that acceleration-dependent terms do not alter the qualitative stability characteristics of the HAPS, but significantly affect its modal properties, including natural frequencies and damping.

title: Tornado-vortex/downwash-vortex coupling mechanism underlying the radial expansion of stall cells in a low-aspect-ratio multistage axial compressor
Transonic flow past the complex cavity-sub-cavity configurations
abstract: The study investigates the physics of unsteady flow in complex cavity geometries operating in the transonic regime. A two-dimensional Detached Eddy Simulation (DES) approach is used for the preliminary analysis. The cavity configuration examined in this work arises from the integration of a scramjet engine with a launch vehicle. In this integrated geometry, the isolator section serves as a deep sub-cavity, while the Single Expansion Ramp Nozzle (SERN) constitutes the primary cavity. The combined arrangement therefore constitutes a complex cavity-sub-cavity system, which is referred to as such throughout the paper. The qualitative analysis revealed a feedback loop within the complex cavity-sub-cavity system, leading to high-pressure oscillations across the geometry. A monotonic increase in pressure loading is observed with increasing Mach number. Varying the cavity topology demonstrated that modifications to the primary cavity geometry strongly alter shear-layer dynamics and significantly affect the pressure distribution within the cavity-sub-cavity system. To mitigate adverse pressure oscillations, passive control strategies, including trailing-edge wall chamfering and a ventilated (slotted) sub-cavity, are investigated. Among the configurations studied, the slotted sub-cavity case exhibits the most pronounced suppression of pressure loads, particularly on the sub-cavity end wall. Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (SPOD) analysis also revealed the restructuring of dominant coherent modes in response to topological variations and to the implementation of passive control, providing insight into the underlying governing mechanism.

title: Design of multilayer heterogeneous graded density impactor for improved planarity in the enhanced hypervelocity launcher

Multi-objective optimization of aircraft spoiler structure with solid-lattice hybrid
abstract: Lattice structures offer superior specific stiffness and specific strength, providing significant potential for lightweight structural design in aerospace engineering. A two-step multi-objective optimization framework is developed for solid-lattice hybrid structures, with structural stiffness and lower-order natural frequencies as the optimization objectives. In the first step, multi-objective topology optimization based on the SIMP method is performed to determine the optimal load-bearing skeleton, where compromise programming and mean frequency method are incorporated to handle multiple performance objectives and ensure stable, balanced optimization results. In the second step, multi-objective lattice size optimization is conducted, aiming to identify the optimal cross-sectional size of lattice struts that satisfy the given mass constraints. At each step, a set of Pareto-optimal designs is derived, enabling the selection of appropriate configurations for different performance requirements. 3D numerical examples are presented, demonstrating that the structural stiffness and natural frequencies are effectively improved by the proposed framework. The framework is then applied to the design of an aircraft spoiler, and the influence of different lattice unit cell types on structural performance is investigated. Among the investigated lattice unit cells, the Octet-truss infill achieves the best overall performance. Compared with the solid spoiler of equal mass, the peak displacement and maximum von Mises stress are reduced by 20.02% and 17.34%, respectively, while the first, second, and third natural frequencies are improved by 20.15%, 39.01%, and 38.59%. The results confirm that the proposed framework effectively enhances the stiffness and natural frequencies of solid-lattice hybrid aerospace structures, and can be generalized to the design of other engineering components.

title: Design and optimization of planform-customized waverider with multistage compression flow
User-centred design of an immersive xr scenario to support risk assessment for specific category drone operations
abstract: European regulatory requires all drone operations the assessment of the risks involved to obtain the required flight mission authorization. In the specific category drone operations the risk assessment procedure must be developed by the drone operator. To effectively identify potential risks and hazards present in the area of interest and to evaluate the feasibility of mitigative solutions, the awareness of the operational scenario is a critical task to be achieved. State of the art tools available on the market for safety assessments usually explore two-dimensional visualizations or screen-based demonstrations of the operational environment, without providing to the operator a proper spatial awareness regarding the risks existing in the environment. This work aims to address this gap by developing a structural methodology to design and develop immersive environments through Extended Reality technologies to effectively convey information regarding spatial distribution of the elements within the operational scenario. A proposed XR application is developed by considering the Specific Operations Risk Assessment developed by the Joint Authorities for Rulemaking on Unmanned Systems as the reference procedure for risk assessment and it enables different points of view of the mission scenario supporting the strategic identification of hazards as well as of elements addressing risk mitigation, such as sheltering, obstacles and sparsely populated areas. The obtained solution was evaluated by addressing the impact of the proposed methodology on the risk assessment procedure and by collecting opinions of drone pilots from surveys conducted during two workshop sessions. Results indicate an enhanced awareness of the operator together with advanced decision-making and contingency management features thanks to the exploitation of Extended Reality technologies.

Active load alleviation of a falcon-inspired morphing flapping-wing aerial vehicle via cable-linkage synergy
abstract: Large-scale flapping-wing aerial vehicles (FWAVs) suffer from a critical ”scale-load” bottleneck, where severe aerodynamic loads during the downstroke lead to excessive peak power demand and elevated structural risks. To address these aerospace engineering challenges, a lightweight, cable-linkage synergistic spatial morphing wing architecture is proposed for active load alleviation, employing a ”downstroke-folding, upstroke-extending” strategy. By coupling unilateral cable constraints with a spatial crank-rocker transmission, the morphing wing achieves a precise, asymmetric wing planform deformation trajectory (40◦ folding and 5◦ extension). A kinematic framework capturing the time-varying topology and a coupled reduced-order aerodynamic model are established to optimize geometric design parameters and characterize the transient load mitigation mechanics. Wind tunnel experiments conducted on a fully integrated flight-worthy prototype successfully validate the aerodynamic performance. The experimental results demonstrate that, compared to a conventional rigid-wing baseline, the proposed morphing wing architecture reduces peak power by 38.2% (from 78.6 W to 48.6 W) and cycle-averaged power by 35.2% (from 26.4 W to 17.1 W) while fully maintaining effective thrust. This work offers a highly energy-efficient aerodynamic and structural framework for the design, load management, and flight efficiency optimization of next-generation variable-geometry aircraft.

abstract: In continuous recognition of urban low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), the widespread deployment of low-cost sensors and autonomous detection technologies has led to multi-view, high-dimensional data exhibiting strong temporal correlations. However, large-scale evidence that exhibits spatio-temporal inconsistencies caused by environmental clutter, building occlusion, and measurement errors leads to high computational complexity, underutilization of informative data, and degraded system stability. Decision-level fusion methods relying on pairwise comparison metrics impose a high computational burden and underutilize the contributions of highquality evidence. The lack of an effective measure for temporal evidence consistency fluctuations restricts system performance in achieving efficient, accurate, and stable recognition. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a spatio-temporal credible evidence fusion method, STCEF, for distributed UAV type recognition in urban low-altitude within a collaborative spatio-temporal fusion framework. Spatially, a conditional credibilitybased fusion method under a fusion-center-based strategy is designed to reduce computational complexity while improving the utilization of high-quality evidence. Temporally, sliding-window Rényi entropy quantifies uncertainty fluctuations to dynamically adjust evidence fusion weights, thereby suppressing transient interference caused by variations in class and belief assignments. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method enhances computational efficiency while achieving more accurate and stable type recognition, improving accuracy by 2.1% and mean belief by 10% compared with conventional methods.

Integrated CFD and machine learning investigation of pressure and temperature distributions on a cone at supersonic and hypersonic Mach numbers
abstract: A comprehensive Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Unified Machine Learning (ML) framework is developed to study high-speed flow regimes over a cone. The study evaluates the distributions of total pressure and total temperature along the slant length of the cone for freestream Mach numbers between 4.2 and 6 and semi-cone angles between 2° and 20°. Flow properties are extracted at non-dimensional positions (x/L) across the range 0 to 1 in 0.1 increments. The CFD results show that the cone tip experiences a significant total pressure loss due to intense shock interactions, leading to downstream pressure stabilization. The total temperature shows a gradual change pattern, resulting from both viscous dissipation and boundary-layer growth, which becomes more pronounced with increasing Mach number and larger cone angles. The CFD results are validated against the Taylor-Maccoll theory. The machine learning models use Support Vector Machines (SVMs), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Ordinal Logistic Regression (OLR) to train on CFD data using k-fold cross-validation method. Later, the models' generalizability was tested on the test dataset. The analysis shows that SVM achieves the best total pressure prediction accuracy, while OLR outperforms other methods in total temperature prediction accuracy. KNN demonstrates moderate accuracy, but it struggles to apply its knowledge to new situations. The combined CFD–ML solution enables researchers to achieve their results with less computational work while delivering accurate predictions. It would serve as a powerful resource for high-speed aerodynamic research and design optimization.

Choking effects influence in the start and unstart limits of supersonic and hypersonic inlets
abstract: Ramjet and scramjet engines are key technologies in hypersonic airbreathing propulsion, operating without mechanical compressors and using atmospheric air as the oxidizer. Their design and operation, however, face major challenges related to internal flow stability, shock wave formation, and choking phenomena. These can lead to unstart, a condition where a detached shock wave forms at the inlet entrance, causing flow spillage and a loss of thrust. Among various choking mechanisms, combustion-induced thermal choking is particularly critical, as it increases back-pressure and can directly trigger unstart. This study introduces a simplified analytical model, the Duct Choking Conversion Model (DC2M), which helps to define an equivalent valve area that captures the effects of common choking mechanisms including geometric, viscous, mass addition, and thermal choking. The DC2M model can be integrated with the existing Duct Shock Speed Model (DS2M), which predicts shock wave motion speed, equilibrium positions, and their stability as functions of flight conditions and internal duct geometry. Together, DC2M and DS2M models allow to perform a unified analysis of shock wave behavior by accounting for flight regime, internal geometry, and choking effects, including the generation of stability maps and the identification of operational limits for ramjet and scramjet systems. The DC2M model can determine the equivalent valve area throughout a wide range of configurations, and the influence in the limits of the fuel–to-air ratio. Moreover, the integrated model provides a powerful tool for examining both stable and transitional regimes, including those with hysteresis. This model offers a consistent theoretical basis for analyzing experimental data under both non-combusting and combusting test conditions, and can give support to both the design of experiments and the optimization of design strategies for hypersonic propulsion systems.

Experimental study on hypersonic retropropulsion aerodynamics for reusable launch vehicles under thrust vectoring
abstract: To address the complex aerodynamic disturbances encountered by the first stage of reusable launch vehicles (RLVs) during Supersonic Retropropulsion (SRP) in the re-entry phase, this study conducts a systematical wind tunnel investigation of a typical slender cylindrical rocket model equipped with thrust vector control (TVC). Aerodynamic forces, surface pressures, and spatial flow field characteristics were measured across varying thrust vector angles (0°, 5°, and 10°) and angles of attack (0°, 5°, and 10°). Experimental results demonstrate that the activation of retropropulsion induces a typical short penetration mode (SPM), which significantly reduces the axial force on the vehicle and alters the surface pressure distribution. The introduction of thrust vectoring disrupts the global symmetry of the flow field, leading to a highly non-linear variation in the pitching moment. A small thrust vector deflection (δ=5°) shifts the center of pressure forward, weakening the restoring pitching moment and potentially inducing local instability. Conversely, a large deflection (δ=10°) shifts the center of pressure rearward, partially restoring static stability, but induces severe interactions between the bow shock and the oblique shock on the windward side. Furthermore, Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) analysis of high-speed schlieren images reveals that as the angle of attack increases, the dominant flow mechanisms transition from high-frequency, globally coherent shock oscillations (with a characteristic frequency of approximately 4263.1 Hz for the first mode 1) to low-frequency, highly chaotic unsteady structures, significantly increasing flow complexity. These findings quantitatively elucidate the non-linear coupling among thrust vectoring, angle of attack, and aerodynamic loads, providing crucial experimental data and theoretical guidance for aerodynamic shape optimization and control law design during the powered descent and landing phase of reusable rockets.

Unsteady aerodynamic characteristics of a high-performance pitching airfoil under light dynamic stall at low reynolds number
abstract: This study investigates the unsteady aerodynamic characteristics of the Ishii airfoil compared to the benchmark NACA 0012 under light dynamic stall at a Reynolds number of Re = 50,000. Aerodynamic loads ( C l , C d , C m ) and Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) flow fields were synchronously measured across reduced frequencies ( k = 0.01 to 0.10). Under static conditions, the Ishii airfoil generates higher C l , a more negative C m , and demonstrates a distinct C d crossover, proving advantageous at low incidence. During dynamic pitching, both airfoils exhibit classical time-lag-induced hysteresis. However, while typical unsteady behavior, demonstrated by the NACA 0012 and Ishii’s pre-stall response, exhibits widening C m hysteresis as k increases, the Ishii airfoil demonstrates a k -independent aerodynamic damping profile exclusively under light stall conditions. In this regime, it maintains a consistently narrow C m hysteresis loop, yielding a constant, low-magnitude aerodynamic damping band ( C w ). PIV and literature comparisons suggest this stability arises from the Ishii airfoil’s unique geometry, anchoring a large, spatially stable Laminar Separation Bubble (LSB) over its mid-chord. Because the upstroke and recovery downstroke phases operate primarily within the incidence range where this massive LSB is present, it is proposed that this structural stability restricts variations in the upper-surface flow field. Furthermore, consistent with other thin-airfoil behavior, the Ishii profile promotes accelerated flow recovery and suppressed C l hysteresis. The combination of superior C l generation, reduced cyclic C l fluctuations, and a narrow, frequency-independent aerodynamic damping response makes the Ishii airfoil a viable candidate for unsteady, low- Re applications requiring the mitigation of temporal load asymmetries.

Three-dimensional integrated guidance and control for leader-follower flexible formation of fixed wing UAVs
abstract: This paper presents a nonlinear integrated guidance and control (IGC) approach for flexible leader-follower formation flight of fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) while accounting for high-fidelity aerodynamics and thrust dynamics. Unlike conventional leader–follower schemes that fix the follower’s position relative to the leader, the follower is steered to maintain range and bearing angles (which is the angle between its velocity vector and its line-of-sight (LOS) with respect to the leader) arbitrarily close to the prescribed values, enabling the follower to maintain formation on a hemispherical region behind the leader. The proposed IGC framework directly maps leader–follower relative range dynamics to throttle commands, and the follower’s velocity orientation relative to the LOS to aerodynamic control surface deflections. This enables synergism between guidance and control subsystems. The control design uses a dynamic surface control–based backstepping approach to achieve convergence to the desired formation set, where Lyapunov barrier functions are incorporated to ensure the follower’s bearing angle is constrained within specified bounds. Rigorous stability analysis guarantees uniform ultimate boundedness of all error states and strict constraint satisfaction in the presence of aerodynamic nonlinearities. The proposed flexible formation scheme allows the follower to have an orientation mismatch relative to the leader to execute anticipatory reconfiguration by transitioning between the relative positions in the admissible formation set when the leader aggressively maneuvers. The proposed IGC law relies only on relative information and onboard sensors without information about the leader’s maneuver, making it suitable for GPS-denied or non-cooperative scenarios. Finally, we present simulation results to vindicate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.

title: Exploration and application of the endoscopic pressure-sensitive paint measurement method in confined compressor cascade environments
Ablation-erosion and failure prediction of MoSi2 coatings under high-temperature, high-speed particle-laden gas flow
abstract: As liquid rocket engines advance toward higher performance, the use of metal-containing particle fuels to enhance specific impulse substantially aggravates the susceptibility of thermal protection coatings to coupled ablation–erosion damage. In response to this issue, the failure behavior of MoSi2 coatings in high-temperature, high-speed particle‐laden gas flow is investigated. Through liquid‐oxygen/kerosene ablation tests, the surface damage morphology and its evolution are revealed, and a synergistic damage mechanism between high‐temperature oxidation and particle erosion is elucidated. Based on this mechanism, a physics‐driven coupled ablation‐erosion mass‐loss model is developed, in which the strain energy density is introduced to characterize normal‐impact‐induced fragmentation, and the effects of impact angle, wall temperature, and flow velocity are incorporated. The model predictions show an error within 16.7% compared to experimental data. Furthermore, by integrating the model into a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver, the dynamic recession of the coating surface is successfully predicted, reproducing the typical pit‐shaped features and depth distributions observed in the tests. This study not only clarifies the previously overlooked synergistic erosion‐ablation effect, but also provides a reliable quantitative tool for lifetime prediction and protection design of hot‐section components in next‐generation particle‐fueled rocket engines.

An experimental parameter study on the formation of plasma on generic sphere-cone geometries and its influence on radar signatures under high enthalpy shock tunnel flow conditions
abstract: The high temperatures arising in hypersonic flight along the surface of a vehicle foster chemical reactions that lead to the formation of plasma. Under re-entry conditions, this plasma can reach densities that make it a highly dispersive medium for microwaves that are used both for radar sensing and communication. The consequence are phenomena like the radio blackout or the distortion of radar signatures. Factors like the vehicle shape and the flight state are wellknown to influence the distribution of plasma around a vehicle. To better understand the complex interplay of plasma formation and microwave scatter, this study considers the influence of these central factors on the radar signature in a systematic way. For this purpose, the radar signature of a series of sphere-cone geometries was measured undervarying high enthalpy flow conditions in the High Enthalpy Shock Tunnel (HEG) at the site of the German Aerospace Center (DLR) in Göttingen. The experiments were guided by combined Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Computational Electromagnetic (CEM) Simulations that first predict the plasma distribution and then determine the microwave response. The results obtained through this approach are subsequently used to identify the impact of thestudied influence factors.

Electronically-throttleable, catalyst-free combustion of ionic liquid-based polymers using transient plasma discharge
abstract: We employ the use of nanosecond pulse transient plasma to initiate catalyst-free thermal decomposition of ionic liquid-based polymers, demonstrating highly repeatable on/off throttling. A cylindrical end-burning combustion device is fabricated with a coaxial center wire electrode filled with hydroxylammonium nitrate (HAN)/polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) propellant. High-voltage (20 kV) nanosecond pulses (20 nsec) generate a plasma discharge at the polymer surface, triggering plasma-driven decomposition and enabling electronic throttling without a catalyst. Real-time imaging characterizes the electrically driven combustion process, capturing plasma initiation and the ignition/extinguishing sequence, which occurs in under 33 milliseconds. The plasma-driven decomposition mechanism involves the generation of highly energetic electrons and reactive atomic species, including hydrogen (H), oxygen (O), and carbon (C), as identified via in situ plasma emission spectroscopy. These radical species act as short-lived reaction intermediates, accelerating new chemical reaction pathways. Spectroscopic analysis reveals sharp emission peaks for monatomic and diatomic species, allowing the identification of key plasma-driven reaction pathways that diverge from conventional thermal catalysis and combustion mechanisms. Complementary chemical kinetics modeling, informed by key intermediates identified through in situ plasma emission spectroscopy, revealed that transient plasma produces reactive radicals—particularly atomic hydrogen — that increases combustion control and accelerates overall burn rates. The modeling also suggests that these species promote chain-branching pathways that are otherwise slow in HAN+PVA combustion. These findings underscore the potential of transient plasma to improve the characteristics of HAN+PVA combustion while emphasizing the critical role of plasma-generated species and mixture composition in governing ignition dynamics.

Thermal control with digital twins for dimensional stability in CubeSat payloads
abstract: Small satellites are on the rise within the context of the so-called New Space industry, driven by the use of cost-efficient, off-the-shelf components as well as miniaturization, modularity, and scalability. While this opens many opportunities, especially in terms of accessibility to space, it also comes with its challenges. When high-precision optical sensors are employed, such as laser-based communication systems, payload temperature gradients often lead to optical aberrations due to the satellite’s uneven thermal expansion. This reduces reliability and hinders the system’s performance in certain stages of the mission. Moreover, traditional methods to alleviate temperature gradients, such as heat pipes, might be infeasible due to limited payload volume, and control routines might fail due to structural degradation and component wear. This paper presents an innovative approach to achieving thermal stability in a Dynamic Optical Ranging & Timing system by exploiting the waste heat of redundant electronic components. An Onboard Digital Twin is defined, composed of a satellite thermal model, model-predictive control to schedule the load of redundant electronic components, and a parameter updating scheme that accounts for time-variant internal and external deviations. The framework was executed off-board in a laboratory hardware-testing environment, with the measured control timings supporting the computational feasibility of future deployment on the target multi-processor onboard computer. During the hardware tests, the presented framework achieved a maximum relative temperature error of under 10 % between model prediction and measurement data, and successfully maintained temperature differences between critical components below the required 5 K.

Generalized engine inoperative performance requirements for future aircraft concepts
abstract: Future transport aircraft concepts leveraging advanced propulsion systems enable more efficient flight, but face major certification barriers prior to entering service. One critical barrier is the poor applicability of “one engine inoperative” (OEI) performance requirements defined in FAA Part 25 and EASA CS-25 regulations that only apply to transport aircraft designed with 2-4 homogeneously sized gas turbine engines, making direct application to heterogeneous and distributed propulsion systems ambiguous. This work constructs generalized OEI performance requirements anchored to existing regulations and are parameterized by the specific excess power lost during a propulsion system failure, maintaining broad applicability to any aircraft and propulsion system architecture. Under the same parameterization, an “engine inoperative correction factor” is also constructed to scale the propulsion system size, enabling seamless integration into the aircraft sizing process. Both contributions are utilized to size a notional Elysian E9X, revealing system-level performance penalties for configurations sized under 4-, 5-, and 6-engine inoperative failure modes. The power loading decreases by up to 28%, thus increasing the aircraft’s maximum takeoff weight and battery energy stored onboard by up to 17% and 19%, respectively. Additional operational constraints prevent attaining system-level benefits for less severe propulsion system failure modes.

Orthogonal stepped-chiral metamaterial for load-bearing morphing skins: Topology-regulated mechanical response and deformation performance
abstract: Load-bearing morphing skins in advanced aerospace vehicles must sustain aerodynamic loads while undergoing large in-plane deformation, posing a persistent stiffness–compliance conflict. To address this challenge, this study proposes an orthogonal stepped-chiral (OSC) metamaterial architecture based on a dual-orthogonality design principle. By integrating global and local orthogonal geometries, the proposed structure decouples load-bearing and deformation pathways, thereby activating a stable pure bending–dominated mechanism that enhances deformation efficiency while suppressing geometric hardening. A topology-regulated configuration strategy enabled by chiral symmetry modulation allows three distinct array arrangements—regular, hybrid, and staggered—to achieve tensile–shear coupling, quasi-zero Poisson’s ratio behavior, and stiffness-enhanced zero Poisson’s ratio responses within a unified architecture. Theoretical analysis, numerical simulations, and experimental validation demonstrate that the OSC structure reduces the effective modulus along the morphing direction by 68% compared with accordion honeycombs and lowers actuation force by a factor of 16 relative to tetrachiral lattices at 10% strain, while maintaining highly linear large-deformation behavior. Prototype demonstrations for variable-sweep wings and morphing forebody structures further confirm its potential for aerospace morphing applications.

title: Aircraft takeoff weight estimation based on optimal control theory and statistical learning
abstract: Accurate estimation of aircraft takeoff mass (TOW) is essential for air traffic management, emissions modeling, and trajectory optimization, yet such information is rarely available in operational surveillance data. Existing statistical approaches can achieve high accuracy but rely on extensive proprietary feature sets and large, region-specific training datasets, limiting their generalizability. This paper introduces a physics-based methodology that integrates nonlinear optimal control with statistical learning to estimate TOW using only a small number of openly available flight parameters. Using the OpenAP performance model and the OpenAP.top trajectory optimizer, we generate a synthetic fuel-optimal dataset covering 36 aircraft types over systematically varied takeoff masses, flight distances, and air temperature. This dataset provides a controlled and physically consistent basis for training TOW estimation models without dependence on sensitive data. We evaluate two regression approaches across four compact feature sets using two to four inputs: altitude, distance, true airspeed, and temperature. Validation against about 390,000 real flights from the EUROCONTROL Performance Review Commission 2024 Data Challenge yields a global mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 6.19 % for aircraft type-specific estimation models. Although purely statistical models trained on the challenge dataset reach 4.12 % MAPE, their performance degrades substantially for underrepresented aircraft types, reflecting overfitting to dataset biases. Sensitivity analyses show that temperature offers modest benefits (0.03–3.7 % MAPE reduction), while consideration of wind yields moderate improvements (up to 4.13 % MAPE reduction). Two-feature models using only altitude and distance remain competitive, with MAPE increases of 0–6.4 % when weather data is unavailable. The methodology is fully reproducible, computationally efficient, and applicable to any aircraft with an available performance model, providing a scalable alternative to data-intensive approaches for operational mass estimation.
