Multi-objective aerodynamic co-optimization methodology and cross-regime coupling characteristics for continuum-transition flow
abstract: Vehicles in the transition flow and high-altitude continuum flow regimes possess irreplaceable strategic significance and substantial potential applications, attracting extensive attention in the development of advanced space transportation systems. However, to date, no mature transition–continuum flow vehicle has entered practical service. The primary reasons are as follows: (1) the mechanisms of rarefied aerodynamics remain unclear; (2) experimental and numerical simulation costs are prohibitively high; (3) significant discrepancies exist between transition flow and continuum flow aerodynamic characteristics, increasing the complexity of collaborative design; and (4) a comprehensive optimization framework applicable to transition–rarefied cross-regime aerodynamic design is still lacking. To address the above challenges, this study integrates numerical simulation methods, optimization algorithms, and surrogate modeling techniques, and proposes an integrated collaborative optimization design methodology for cross-regime vehicles. The proposed optimization framework demonstrates excellent performance across three optimization strategies, exhibiting strong search capability, multi-objective balancing ability, and robustness under complex conditions. The optimization results indicate that, without loss of lift, the continuum flow drag of an X-38-like configuration is reduced by 19.8%, and the lift-to-drag ratio is increased by 27.9%. In the transition flow regime, the drag coefficient is reduced by 9.28%, and the lift-to-drag ratio is improved by 12.5%, achieving an effective balance between continuum and transition aerodynamic characteristics. Furthermore, a coupled optimization strategy for transition–continuum flow is investigated for the X-38-like vehicle, leading to an important conclusion: the lift-to-drag characteristics in the transition flow regime are more significantly influenced by drag–lift coupling effects, and lift enhancement is more easily constrained by drag reduction. In addition, a mechanism analysis of cross-regime aerodynamic differences is conducted, revealing that substantial discrepancies exist between continuum and transition flow aerodynamic characteristics. Compared with continuum flow, the transition flow exhibits increased drag coefficient and reduced lift coefficient, and the surrounding flow field is more sensitive to geometric variations. Finally, five cross-regime multi-objective aerodynamic design principles for continuum–transition flow are summarized.

title: Predefined-time cooperative guidance law for multiple interceptors with LOS angle constraints and smooth switching topologies
A few-shot and physically restorable symbolic regression turbulence model based on normalized general effective-viscosity hypothesis
abstract: Turbulence is a complex, irregular flow phenomenon ubiquitous in natural processes and engineering applications. The Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) method, owing to its low computational cost, has become the primary approach for rapid simulation of engineering turbulence problems. However, the inaccuracy of classical turbulence models constitutes the main drawback of the RANS framework. With the rapid development of data-driven approaches, many data-driven turbulence models have been proposed, yet they still suffer from issues of generalizability and accuracy. In this work, we propose a few-shot, physically restorable, symbolic regression turbulence model based on the normalized general effective-viscosity hypothesis. Few-shot indicates that our model is trained on limited flow configurations spanning only a narrow subset of turbulent flow physics, yet can still outperform the baseline model in substantially different turbulent flows. Physically restorable means our model can nearly revert to the baseline model in regimes satisfying specific physical conditions, using only the symbolic regression training results. The normalized general effective-viscosity hypothesis was proposed in our previous study. Specifically, we first formalize the concept of few-shot data-driven turbulence models. Second, we train our symbolic regression turbulence models using only direct numerical simulation (DNS) data for three-dimensional periodic hill flow slices. Third, we evaluate our models on periodic hill flows, zero pressure gradient flat plate flow, NACA0012 airfoil flows, and NASA Rotor 37 transonic axial compressor flows. One of our symbolic regression turbulence models consistently outperforms the baseline model, and we further demonstrate that this model can nearly revert to baseline behavior in certain flow regimes.

title: Adaptive predefined-time control of PMSM drive system for suppressing hose whipping in aerial refueling
abstract: Hose whipping during the docking phase of aerial refueling poses a significant threat to operational safety. To address this challenge via precise and rapid hose length regulation, an adaptive predefined-time control (APTC) scheme is proposed for the permanent magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) drive system of the hose reel mechanism. A radial basis function neural network (RBFNN) is utilized to approximate and compensate for lumped uncertainties and unmodeled dynamics. Furthermore, a novel predefined-time command filter is developed to estimate the derivatives of virtual inputs and resolve the control singularity issue. Building upon these components, the predefined-time controllers and parameter adaptive laws are systematically synthesized via the backstepping framework. Rigorous theoretical analysis guarantees that the PMSM rotor position tracks the desired trajectory within a predefined time, and all signals in the closed-loop system remain uniformly ultimately bounded. Comprehensive simulations and hardware-in-the-loop experiments, including comparative analyses with a fixed-time control scheme, demonstrate that the proposed APTC achieves faster convergence and precise hose retraction, effectively suppressing the hose whipping.

A novel approach for pole erosion mitigation in Hall thrusters: Design and mechanism of an internally loaded magnetic field
abstract: Permanent magnet Hall thrusters with large height-radius ratios are ideal for the miniaturization and lightweighting of spacecraft propulsion systems due to wide channels and compact radial dimensions. However, severe magnetic pole erosion induced by divergent magnetic fields and compact structures limits their long-term stability. To solve this problem, this paper proposes an internally loaded magnetic field (ILMF) design with a segmented magnetic screen and optimized magnetic circuit. This scheme moves the ionization zone inward and lowers the magnetic pole end face, lengthening the particle bombardment path and reducing the potential difference near the channel exit. Numerical simulations show that the ILMF-configured Hall thruster reduces the peak ion flux and energy on magnetic poles by approximately 90% and 91%, respectively, and also decreases electron flux and energy, thus significantly suppressing magnetic pole erosion. Moreover, it improves magnetic utilization efficiency, enabling a height-radius ratio of 0.81 and a 5% reduction in outer channel radius, achieving further lightweighting with weakened ion wall losses. For a 1.35 kW Hall thruster, the ILMF-configured Hall thruster enhances thrust by 6.3%, specific impulse by 6.1%, and discharge efficiency from 54.2% to 60.5%. This design integrates long service life, high performance, and lightweighting, providing a novel solution for the optimization and engineering application of large height-radius ratio permanent magnet Hall thrusters and a reference for the development of space electric propulsion.

Dipole-field magnetic windows for radio-frequency transmission through hypersonic plasma sheaths: A reduced-order scaling model
abstract: Hypersonic vehicles and atmospheric-entry bodies can experience radio-frequency communication blackout when shock-heated gas surrounding the vehicle becomes sufficiently ionized that plasma cutoff and collisional attenuation restrict electromagnetic transmission. Magnetic-window approaches attempt to reduce this loss by exploiting the anisotropic dispersion of a magnetized plasma, in which selected right-hand or whistler-like modes may propagate along preferred directions. This paper develops a reduced-order scaling model for magnetic-window transmission through a finite-thickness hypersonic plasma sheath when the magnetic source is represented as an onboard axial dipole. The model gives a closed-form estimate of the collisionless angular aperture, compares the underlying projected-cyclotron criterion with full cold-plasma dispersion roots, and extends the aperture estimate to a loss-limited cone using a collisional optical-depth approximation. A simplified neutral-density, speed, and ionization closure is used only to generate qualitative parametric maps and sensitivity trends. The results clarify how dipole-field decay, sheath thickness, radio frequency, vehicle scale, electron density, and collisions jointly constrain the candidate transmission window. The contribution is intended as a screening framework for selecting cases for full-wave electromagnetic simulation, nonequilibrium aerothermochemistry, antenna-coupling analysis, and laboratory validation, rather than as a demonstrated engineering solution to plasma blackout.

Implicit simplified unified gas-kinetic scheme for diatomic rarefied flows based on OpenFOAM
abstract: An implicit simplified unified gas-kinetic scheme (ISUGKS) for diatomic gas flows is developed and implemented within the OpenFOAM framework. The solver integrates the Rykov kinetic model to characterize translational–rotational energy exchange and nonequilibrium effects, adopting an implicit macro–micro coupling strategy to eliminate the time-step limitation of explicit schemes. The macroscopic conservation equations are discretized using vector flux splitting, while the microscopic distribution function is solved with a first-order upwind scheme. Both systems are solved by a matrix-free point-relaxation symmetric Gauss–Seidel (PR-SGS) method for low cost and fast convergence. A dual-time-stepping approach is employed to preserve multiscale flow characteristics and accelerate steady-state convergence, and an error compensation technique is introduced to suppress conservation errors caused by velocity-space discretization. The interface flux is reconstructed via the right rectangular integration rule to simplify computation and improve efficiency. Validations are conducted through benchmark cases including a supersonic rarefied flow over a flat plate, a 3D supersonic/hypersonic flow over a sphere, an Apollo re-entry capsule, and a lifting-body vehicle, covering supersonic to hypersonic rarefied flow regimes. Numerical results show good agreement with experimental data, implicit UGKS, and DSMC solutions. Compared with the explicit counterpart, the proposed solver achieves more than one order of magnitude speedup under the same parallel configuration, demonstrating significantly improved efficiency for large-scale engineering simulations. The developed ISUGKS solver fills the gap of implicit multiscale kinetic solvers for diatomic gases in OpenFOAM and provides a reliable tool for hypersonic rarefied aerothermodynamic predictions.

Design and optimization of spacecraft architectures for asteroid impact mitigation
abstract: In a planetary defense setting, mitigation is the act of preventing a hazardous object from impacting or causing damage to Earth. This study addresses the question of how best to pre-position a set of mitigation spacecraft launching from Earth or maneuvering from a selection of in-space orbits in the Sun-Earth system for rapid use when a hazardous asteroid threat is discovered. Here, mitigation includes two approaches: kinetic deflection, in which a spacecraft impacts the asteroid to impart momentum and alter its orbit away from Earth, and robust disruption, in which the spacecraft impacts the asteroid with sufficient energy to deliberately break it apart so that none of the resulting fragments pose a danger to Earth. This study finds that kinetic deflection with a single impactor is an unreliable option for mitigation when accounting for the potential for partial asteroid fragmentation, which introduces stringent performance constraints and reduces the success rate by nearly an order of magnitude. Robust disruption via kinetic impact is more broadly successful for low warning times. However, its maximum effectiveness is limited to asteroids of approximately 200 m in diameter. The most successful single spacecraft approach, for kinetic deflection and robust disruption, is to use a 8,000 kg and 10,000 kg class spacecraft launched by a heavy class vehicle, respectively. In general, architectures incorporating ground-launched spacecraft achieved higher success rates than space-based-only architectures. Nevertheless, the highest-performing locations for space-based spacecraft augmenting near-Earth spacecraft included L3 vertical and L4/L5 short-period orbits, although the specific trends vary between scenarios. For objects larger than roughly 200 m—particularly when warning times are short—alternative mitigation approaches, such as multiple kinetic impactors or nuclear explosive devices, should continue to be investigated.

title: Mission-level assessment of subsystems electrification in hybrid-electric turboprop aircraft conceptual design
abstract: Electrification of aircraft subsystems has been widely studied in the context of more-electric aircraft; however, its potential benefits may be more pronounced with electrified propulsion architectures, because subsystem electric loads are more directly coupled to onboard power and energy management. Nevertheless, the mission-level impacts of subsystem electrification in hybrid-electric propulsion concepts remain insufficiently quantified. This study develops a unified assessment framework to quantify how subsystem-level variations in mass, drag, and secondary power demand influence aircraft-level performance metrics, including fuel burn, energy consumption, and range capability. The framework is applied to a hybrid-electric regional turboprop aircraft, focusing on two major pneumatic power consumers: the environmental control system (ECS) and the ice protection system (IPS). Beyond the electrification of ECS and IPS themselves, this study proposes and analyzes novel subsystem architectures in which the electrified subsystems are powered directly by the main battery in the hybrid propulsion system. Results show that, despite a modest weight penalty, ECS electrification reduces mission fuel burn and energy consumption primarily through improved engine efficiency enabled by eliminating its bleed air extraction. IPS electrification improves fuel burn, energy consumption, and range capability under icing conditions by reducing aerodynamic drag penalties. Finally, powering the electrified ECS and IPS directly from the main battery increases battery energy utilization on short missions, yielding approximately 1% additional fuel savings and 0.5% energy savings, at the cost of a slight reduction in range capability.

Shadow modeling with warm-up time for multi-revolution low thrust transfers
abstract: Low thrust solar powered missions are challenging for their requirement of long duration missions with extended periods of thrusting. The complexity of the mission design and trajectory optimization is enhanced by the occurrences of eclipses when the solar arrays generate no power for the duration of the eclipse forcing the spacecraft to coast and leaving the essential systems to be supported by the battery. Therefore, the charge depletion of the battery and the temperature drop of the engine are consequent events that deter automatic retrieval of thrusting capability even when the spacecraft just ventures out of the shadow region. This is called as warm up period which typically depends on the duration of the eclipse. Though important in practice, warm up time has never been formally included as a factor at the level of trajectory optimization. This work shows the capability of accommodating such discrete events like warm up time in the indirect optimization to obtain a more realistic eclipse constrained fuel-optimal solution for the first time.

Design and analysis of a high-precision separation mechanism for on-orbit launch of micro-spacecraft
abstract: With the sharp increase in the amount of space debris, space debris removal technologies have become a research hotspot in the aerospace field. Utilizing micro-spacecraft for on-orbit launch to perform rapid debris deorbiting missions has emerged as a key research direction, and the launch attitude is a critical factor determining mission success. This study establishes launch dynamics models of separation mechanisms with different configurations using ADAMS software under multiple operating conditions. Based on these models, the influence of the mechanism configuration on the launch disturbance of the micro-spacecraft is analyzed, and the mechanism responsible for generating large disturbances is revealed. On this basis, by comprehensively considering the advantages of various separation mechanisms, a novel high-precision separation mechanism is proposed. Theoretical analysis, transient collision cross-section design, and guide rail fit parameter optimization are performed. The research results show that, in terms of suppressing the launch disturbance of the micro-spacecraft, the cylindrical separation mechanism delivers the best performance, and the continuous-contact straight guide rail outperforms the gradient guide rail. After integrating all factors, the newly designed separation mechanism achieves its optimal parameter combination with a guide rail length of 270 mm and a fit clearance of 0.2 mm. Compared with the currently used circular-guide-rail separation mechanism, the overall launch accuracy is improved by 82.76%.

Impact of non-equilibrium radiation in a high-enthalpy inductively coupled plasma wind tunnel
abstract: High-power inductively coupled plasma (ICP) wind tunnels are widely used to reproduce high-enthalpy environments relevant to atmospheric entry and hypersonic testing. Despite their importance, radiative heat transfer in ICP facilities is commonly neglected or modeled using simplified optically thin assumptions, and the impact of non-equilibrium radiation on plasma dynamics remains poorly quantified. In this work, a loosely coupled, multi-physics framework is developed to systematically investigate radiative cooling effects in the 350 kW Plasmatron X facility at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The approach self-consistently couples a magnetohydrodynamic plasma framework with a spectral radiative transport solver, eliminating the need for optically thin or empirical models. Simulations are performed for nitrogen and air plasmas over a wide range of operating pressures (1-101 kPa) and powers (100-350 kW). The results reveal a strong pressure dependence of radiative losses, with radiation contributing negligibly at low pressures, but becoming a dominant energy sink at elevated pressures. At atmospheric pressure, radiative losses account for up to approximately 32% and 22% of the input power for nitrogen and air plasmas, respectively, leading to substantial reductions in core plasma temperatures. Nitrogen plasmas consistently exhibit higher radiative losses than air as a result of increased concentrations of radiatively active species and higher electron number densities. Pressure-power maps of radiative heat loss relative to input power are constructed to quantify combined operating effects and to provide guidance for facility operation and modeling fidelity. Finally, an assessment of self-absorption demonstrates that the Plasmatron X torch operates predominantly in an optically thin regime, even at the highest power and pressure conditions considered.

Impact vector guidance with monotonically decreasing look angle
abstract: This paper addresses the impact vector control guidance (IVCG) problem under field-of-view (FOV) constraints for missiles equipped with strap-down seekers. Through an angle shaping approach, an auxiliary variable is introduced to combine the look angle and the three-dimensional (3D) impact angle error, which ensures the convergence of both quantities through the convergence of this single variable. Theoretical analysis is conducted to reveal the feasible achievable impact vectors that ensure the look angle decreases monotonically, thereby strictly satisfying the FOV constraint throughout the engagement. The main benefit of the proposed 3D approach is that it enables the look angle of the strap-down seeker to decrease monotonically under a looser constraint than existing two-dimensional (2D) methods, while guaranteeing convergence of the terminal guidance command. The efficacy and superiority of the proposed guidance law are demonstrated through comprehensive numerical simulations.

Ignition thresholds of HTP-ethanol bipropellants with an electrothermal mesh igniter
abstract: Reliable low-power ignition is essential for replacing toxic hypergolic propellants with green bipropellant systems in spacecraft propulsion. This work experimentally evaluates a Nickel–Chromium (NiCr) thermal wire mesh igniter for high-test peroxide (HTP) with ethanol and Jet A in two laboratory configurations: open premixed surface ignition and confined spray-through hot-mesh ignition. Each power condition was repeated five times, and thresholds were defined as the minimum power producing at least 80% self-sustained ignition success ( ≥ 4/5). In the open configuration, ethanol–HTP and Jet A–HTP reached self-sustained ignition at 12.5 W and 10.0 W, respectively, corresponding to an estimated pre-contact mesh temperature of approximately 420 ∘ C and 380 ∘ C, respectively. In the confined configuration, thresholds decreased to 10 W for ethanol–HTP and 7.5 W for Jet A–HTP, corresponding to approximately 380 ∘ C and 320 ∘ C, respectively. Ignition delay time, estimated from 240 fps video, decreased from approximately 500–700 ms near threshold to 50–75 ms at the highest tested powers. The results indicate that NiCr mesh ignition can provide repeatable, low-power ignition of HTP-based green bipropellants, while confinement improves ignition by increasing heat retention and reactant residence near the heated mesh.

Distribution-agnostic robust trajectory optimization via chance-constrained reinforcement learning
abstract: This paper presents a distribution-agnostic robust trajectory-optimization framework based on chance-constrained reinforcement learning. The uncertainty is represented here through initial conditions and process noise, with the only requirement being that it can be sampled. A deterministic nominal trajectory is first computed offline, and reinforcement learning is then used only to robustify that baseline through a structured affine closed-loop correction law comprising a feedforward control adjustment and time-varying feedback gains. Probabilistic feasibility is enforced empirically through rollout-based upper-tail quantiles, while terminal dispersion is regulated through covariance-feasibility penalties. The framework is assessed on two materially different trajectory design problems. The flagship case study is a three-dimensional multi-impulse Earth–Mars transfer, where the learned policy is benchmarked against a recent robust trajectory-optimization reference under Gaussian uncertainty and then evaluated under bounded uniform uncertainty and under process disturbances not seen during training. The second case study is a stochastic atmospheric pinpoint rocket landing problem, used to assess portability to a short-horizon continuous-thrust setting with drag, mass depletion, and glide-slope constraints. The results show that the proposed framework can remain competitive in upper-tail fuel cost while preserving probabilistic feasibility, and that the same robustification scaffold can be carried across heterogeneous spacecraft trajectory planning problems without redesign of its core stochastic-control structure.

title: An explainable safety assessment and decision framework for UAV emergency landing in urban low-altitude airspace
abstract: Emergency landing is a critical safety function for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) operating in urban low-altitude airspace, where complex environments and ground-risk exposure impose stringent requirements on both landing-site selection and approach-trajectory safety. To address this challenge, this paper presents a semantic-driven and explainable safety assessment and decision framework for UAV emergency landing. From scene-level semantic information, the proposed method constructs complementary safety representations that explicitly characterize touchdown-area feasibility, overflight risk distribution, and hard exclusion zones around high-risk entities. Based on fixed feasibility constraints, a diverse set of non-overlapping emergency landing zone (ELZ) candidates is generated to support consistent and reproducible evaluation.To enable end-to-end assessment, a unified safety evaluation protocol is further developed to quantify site-level safety, path-level safety, and their combined global safety. This formulation provides an interpretable decomposition of safety factors and enables direct comparison across different decision strategies. Experimental results in simulation-consistent urban environments demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves end-to-end emergency landing safety compared with representative site-only and path-only decision baselines. In particular, the joint decision strategy achieves the best global safety performance with improved robustness, while the heading-aware planner yields higher overflight safety than geometric shortest-path and semantic A* baselines. These results indicate that explicitly coupling landing-site feasibility and trajectory safety is beneficial for reliable emergency landing decision-making. Beyond algorithmic design, this work establishes a standardized and data-driven safety assessment benchmark, providing a principled foundation for future learning-based and safety-critical UAV emergency landing systems.

title: Adaptive trajectory prediction for RGV: A physical-prior intelligent dynamic algorithm
abstract: In the field of air defense, high-speed and highly maneuverable Reentry Glide Vehicles (RGVs) pose a significant threat to intercepting parties. Achieving high-precision trajectory prediction for RGVs is a core challenge for effective interception. Existing methods often lack adaptability when the target's maneuvering pattern changes abruptly, leading to large prediction errors. To address this issue, this paper proposes a physics-prior-driven intelligent adaptive prediction framework called the Physical-prior Intelligent Dynamic Algorithm (PIDA).First, the rate of change of flight path angle and the rate of change of heading angle are extracted as kinematic features. Real-time identification of maneuvering patterns is realized based on Random Forest, and the identification results are used as physical prior information. Subsequently, a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is constructed to predict aerodynamic acceleration and control parameters respectively. The pattern probability output by the Random Forest is used as weights to perform adaptive weighted fusion of the two integrated trajectories. Simulation results show that the Mean Euclidean Distance (MED) of PIDA in equilibrium gliding and skip gliding modes is stably maintained at 0.6620 km and 1.5614 km respectively, which is significantly superior to traditional parameterized methods and various deep learning models in multi-index comparison. Ablation experiments further verify the effectiveness of the pattern recognition module and physical prior information. This study provides a solution with high precision, strong adaptability, and physical rationality for trajectory prediction of highly maneuverable targets, which has important reference value for improving the actual combat capability of interception systems.

title: Corrigendum to “flow mechanism-embedded deep learning for modeling geometric uncertainty effects on aerodynamic stability” [Aerospace science and technology, volume 179 part 1, 2026, 113198]
Full-gap kinetic limitation of thermionic-electron transport for electron transpiration cooling
abstract: Electron transpiration cooling (ETC) can reduce aerothermal loads on sharp hypersonic leading edges, but its performance is governed by whether thermionically emitted electrons escape the hot surface or return as cathode-directed backflow. Here, a one-dimensional-in-space, three-dimensional-in-velocity electrostatic particle-in-cell/Monte Carlo collision model is developed for a full cathode--anode plasma diode, resolving thermionic emission, collisional plasma transport, emitted-electron backflow, and downstream collection. A helium benchmark is used to examine emitted-electron transport and backflow-limited current flow. With increasing imposed emission, the diode first remains in a weak-backflow regime, where net emitted-electron transport and downstream collection both increase with emission. Further increasing the emission produces a sharp transition to backflow-limited transport between $7.0\times10^{19}$ and $7.5\times10^{19},\mathrm{m^{-2},s^{-1}}$. At $7.25\times10^{19},\mathrm{m^{-2},s^{-1}}$, the backflow ratio reaches $54.03%$, while the net transport and downstream collection efficiencies fall to about $46%$. Above this transition, added backflow overcompensates the imposed emission increase, reducing useful emitted-electron transport rather than causing saturation. Boundary energy diagnostics show that stronger emission may still increase the nominal cathode-side cooling metric, but after transition this metric no longer indicates improved emitted-electron escape or full-gap transport. These results show that the present PIC-MCC framework captures the key kinetic processes governing ETC-relevant emitted-electron escape and backflow limitation.

title: Deep reinforcement learning-based thrust recovery control strategy for STOVL propulsion systems
Predefined-time disturbance-rejection tracking control applied to vertical take-off and landing aircraft systems
A generalised inverse-design framework for variable camber wings: A supersonic thin airfoil case study
Experimental and numerical investigation on lean ignition and blowout performance of a pilot flameholder with aerodynamic shielding in dual-channel flows
Flutter optimization of variable stiffness composite skins in supersonic viscoelastic sandwich panels
abstract: This study explores optimization of flutter stability in viscoelastic sandwich panels with variable stiffness composite (VSC) skins under supersonic airflow, using a Genetic Algorithm with manufacturing constraints on fibre curvature. Both constant stiffness composite (CSC) skins with unidirectional fibres and VSC skins with curvilinear fibres, parametrized by linear and sinusoidal fibre angle distributions, are examined under simply supported and clamped boundary conditions. Aeroelastic flutter analyses are performed resorting to a numerically accurate and computationally efficient layerwise finite element model coupled with the first-order piston theory. Design optimization results indicate that carefully tailored VSC skins significantly enhance flutter performance as compared to conventional skins made of metal or CSC laminate, with improvements ranging from 0.3% to 15% in flutter dynamic pressure parameter and 0.5% to 19% in flutter Mach number. These flutter improvements are strongly influenced by boundary conditions, parametrization of spatially varying fibre orientations, and maximum curvature constraint, highlighting the importance of balancing aeroelastic benefits against manufacturability.

title: Numerical–experimental investigation of the aeroacoustic environment of a launch vehicle in transonic descent
A two-layer predictive guidance method for powered landing via online trajectory planning based on convex optimization
Investigation of flared folding wing tips on gust load alleviation potential based on URANS simulations
abstract: Gust loads pose a significant structural challenge in the design of highly flexible modern aircraft. Flared folding wing tips (FWT) offer a promising passive load alleviation mechanism by enabling targeted aeroelastic morphing. This study investigates the aerodynamic performance and structural load alleviation potential of a flared FWT during a standard CS-25 related 1-minus-cosine discrete gust encounter. A comprehensive computational framework, integrating high-fidelity RANS and URANS simulations with Gaussian Process (GP) surrogate modeling, is deployed to evaluate the complex design space governing the wing tip kinematics. The initial static GP assessment maps a parameter space spanning fold angles from 0 ∘ to 15 ∘ and flare angles from 0 ∘ to 45 ∘ , identifying the flare angle Λ = 45 ∘ flare configuration as the load alleviation most promising case. Subsequent URANS analyses reveal that the gust-induced actuation of the FWT drives a localized reduction in the angle of attack through kinematic coupling. This highly effective aerodynamic tailoring sheds extreme outboard lift and redistributes the spanwise aerodynamic loads inboard. The structural hinge stiffness K , evaluated across a range from 5 kNm/rad to 150 kNm/rad alongside a free-floating idealization, is identified as the dominant parameter governing this transient aerodynamic response. A free-floating hinge maximizes geometric morphing, actively neutralizing localized lift surges and yielding, albeit idealized, reduction in the peak wing root bending moment compared to a rigid baseline. While real-world aeroelastic wing bending and torsion would dynamically alter the local inflow conditions, this rigid-wing framework establishes the theoretical upper bound of the mechanism’s load alleviation potential. Conversely, introducing higher structural hinge stiffness systematically suppresses the dynamic fold mechanism, restricting aerodynamic unloading and proportionally degrading the load alleviation potential. While highly compliant, large-flare designs represent the theoretical aerodynamic ideal case, preliminary multidisciplinary assessments regarding aeroelastic stability boundaries might indicate that a tailored structural stiffness combined with an intermediate flare angle is required to realize optimal, safe gust load alleviation in future aircraft designs. Consequently, detailed aeroelastic fluid-structure interaction (FSI) investigations remain a critical necessity to address these complex boundary conditions.

Leading-edge surface contamination effects on boundary-layer separation and wake dynamics of a low-Reynolds-number wind turbine blade
abstract: This study investigates the aerodynamic impact of leading-edge surface contamination on a NACA 63 (3) -418 horizontal-axis wind turbine blade section operating in a low-Reynolds-number regime. While conventional high-Reynolds-number aerodynamics characterises surface roughness as strictly detrimental, this research evaluates the regime-dependent potential of surface roughness to act as a beneficial flow-control mechanism. Utilising Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), we quantified the effects of varying roughness severities (P80 and P40 grits), suction-side chordwise extents (2 %, 6 %, and 10 %), and contamination densities (3 % and 4 %). Results demonstrate an angle of attack (α) dependent dual aerodynamic response. In the pre-stall regime (α ≤ 4°), leading-edge roughness acts as a parasitic disturbance, forcing premature boundary layer transition and increasing the recirculation area by approximately 35 % compared to the clean baseline. Conversely, at the transitional angle of α = 8°, coarser P40 grit reduced the recirculation area by 94 % relative to the clean baseline recirculation area. This was achieved by inducing a micro-recirculation bubble that injected turbulent kinetic energy into the near wall region, forcing rapid flow reattachment. Under deep stall conditions (α = 12°), restricting the finer P80 grit to a 2 % suction-side extent at 3 % contamination density proved optimal. This configuration injected concentrated near-wall turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), delaying separation from x/c ≈ 0.16 to x/c > 0.9. These findings reveal that highly localised degradation functions effectively as a passive stall-delay mechanism. Critically, for condition-based maintenance of low-speed rotors, the chordwise extent of leading-edge contamination is a more aerodynamically significant parameter than its mere presence.

GNN guided hierarchical reinforcement learning for resilient reconfiguration of heterogeneous satellite cluster
abstract: To address the critical challenges of noneuclidean topology awareness, realtime decision-making, and strict constraint satisfaction in future large scale heterogeneous satellite clusters, this paper proposes a topology-semantic guided hierarchical framework: GNN-HDRL. The architecture leverages Heterogeneous Graph Attention Networks (GAT) to transform complex, dynamic topologies into informative latent embeddings, effectively capturing the intricate relational semantics among diverse satellite types. A Manager-Worker hierarchical structure is employed to decouple high level reconfiguration planning from low level atomic control, successfully mitigating the dimensionality curse inherent in massive, multiagent space systems. Crucially, we introduce a State Aware Dynamic Action Bias mechanism that integrates hard physical constraints—such as energy safety and collision avoidance directly into the forward propagation path of the policy network. This ensures 100% action validity and resolves exploration inefficiencies in sparse-reward space environments. Simulations under J2 perturbed dynamics demonstrate that GNN-HDRL achieves a 4.6% higher reward than MAPPO and maintains a 95.2% completion rate under extreme 42% satellite failures. Most importantly, the framework exhibits robust topology invariant representation, achieving a 97.2% completion rate when transferred zeroshot from a 12 satellite training set to a 72 satellite scenario. These results provide a scalable and resilient paradigm for the autonomous management of future heterogeneous mega-constellations.

title: Roll control using Co-Flow jet actuators: Modeling, control and experiments
Robust safety-critical control for attitude tracking on TSO(3)
A physics-based correction model for swirl number prediction in axial swirlers with surrogate-assisted calibration
Receding horizon control for quadrotors under semi-Markovian intermittent measurements and quantization
abstract: Visual positioning systems are crucial for quadrotor trajectory tracking, but mechanical vibrations and environmental variations often cause bursty intermittent measurements, which are better characterized by a semi-Markovian process. To overcome these issues, this paper proposes a novel visual receding horizon control method for quadrotors subject to semi-Markovian intermittent measurements and quantization. First, a linearized tracking error model is established, explicitly accounting for the quantization effects and the time-correlated nature of feature extraction failures. Furthermore, a min-max optimization problem involving a stochastic variable and a terminal penalty function is formulated to guarantee robustness against worst-case quantization errors. Based on Lyapunov stability theory for semi-Markovian jump systems, sufficient conditions are derived to guarantee the mean-square asymptotic stability of the closed-loop system. The terminal weighting matrix is solved offline via linear matrix inequalities (LMIs), while the control law is computed online. Finally, numerical simulations and flight experiments validate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.

title: Adaptive weighted robust control for flexible launch vehicles based on rigid-elastic coupling analysis
abstract: This paper focuses on the attitude control problem of flexible launch vehicles subject to strong rigid-elastic interaction and parameter uncertainties. A systematic analysis and control design framework is developed by combining rigid-elastic coupling evaluation, uncertainty sensitivity assessment, and adaptive robust control. First, two indicators are established to describe the bidirectional coupling between rigid-body motion and elastic vibration, which enables the coupling intensity to be evaluated along the flight trajectory. The analysis shows that the rigid-elastic interaction reaches a pronounced level around the maximum dynamic pressure condition, where the closed-loop system is also more sensitive to controller and model parameters. To improve the efficiency of robust controller synthesis, the influence of uncertain parameters on the system sensitivity characteristics is further examined, and the dominant uncertainty factors affecting robustness are determined. On this basis, two μ-synthesis controllers with different design emphases are developed for low-frequency attitude tracking and mid-to-high-frequency vibration attenuation, respectively. An adaptive weighting mechanism is then introduced to coordinate the two controllers according to flight and disturbance conditions, so that the control system can adjust its robustness preference online. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach provides accurate attitude tracking while effectively suppressing elastic vibration, and it enhances disturbance rejection and robustness against parameter variations over a broad frequency range.

title: Multiphysics aeroelastic stability of axially moving functionally graded perovskite‑piezoelectric plates under yawed supersonic flow: A hybrid numerical‑machine learning framework
A physics-informed generative framework for predicting symmetry-plane unstart flow evolution in a turbine-based combined-cycle inlet
abstract: Unstart in turbine-based combined-cycle (TBCC) inlets is characterized by highly unsteady shock dynamics and complex flow separation, posing substantial challenges to existing intelligent models for accurate flow prediction. To address this issue, this work proposes a physics-informed multimodal temporal-spatial Diffusion Transformer (PI-MTSDiT) framework for predicting unstart-flow evolution in a TBCC inlet. The model is built upon a Diffusion Transformer backbone, augmented with multimodal conditional injection and an interleaved temporal-spatial attention mechanism to capture long-range dependencies among flow variables. Discrete residuals of the unsteady compressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations are evaluated using finite-volume operators and incorporated into the training process as physical constraints. With limited training data, the proposed model can predict unstart evolution beyond the training set and capture key flow features unseen in the training data, including flow separation and shock spillage at the cowl lip. Compared with the purely data-driven MTSDiT, Transformer, and convolutional long short-term memory (ConvLSTM) baselines, PI-MTSDiT reduces the average root-mean-square error (RMSE) of the physical fields during unstart evolution by 20.98%, 70.18%, and 81.00%, respectively. For near-wall parameter prediction under the unstart state, the average relative error is reduced by 20%~75%. These results demonstrate that integrating Diffusion Transformer modeling with physics-constrained training provides a promising and efficient framework for enhancing both the extrapolation capability and physical consistency of unstart-flow prediction.

title: Analysis of formation flight aerodynamics using vortex lattice method and convolutional neural networks
Ejection-based payload deployment for efficient on-orbit servicing of mega-constellations
abstract: The prevailing assumption holds that on-orbit servicing (OOS) of mega-constellations is infeasible due to the prohibitive fuel consumption incurred by multiple rendezvous maneuvers across vast and dispersed satellite populations. To address this challenge, a novel OOS architecture termed Ejection-based Payload Deployment (EPD) is proposed in this paper. Within this framework, a service spacecraft (SSc) ejects micro-payload spacecraft (PSc) into transfer orbits, after which the PSc autonomously rendezvous with target spacecraft (TSc). By confining propulsive maneuvers to the much lighter PSCs, total fuel consumption is significantly reduced. This paper develops a phase-based approximation algorithm to resolve the scheduling problems arising from cumulative recoil-induced orbital perturbations. Numerical simulations for a constellation of over 100 satellites demonstrate that this algorithm reduces computation time by over 90% while maintaining ejection velocity errors below 1%. Further analysis yields an analytical formula for evaluating the deployment capability of the EPD system, providing planning estimates with less than 2% error within low Earth orbit (LEO) regimes. Finally, a case study of the Starlink Gen2 constellation confirms the EPD system’s substantial propellant economy relative to conventional methods.

title: Dynamics and cascade control of a solar sail on a displaced solar orbit
abstract: Solar sails represent a promising propulsion technology for long-duration space missions. This study investigates the modeling and control of a large-scale square solar sail operating on a displaced solar orbit. A high-fidelity coupled orbit-attitude-flexibility dynamic model is developed, incorporating the synergistic effects of orbital thermal loads, solar radiation pressure (SRP), and gravity. To achieve precise station-keeping on this non-Keplerian orbit, a novel cascade control architecture is designed. This architecture strategically decouples the control problem: the outer loop handles orbit tracking and dynamically allocates the required thrust between SRP and electric propulsion, while the inner loop implements a fault-tolerant strategy to ensure robust attitude control in the presence of actuator anomalies. Numerical simulations reveal that orbital thermal loads can induce a reduction in structural natural frequencies and may even lead to local structural slackness. The controller's performance is validated in displaced orbit scenarios. Results demonstrate that the system robustly converges from initial state errors and maintains the desired orbit, primarily utilizing SRP with only minimal supplemental electric thrust. This work establishes a comprehensive modeling and control framework, confirming the feasibility and superior energy efficiency of solar sails for sustained orbital missions.

title: Risk-aware rolling scheduling for continuous paired-satellite surveillance in LEO constellations
Linear and nonlinear buckling analysis of bi-directional FG‑TPMS sandwich panels: a Chebyshev–Ritz, bagging ensemble, GA–PSO, and experimental approach
Numerical analysis of quad-rotor aerodynamic and aeroacoustic performance with automated trimming algorithm
abstract: The current work introduces a novel and affordable Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) methodology for the purpose of assessing the aerodynamic and aero-acoustic performance of multi-rotor systems under trimmed flight conditions. The approach couples a simple Proportional-Integral (P-I) based trim algorithm and steady state CFD solver to automate the process of determining the set of control variables that results in balanced flight conditions. The methodology’s low computational cost is primarily achieved by including the rotors’ effects on the flow field with actuator models. A partial validation of the rotor modeling approach in isolated hover conditions reveals slight discrepancies in the computed aerodynamic loads but good agreement with experimental results in terms of the prediction of tonal noise. The CFD procedure is subsequently applied to evaluate a quad-rotor Unmanned Aerial Vehicle’s (UAV) performance in varied flight scenarios. The obtained results demonstrate that this automated approach effectively predicts quad-rotor performance trends, aligning with previously published data. Key findings include the fact that a hybrid over-mounted fore rotor and under-mounted aft rotor configuration negatively affects forward flight performance, and that the airframe’s geometry and distribution around the Center of Gravity can have a significant impact on flight characteristics. Finally, comparisons between the automated trim procedure and manually imposed trim parameters in transient aero-acoustic simulations reveal a more accurate approximation of trim when using the automated method. The comparison additionally highlights the importance of simulating multi-rotor systems in physically representative flight conditions as notable differences in the UAV’s acoustic footprint are observed between cases.

title: Exploiting control surface reversal for active and passive manoeuvre load alleviation
abstract: High-aspect-ratio wings offer significant aerodynamic efficiency gains but face substantial structural mass penalties because wing sizing is strongly driven by manoeuvre loads. Effective manoeuvre load alleviation is therefore a key enabler of such configurations. However, current manoeuvre load alleviation strategies still require trade-offs: active systems demand high torsional stiffness and therefore increase structural mass, whereas passive manoeuvre load alleviation through composite tailoring reduces roll control authority. This paper shows that intentionally operating control surfaces beyond their reversal point can combine key elements of both approaches within a single aeroelastic design framework, enabling simultaneous active and passive manoeuvre load alleviation while satisfying a prescribed steady-roll authority requirement. An aeroelastic optimisation framework incorporating analytical control-deflection sensitivities is developed and applied to a representative mid-range transport wing. Detailed aeroelastic analysis reveals that, in swept composite wings, control surface reversal is governed by wing-level spanwise load redistribution arising from bending-torsion coupling and elastic-flexural-axis misalignment, rather than by a purely local sectional effect. Load redistribution extends far inboard of the control-surface region, providing an effective mechanism for shifting manoeuvre loads away from the outboard wing. The reversal-enabled design achieves 13.3% structural mass reduction compared to a conventionally optimised baseline while meeting the prescribed steady-roll requirement in nominal operation and in a representative single-surface loss-of-function case with the midboard control surface disabled. These results indicate that, within the present modelling scope, control surface reversal can be purposefully exploited for manoeuvre load alleviation and structural-mass reduction in high-aspect-ratio wings.

title: Effects of combustor exit non-uniform flow on aerodynamic excitation characteristics of high-pressure turbine rotor blades

Modeling of the ion environment in very low earth orbit and assessment of its erosive effects on spacecraft surface materials
abstract: The development and utilization of very low Earth orbit (VLEO, 70–300 km) have become increasingly important in space activities. However, the complex space environment poses significant erosion threats to spacecraft surface materials. Beyond atomic oxygen (AO) oxidation, erosion induced by charged ions has attracted growing attention. Nevertheless, the generation mechanisms and spatial distribution of ion components in VLEO remain insufficiently understood, limiting accurate material erosion assessment, protective design, and ground-based simulation experiments. To address this issue, a multiphysics coupled simulation model was developed to investigate the generation mechanisms and spatial distribution of the VLEO ion environment. The results show that, driven by solar radiation, atmospheric species undergo photoionization and electron-impact ionization, forming a multicomponent ion environment primarily composed of O+, N+, NO+, O2+, and N2+. Among these ions, O+ is the dominant species, with a peak number density of 1.71×1012 m-3 at an altitude of approximately 300 km, while molecular ions (NO+, O2⁺, and N2⁺) are mainly distributed at lower altitudes. In addition, the effects of realistic factors, including solar activity, on the evolution of the ion environment were further analyzed. Based on the simulated ion densities, material erosion at a representative altitude of 300 km was evaluated. The results indicate that O+ can cause an annual erosion depth of 107.7 μm and a mass loss of 1129.5 g·m⁻² on silver interconnect materials in solar arrays, potentially exceeding the damage caused by AO-dominated chemical erosion and posing a serious threat to spacecraft operational safety.

Enhancing the diversity of solutions in system design optimization
abstract: During the design and optimization of complex systems, decision makers may be interested in obtaining a set of high-performance solutions that present a diversity of characteristics of interest. Quality-Diversity (QD) optimization algorithms model the latter as feature functions which are discretized. The aim is to find a single performing solution with respect to the objective function inside each combination of feature function intervals (called a niche). For example, in sounding rocket design, one may want to find the lightest architecture for a set of orbit and payload specifications. However, several system architectures embedding different technologies ( e.g. , number of rocket stages, type of rocket propulsion) can grant equivalent performances in a given niche. Current QD approaches only allow to identify the most performing one. This work proposes a novel QD framework where different solutions can occupy the same niche to provide more knowledge to the decision makers when deciding which solution to adopt for future design phases. In this paper, a mathematical formulation of the problem is developed. Four methods are proposed and their associated algorithms are detailed. Numerical simulations are done on an analytical test case and a sounding rocket design problem to assess their performances. It is shown that one of them is able to find the very best solutions in each niche and two others grant the discovery of a large batch of solutions. The last one allows to find a tradeoff between finding performing solutions and enhancing a great diversity of designs.

Challenges and remedies for accurate performance prediction of a multistage large-clearance axial compressor
abstract: This paper addresses the challenges of conventional steady Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) simulations in predicting the aerodynamic performance of large-clearance multistage axial compressors and proposes practical remedies to enhance prediction accuracy. The study is based on a 4-stage high-speed Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) compressor, which represents the middle-rear stages of a one-shaft gas turbine compressor. Conventional RANS simulations predict the performance well for the small-clearance case, but they over-predict the 3D tip blockage and losses in the front stages of the large-clearance case, leading to premature stall onset. To address these shortcomings, an advanced combination of turbulence model corrections is identified, which includes the quadratic constitutive relation (QCR) correction, relaxing the linear constitutive relation assumption of the Boussinesq approximation, and the vortical pressure gradient correction, incorporating the vortex stretching effect due to the pressure gradient in non-equilibrium 3D separated flows. The advanced turbulence model effectively reduces the prediction error of the conventional model by about 76% for total pressure ratio, 50% for isentropic efficiency, and 77% for stall margin. It also demonstrates strong predictive accuracy for overall performance and stage matching for both small and large clearance compressors. The proposed advanced turbulence model could be a promising tool for future small-core engine compressor design cycles.

A numerical study of additively manufactured lattice structures for bird strike resistance in UAV leading edges
abstract: Bird strikes remain a major threat to lightweight composite aircraft structures, particularly leading-edge (L.E) components that experience severe impact loading. This study investigates the bird-strike performance of a composite UAV L.E reinforced with additively manufactured lattice structures using three topologies (Body-Centred (BC), Body-Centred Cubic (BC-cubic), and Face-Centred Cubic (FC-cubic) combined with uniform (1.5 and 2.0 mm) and functionally graded (1-2 mm) strut configurations. A validated Abaqus/Explicit finite element model employing a Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) bird model was used to evaluate the structural response. The influence of lattice topology and functional grading on stress transfer, energy absorption, plastic deformation, structural displacement, and mass efficiency was systematically assessed. The results show that lattice topology governs the impact load-transfer mechanism, whereas functional grading improves structural efficiency through optimized material distribution. The BC topology promoted extensive lattice deformation and high specific energy absorption but resulted in larger structural deformation and increased loading of the composite skin. In contrast, the FC-cubic topology exhibited higher stiffness but transferred a greater portion of the impact load to the composite, causing localized damage. The BC-cubic topology achieved the most balanced response by concentrating plastic deformation within the lattice while preserving the composite skin. Among all configurations, the functionally graded BC-cubic lattice demonstrated the best overall structural efficiency, providing an optimal compromise between lightweight design, stress redistribution, controlled plastic deformation, and bird-strike resistance.

Schur-complement iterative SOCP strategy for free-final-time fuel-optimal orbital rendezvous
Deformation compatibility and clearance stability of a ceramic matrix composite turbine outer shroud support structure under thermal cycling
Hybrid offline-to-online kickstarting with advantage-weighted regression for agile fixed-wing UAV flight control
abstract: High-fidelity fixed-wing UAV flight control requires policies that can coordinate altitude, speed, and heading during rapid maneuvers while avoiding early exploration failures.This paper proposes Hybrid Offline-to-Online Kickstarting with Advantage-Weighted Regression (HOK-AWR), a single-stage hybrid training framework for agile fixed-wing flight control. HOK-AWR combines dynamic expert-student sampling, online relabeling of expert-action likelihoods under the current policy, and an advantage-weighted regularizer that down-weights conservative or low-advantage demonstrations as training progresses.To improve transient agility, we further design a sparse-then-dense hybrid reward that first encourages rapid maneuver completion and then stabilizes terminal tracking. Experiments in the JSBSim F-16 simulator show that HOK-AWR improves learning stability and maneuver execution over the evaluated imitation-augmented and DRL baselines, including an average 20% reduction in climbing settling time and improved 3D pursuit performance.

title: Adaptive broad learning neural network for integrated guidance and control of maneuvering targets
abstract: This paper addresses the integrated guidance and control (IGC) problem for interceptors engaging maneuvering targets under terminal line-of-sight (LOS) angle constraints, model uncertainties, and external disturbances. To estimate unknown target maneuvers within a prescribed time, a prescribed-time extended state observer (PTESO) is developed, in which a trigonometric time-scaling function is introduced to suppress transient peaking and enhance estimation robustness. To handle strong nonlinear uncertainties, an adaptive broad learning neural network (BLNN) with online node growth is proposed to achieve real-time structural adaptation and improved approximation capability with compact network complexity. Moreover, a smooth switching mechanism is introduced to coordinate neural approximation with adaptive robust compensation, thereby improving disturbance rejection performance under varying operating conditions. Furthermore, an adaptive command-filter-based backstepping IGC scheme is developed within a logarithmic Lyapunov framework. Unlike conventional backstepping designs based on quadratic Lyapunov functions, the proposed approach guarantees inherent boundedness of closed-loop signals. The adaptive command filter effectively avoids the explosion of complexity caused by repeated differentiation of virtual control laws and removes the restrictive requirement that virtual control laws be explicitly bounded. Rigorous stability analysis shows that all closed-loop signals are semi-globally uniformly ultimately bounded (SGUUB). Simulation results demonstrate effective interception and satisfactory terminal LOS angle tracking performance, while Monte-Carlo simulations further confirm strong robustness against model uncertainties and external disturbances.

Lossless Convex Trajectory Optimization for Solar-Sail Transfers from Earth–Moon NRHOs to Sun–Earth Halo Orbits
abstract: This paper presents a convex-optimization-based framework for time-optimal solar-sail transfers from an Earth–Moon near rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) to Sun–Earth halo orbits in the bicircular restricted four-body problem (BCR4BP). A dynamical-structure-driven initialization strategy is first developed to mitigate the sensitivity of cross-system trajectory design. Direct escape trajectory families from the solar-sail NRHO are identified to significantly reduce the search space, after which forward escape trajectories are patched with stable manifolds of the target halo orbits, and particle swarm optimization is employed to generate feasible initial guesses satisfying position and velocity matching constraints. For trajectory optimization, a lossless control-convex reformulation is introduced to handle the intrinsic nonconvex solar radiation pressure control, enabling the original optimal control problem to be transcribed into a convex form without loss of optimality. The resulting problem is solved using a successive convexification framework with first-order-hold discretization, hard trust-region constraints, and time-dilation techniques to address the free-final-time objective. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves reliable convergence and efficiently computes time-optimal transfers between Earth–Moon solar-sail NRHOs and Sun–Earth halo orbits. This work extends lossless control-convex solar-sail optimization to BCR4BP-based transfers between Earth–Moon and Sun–Earth libration-point orbits, offering a computationally tractable approach for solar-sail mission design in strongly nonlinear multi-body dynamical environments.

title: Adaptive Event-Based Control for Spacecraft Attitude with Full State Constraints
Separated flow control in a variable-cross-section S-shaped diffuser: An experimental study with pulsed jet actuation
abstract: To address severe flow separation and swirl distortion in an S-shaped diffuser with variable cross-section under different working conditions, experiments were conducted to investigate the control effects of a pulsed jet driven by an oscillator. For incoming Mach numbers of 0.15, 0.25, and 0.4, the flow-field performance of different pulsed-jet intensity and layout schemes was evaluated using a five-hole probe and wall static pressure measurements. The results indicate that, under uncontrolled conditions, the low-energy fluid is separated, leading to central loss and streamwise vortices that cause significant swirl distortion at the outlet. The pulsed jet can effectively improve the uniformity of the outlet total pressure. With the increase of jet intensity, the control effect of the pulsed jet is significantly improved. When the jet intensity is 100kPa, the distortion coefficients are reduced by 47.17%, 16.82% and 11.9% under different conditions. Furthermore, the jet layout mainly affects the action region of the pulsed jet. The two-sided jet reduces the center loss and the core loss range. The middle jet demonstrates a more pronounced effect on the streamwise vortex loss. The global jet can minimize distortion to the greatest extent, especially at low speeds. Ultimately, the pulsed jet is effective at controlling unsteady flow separation in the S-shaped diffuser, and its effect depends on the jet intensity and layout. Future work should focus on adaptive matching between diffuser flow-field characteristics and jet parameters.

When Better Fuel Shortens Safe Return: A Redispatch Rule for SAF Flight Planning
abstract: Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) can increase mass-specific energy while reducing density, creating a flight-planning trade-off that is hidden when fuels are ranked by LHV or nominal range alone. This study asks four linked questions: which density–LHV combinations preserve the Jet-A protected point of no return (PNR); what physical term controls any reversal; how blending and property uncertainty move the boundary; and when reduced-contingency-fuel (RCF) redispatch becomes beneficial after physical reversibility has been checked. A constraint-first analytical framework couples source-traceable fuel properties, manufacturer aircraft envelopes, an energy-scaled Breguet relation, protected reserve, wind, and exact RCF branch logic across 95,847 evaluated states. The central finding is a measurable reversal: neat HEFA-SPK raises LHV by 2.60% but lowers density by 6.35%, retreating the protected PNR by 3.33%, 3.22%, and 2.66% for the A220-300, A320ceo, and 787-9, respectively. At 50% HEFA by mass, the retreat is already 1.71%, 1.66%, and 1.36%; a 1% retreat occurs at 28.8%, 29.9%, and 36.4% HEFA, respectively. The ±1.5% property-source envelope preserves the negative sign for the two narrowbodies but makes favorable 787-9 states boundary-sensitive. Redispatch follows the independent threshold S crit =δ/(1−α): when the route-geometry condition is satisfied, it can provide a fuel benefit after Gate 1, but it cannot restore a lost physical return boundary. For aviation practice, the resulting two-gate rule converts measured fuel properties into an aircraft-specific protected-return margin before route optimization, providing a transparent screening layer for airline performance/dispatch teams, fuel developers, and aircraft designers while remaining distinct from certified flight-planning calculations.

Development and application of a hydrogen aircraft fuel system mass estimation framework
abstract: Liquid hydrogen aircraft require fundamentally different fuel storage, distribution and conditioning systems from conventional kerosene-fuelled aircraft, making existing empirical fuel-system mass-estimation methods unsuitable for early-stage design. This study develops an integrated mass-estimation framework for liquid hydrogen aircraft fuel systems that directly links component thermodynamic performance to geometry and mass. Thermodynamic models of the storage tank, pipeline and heat exchanger are coupled with corresponding geometry- and material-based mass models through an iterative sizing procedure, in which component dimensions are adjusted until specified thermal and hydraulic requirements are satisfied. The thermodynamic models are assessed against published liquid-hydrogen experimental data, while the integrated thermodynamic and mass-estimation framework is evaluated using recent published component studies and two conceptual hydrogen aircraft case studies. Comparisons with published mass-estimation studies show differences of approximately 4–10% for the investigated pipelines and approximately 11% for the comparable tank case. In the aircraft case studies, differences of 15.1% for tank mass and 44.9% for pipeline mass were observed, with the larger discrepancy primarily associated with differences in component architecture and structural assumptions. The framework provides a computationally efficient approach for estimating liquid-hydrogen fuel-system mass during conceptual and early preliminary aircraft design, while allowing the influence of operating conditions, system architecture and component design assumptions to be investigated systematically.

title: A Numerical Decomposition of the Tonal Noise Sources of an Electric Ducted Fan
abstract: This paper investigates the tonal noise produced by an Electric Ducted Fan (EDF) designed for Unmanned Aircraft Systems using computational methods. The main contribution of this study is the decomposition of tonal noise into its fundamental sources, namely the steady and unsteady pressure distributions on the surfaces of the rotor, stator, hub and nacelle. Computational Fluid Dynamics simulations are used to predict the pressure distribution on the surfaces of the EDF, and the resulting time-averaged thrust is compared with experimental measurements for validation. The steady and unsteady components of pressure distribution are visualised as contour plots. These reveal that the unsteady pressure caused by the rotor-stator interaction causes disturbances on the surfaces of the rotor, stator, hub and nacelle, which produce acoustic radiation and contribute significantly to the total tonal noise of the EDF. A frequency-domain acoustic analogy method is presented which is used to calculate the tonal noise produced by the pressure distributions on the surfaces of the EDF at various observer locations. Predictions of the sound pressure level of the tonal noise at various observer locations are presented and show the relative contributions of the loading sources on the different surfaces to the total noise level. The pressure distributions on the hub and nacelle (particularly the area close to the stator) are shown to contribute significantly to the total tonal noise produced by the EDF. By explicitly decomposing the tonal noise into contributions from specific surfaces (e.g., rotor, stator) and loading types (steady or unsteady), this work clarifies the dominant physical sources of EDF tonal noise. This detailed source identification provides an important foundation for developing analytical models as it details which loading types are critical to model accurately. This analysis also directly supports the design of low-noise EDFs by showing which sources should be targeted for noise reduction.

Safe learning-scheduled allocation for spacecraft with variable-speed control moment gyroscopes
abstract: Agile spacecraft using variable-speed control moment gyroscopes (VSCMGs) require online allocation choices among torque tracking, singularity management, wheel-speed margins, gimbal motion, command smoothness, and degraded-actuator usage. This paper develops a safety-constrained steering architecture in which supervised learning is used only for bounded scheduling of these secondary allocation objectives. An extreme learning machine maps online risk indicators to positive objective multipliers, bounded wheel-speed and gimbal-angle bias targets, and a bounded robust-compensation authority. The physical actuator command is not produced by the learner; it is selected by a torque-priority finite-preview allocator that projects candidate wheel-acceleration and gimbal-rate commands onto actuator limits and retains an unscheduled torque-residual penalty. A metric-triggered transient layer activates admissible internal-motion profiles when conditioning, singular-value, wheel-margin, or actuator-health indicators show elevated risk. The final trained setting is evaluated through deterministic stress tests and a 500-case Monte Carlo campaign including near-singular configurations, tracking, inertia uncertainty, bounded disturbances, and partial actuator-effectiveness loss. The campaign achieves 478 successful trials, corresponding to a 95.6\% success rate with a 95\% Wilson confidence interval of 93.4--97.1\%. A stage-wise ablation against profile-disabled, fixed-weight, heuristic-labeler, null-motion, singularity-robust damped-inverse, and weighted-inverse alternatives shows that the learning scheduler improves the allocation tradeoff without replacing the analytical attitude-control and actuator-feasibility layers.

Design of Experiments Framework for Experimental Total Impulse Optimization of a Reduced-Scale Solid Rocket Motor
abstract: This study presents a structured experimental framework for optimizing the total impulse of a reduced-scale solid rocket motor under the practical constraints of static firing campaigns. Because solid rocket motor development is typically limited by cost, infrastructure, safety requirements, and hardware availability, a two-stage Design of Experiments (DoE) and Response Surface Methodology (RSM) strategy was adopted to maximize information from a reduced number of tests. In the screening stage, a fractional factorial design was used to evaluate the effects of ignition-pellet number, operculum thickness, propellant inhibition, and nozzle geometry on total impulse. The screening results identified nozzle geometry and operculum thickness as the strongest fitted effects, while ignition-pellet number was retained for optimization because of its positive coefficient and physical relevance. Inhibition percentage showed a negligible effect within the range investigated. In the optimization stage, a Doehlert design was employed to fit a quadratic response surface and identify the operating region associated with improved propulsion performance. The best model-predicted condition corresponded to an operculum thickness of approximately 2.04 mm and six ignition pellets, with a predicted total impulse of about 420.78 N·s. The predicted response represents a model-based candidate result rather than an independently validated performance improvement. Direct comparisons with screening-stage measurements are limited by nozzle re-machining between the two experimental stages. In addition to the optimization outcome, the study emphasizes the importance of measurement reliability in static firing evaluation, since the response variable is obtained from integration of the thrust-time signal. The proposed DoE-RSM workflow provides a practical and experimentally efficient route for propulsion-oriented optimization when test resources are restricted and offers a transferable methodology for reduced-scale solid rocket motor development in aerospace applications.
